a14-0023857.text: Okay, Gordon. We have your - have good signal strength for you now. And I might say the Earth is starting to drop away very rapidly at this point.

a14-0023857.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0023857.text: Stu and Al have started to change seats. We're going into our...

a14-0023857.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0023857.text: Apollo 14, Houston. I have an update to your High Gain gimbal angles as shown on page 3-3 when you're ready.

a14-0023857.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0023857.text: Okay, about five lines from the bottom, this is the High Gain angles after pitch around for docking. It should be pitch, plus 11; and yaw, plus 306. [Pause.]

a14-0023857.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0023857.text: Understand. Pitch, plus 11; and yaw, plus 3 - plus 306.

a14-0023857.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0023857.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 2 hours, 43 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. The Booster [flight controller] has advised our Flight Director that the maneuver to separation attitude should begin at 2 hours, 49 minutes, 23 seconds. About 3 minutes, the time duration for the maneuver separation. We're now looking at 2 hours, 59 minutes, 23 seconds; we'll stand by and continue to monitor. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: Apollo 14, Houston. I have some updates for your - for you now. Over.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: I've got the S-IVB maneuver time and Sep time that goes on 3-1, and then a new S-IVB viewing attitude.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: The S-IVB maneuver time, 2:49:23. Maneuver will be complete in 3 minutes, and the nominal Sep time is 2:59:23. [Pause.]

a14-0024300.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0024300.text: Understand. S-IVB maneuver, 2:49:23 and it'll maneuver for 3 minutes. Sep is 2:59:25 - 23.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: That's correct, Ed. And then on page 3-7 - stand by 1. [Pause.]

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: Terminate the cabin repressurization. We show you over 6 psi.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: Okay. And we have 3.7 [means page 3-7] in front of you. I'll give you the new S-IVB view-attitude Noun 22 angles.

a14-0024300.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0024300.text: Okay, it's about a quarter of the way down where it reads 93, 39.6, and 355.8. Change them to read same for roll, 090; pitch, plus 349.0; and yaw, plus 356.0. [Pause.]

a14-0024300.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0024300.text: Rog; understand. Roll is the same, pitch is 349.0, yaw is 356.0.

a14-0025325.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0025325.text: Apollo 14, Houston. Give us Omni Charlie, please.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0025325.text: All right, Houston. You have Charlie.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: Apollo 14 now 2,744 nautical miles [5,082 km] away from Earth. We're at 2 hours, 53 minutes into the flight.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: 2 hours, 54 minutes; our Booster reports maneuver to separation attitude has been completed.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: 2 hours, 55 minutes; and Mission Control Flight Director Pete Frank taking a status check for Transposition and Docking.

a14-0025325.speaker: Shepard
a14-0025325.text: Houston, 14. The S-IVB tank pressures: oxidizer, 24, and fuel is 9.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: We now show 14 at an altitude of 3,126 nautical miles [5,789 km].

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 14 now 3,369 nautical miles [6,239 km], 3,404 nautical miles [6,304 km] at 2 hours, 57 minutes.

a14-0025325.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0025325.text: Roger; you are Go for Transposition and Docking, and we're to have a site handover from Guam to Goldstone at 3 hours even; over.

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Okay, understand. We're going to Goldstone at 3, and we have a Go for T&D.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: We presently show 14 at a distance of 3,858 nautical miles [7,145 km] from Earth.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0025325.text: ...you can get Go for pyro arm.

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Houston, 14. I'd like a Go for pyro arm.

a14-0025325.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0025325.text: 14, Houston. You're Go for pyro arm.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0025325.text: Okay, you can start your DET .

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: Standing by for a report of separation.

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Okay. What we're going to do here is start the DET . 59:50, I'll go to Auto; 59:58, I'll hit it with some thrust. I'll punch this and check and make sure these go to zero. You - you did do a Verb 62? Is that...

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: So we'll come off and, if this needle is negative, I'll go to Pitch to Accel Command, start it up, and, when she goes across, you'll give me two Pros...

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: ...I'll go to Rate Command, and we'll come on around. Okay?

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Okay. And we're going to start.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0025325.text: ...no. Just do it slow and easy.

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: We're Auto. At 8:58, plus-X thrust and zero - 56, 57,...

a14-0025325.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0025325.text: Is your launch vehicle tank pressure full scale low?

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Okay, I'm going to start her...

a14-0025325.speaker: Roosa
a14-0025325.text: Okay. Give me a couple Pros.

a14-0025325.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0025325.text: Our data shows that we have separation. We're at 3 hours, 3 minutes.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: Look out that window!

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Yes, look at all that crap.

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: Okay, Houston. We've separated. Turnaround started.

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: Roger.

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: And we have the usual couple of Parker valves.

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Okay. Service Module RCS Second Propellant Fuel Press, low - or Close, and the Reactants valve, Normal.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: [Garble].

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: ...want to verify...

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: Fuel propellant [Garble].

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Okay.

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: Okay.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: Okay. Can you see anything out there good?

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: Okay, you don't want to change the DAP early on this...

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: No, not until after I've given 4 seconds of ullage forward.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Okay, I just wanted to verify...

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: You should be looking for the S-IVB - there goes a panel out there. You can see it drifting out.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Yes, there it is.

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: There it is, yes. Oh, man. That's beautiful.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: What's our range?

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: What?

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: Are we within - Oh, yes.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Oh, yes.

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: I'd say it's - Oh, yes, we're real fine, Stu.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Come right on down to - Steady as a rock.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: Go ahead, Ed.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: You should have the television here in a minute. There it comes.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: Okay, come right on with that...

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: Roger. We're not seeing it yet. [Long pause.]

a14-0030254.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030254.text: Ed Mitchell reporting, the television should be coming through. We're receiving an image now.

a14-0030254.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030254.text: ...shit. It's not quite lined up, damn it. Okay. 1, 2, 3, 4. Okay?

a14-0030254.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030254.text: Okay. You doing a...

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: Roger, Ed. We're getting a great picture now.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Okay.

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: We can see the drogue down toward the bottom of the picture and slightly left. You might move the camera a little bit left and down about a half a frame. [Pause.]

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: That's real good. Right there. [Long pause.]

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Houston, how's the television look to you now? Anything I can do to the picture?

a14-0030254.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030254.text: No. I wouldn't change a thing, Ed. Looks really good. It's right in the middle and steady.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030254.text: Okay.

a14-0030254.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030254.text: 14 now 5,168 nautical miles [9,571 km] away from Earth.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: ...a little more at it here [garble]. I gave it a solid [garble].

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Looks to me like you're still closing, Stu.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: I'm closing slowly. Now, wait until I get in, and see how it - We've got lots of time.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Going to break the record, man. Take it slowly.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: We've already used a little more than I do in the simulator for some reason.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Go ahead.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Just for your information, we've lost data with the LVDC. We don't have any procedures for you with regard to that.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Say again, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: We've lost data with - all data from the LVDC, but we have no change in the figures. Go ahead with normal procedures.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Okay.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: That's the Launch Vehicle Digital Computer, the LVDC. We're at 3 hours, 9 minutes now into the flight.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 9 minutes on 14. Presently 5,441 nautical miles [10,077 km] away from Earth.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: You see Kitty Hawk moving in before docking now. We're at 3 hours, 10 minutes into the flight. We show an altitude of 5,577 nautical miles [10,329 km].

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: Houston, 14. Do you need any commentary to help you identify what you're seeing on the TV?

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: We're - we're picking out things pretty well here. If you have anything for - the rest of the country, you might go ahead and talk if it won't interfere with the operation there.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: Okay, I'll chat for a minute. The S-IVB is surrounded here by typical thousands, or millions of particles that came out when we separated. They look like little winking stars, floating around in a very random pattern. The sunlight is shining very strongly off the top of the Lunar Module as we drift into it. Stu's doing an excellent job of sliding in here very slowly. As you can see that - our approach speed is a few tenths of a foot per second, probably. And the LM is starting to get very large in our field of view; starting to cover the window, out my plus-X window. And the LM and the S-IVB a

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Hi, Ed, this is Houston. About how far out in range are you now, would you estimate?

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: About 5 feet.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: [Garble]. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: And Houston; we're about to dock.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: That was Ed Mitchell reporting they're getting ready to dock and we're at 3 hours, 13 minutes now into the flight.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: We're probably a foot - 18 inches to 2 foot out now.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 14 minutes into the flight. We show Apollo 14 at a distance of 6,184 nautical miles [11,453 km].

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: And we docked.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. We could see a slight oscillation. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: Ed Mitchell reporting that Apollo 14 Command Module Kitty Hawk has docked in with the Lunar Module.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 14 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 14 presently at 6,318 nautical miles [11,701 km] away from Earth.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay, Houston. We hit it twice and - Sure looks like we're closing fast enough. I'm going to back back out here and try it again.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Well, there goes the record.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: Don't worry about it. Let's get him picked up.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Man, we'd better back off here and think about this one, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: We're unable to get a capture.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger, Ed. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay, Houston. We backed out a little bit, and that last time I hit it pretty good and we're just not getting - getting the capture latches in there.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. We suggest you verify, if you haven't already, the docking probe circuit breakers on panel 8.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: That's verified.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: And - stand by 1. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: And, Stu, we suggest you go to Extend on the Docking Probe Extend/Retract switch and check the talkback's gray.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay. We did that when we extended them, but we'll sure do it again.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: And then back to Retract. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay. We get both gray in the Extend position.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: And we go Retract and both gray. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: 14, Houston. One other suggestion. Go to panel 229 and check the EPS group 4 circuit breakers. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay. They're both in.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: ...Houston. We're about out of ideas here. Suggest you verify you got it - the switch back in Retract and then give it another try at docking.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: That's Stu Roosa and Ed Mitchell reporting that, at least at this point, that they're unable to get a capture. We'll stand...

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 20 minutes. Apollo 14 will be coming forward for another try at docking. 3 hours, 21 minutes. We show [Apollo] 14 [at] 7,372 nautical miles [13,653 km] from Earth."

a14-0030637.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0030637.text: Houston, we're starting to drift back in now.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger, Ed.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Go ahead.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: We suggest that at the initial contact that you hold plus-X for 3 seconds or so at least.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Okay, Houston. We tried it before, but not quite 3 seconds.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Okay.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: And [garble] a good rate coming in this time.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: I'm glad we've been through it.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: And here we come in again.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: 1, 2, 3, 4 - Son of a bitch - nothing!

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay, Houston. I hit it pretty good and held 4 seconds on contact and we did not latch.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. We're seeing it all on TV here. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: You heard Stu Roosa. Still no latch. The crew has a period of time that they can continue with this attempt. The restricting item would be as long as we have attitude holding on the S-IVB .

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: (Sigh) Shit.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: [Garble] one more time.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 25 minutes.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: For your information, at 3 plus 34:24, a nonpropulsive vent in the booster will be sequenced open. We don't expect to see much from it. Over.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Say that again, please.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: At 3 plus 34:24, a nonpropulsive vent in the booster will be sequenced open. Over.

a14-0030637.speaker: Shepard
a14-0030637.text: Okay, we got you.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Okay, Houston; 14. I can look in the drogue and I can see three marks 120 degrees apart, like the capture latches are scratching the drogue. They're about - I don't know - inch and a half long going into the hole in the drogue about - spaced about 120.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: 14, Houston. Can you describe the scratches? Are they sharp scratches or rounded off? Over.

a14-0030637.speaker: Roosa
a14-0030637.text: Well, I didn't really see that good. I can move back in, I guess. We can take a look at them. They look like fairly distinct - scratches coming into the hole, but - let's move up. We'll take another look.

a14-0030637.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0030637.text: Roger.

a14-0030637.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0030637.text: We're at 3 hours, 29 minutes now into the flight. We show 14 8,683 nautical miles [16,081 km] into the flight.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Go ahead.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Okay, Gordon. I'm sure you're all thinking along the same lines, but - you know, if the capture latches were depressing as they slide into the drogue, I don't see why they would have made those marks.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Yes, that's been discussed here. We think probably something is holding them out. One possibility is a sort of a shearpin that gets pulled off when the tower is jettisoned and - First look at it looks - We're thinking maybe that may not be - may not allow the capture latches to depress. I guess we'll just have to tell you to stand by while we talk it over here more.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Okay. We're - we're nice and comfortable. And I'm just going to drift around here about this range and try not to use any more fuel than I have to.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Roger. A reminder. You have about 3 minutes until that vent will come open. Keep an eye on that booster when that happens.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Okay. How about you give me a mark on that beauty?

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Will do.

a14-0032900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0032900.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. They're 3 hours, 32 minutes. That was Stu Roosa troubleshooting with the ground. As you have heard, 14 at this point has been unable to effect a capture in the docking procedure with the Lunar Module. We're at 3 hours, 32 minutes; continuing to monitor. We show Apollo 14 presently 9,150 nautical miles [16,946 km] from Earth.

a14-0032900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0032900.text: We're less than a minute now away from the time of non-propulsive venting of the S-IVB .

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Stu, this is Houston. That vent is due in 30 seconds.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: 10 seconds.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Ready...

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Mark. It should be on now.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Man, it's beautiful.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: We can see one-half of it from here.

a14-0032900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0032900.text: Okay, I'll back down a little bit and let you watch this.

a14-0032900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0032900.text: There's lightning - the whole sky. Of course, it's the source of another 10 million particles floating out in front of us.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Roger, Ed.

a14-0032900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0032900.text: As I was going to say when we were - got busy there a little while ago - look out our left window across Stuart, we could see the Earth receding.

a14-0032900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0032900.text: Roger.

a14-0032900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0032900.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 3 hours, 39 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. Discussions continuing to take place here in Mission Control attempting to come up with a solution to...

a14-0033900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0033900.text: Houston, we observe that the S-IVB is slowly rotating, now.

a14-0033900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0033900.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 3 hours, 40 minutes into the flight. Discussions are continuing in Mission Control concerning our docking problem. The...

a14-0033900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0033900.text: Gordon, how do you read me now?

a14-0033900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0033900.text: Okay, I'm not sure what we might be doing to the windows. I guess it's a minor problem at this point, but is everybody happy with us sitting here in this vent?

a14-0033900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0033900.text: I don't think that point's been raised. Let me ask it around here.

a14-0033900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0033900.text: Apollo Control, Houston. The pacing item would be the attitude control on the S-IVB . The battery power is the major constraining item on that, however it does allow us a fair amount of time, approximately 6 to 8 hours. Continuing to monitor the troubleshooting operation here at Mission Control; this is Apollo Control, Houston. We presently show Apollo 14 at an altitude of 10,643 nautical miles [19,711 km], and we're at a Ground Elapsed Time of 3 hours, 42 minutes.

a14-0033900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0033900.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 3 hours, 43 minutes into the flight. Troubleshooting continuing in Mission Control. To quickly repeat, we have been unable to latch with the Lunar Module. We have quite a while to consider an approach to this problem. The battery power on the S-IVB is perhaps our major constraining item, allowing us perhaps 6 to 8 hours of time. However, if we're not able to extract the Lunar Module, of course the lunar landing Mission would not be possible. We're at 3 hours, 44 minutes; continuing to monitor.

a14-0033900.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0033900.text: While we're working on the problem here, we suggest that you go to a 5-degree deadband in the DAP . That will be a DAP load 11112 to save RCS , and nobody's come up with a good suggestion on what to do about the windows, so I guess we just won't worry about it now.

a14-0033900.speaker: Roosa
a14-0033900.text: Ah, Rog. Like I say, I think it's a minor problem.

a14-0033900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0033900.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 3 hours, 53 minutes now into the flight. We presently show 14 at an altitude of 12,310 nautical miles [22,798 km] away from Earth. To again go over our problem, the capture latches have not been working. One of the plans being considered here, and will very probably be passed along to the crew, is to retract the probe and attempt to bypass the capture latches hoping to get the - to the docking latches. There are 12 docking latches and to successfully dock we would need 3 to work. If we're not able to extract the Lunar Module - I repeat, our lunar landing mis

a14-0035849.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0035849.text: I'd like you to try one thing. Take the Extend/Retract switch to Retract and tell us what the talkbacks read in Retract as you have on others before. [Pause.]

a14-0035849.speaker: Roosa
a14-0035849.text: Okay, Gordon. I - You want the switch in Retract and a read - readout of the talkback?

a14-0035849.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0035849.text: That's affirmative; while the switch is in Retract.

a14-0035849.speaker: Roosa
a14-0035849.text: Rog. It's in Retract now and the talkbacks are gray.

a14-0035849.speaker: Flight controller
a14-0035849.text: Okay. That tells us right there that the capture latches are indeed cocked and that kind of says that there's something in there that's keeping us from releasing them when we go ahead and dock. And it says that we cannot fire bottle.

a14-0035849.speaker: Flight controller
a14-0035849.text: It just wouldn't fire, is that the true indication? It would not fire. Right?

a14-0035849.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0035849.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours now into the flight. We in Mission Control continuing to troubleshoot our docking problem. The discussions still underway, both in the Mission Control Room operation floor proper and with the SPAN [Spacecraft Analysis] or the backroom experts. The capture latches has not been working. It is a problem which can be considered and discussed and played with for a while. The constraining item would be the attitude on the third stage, the S-IVB and perhaps the most critical point there is the battery power and this approximate lifetime of some 6 to 8 hours. A

a14-0040738.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0040738.text: Another question. Can you remember back to the initial probe extension, did you hear a thud as though it did extend out?

a14-0040738.speaker: Roosa
a14-0040738.text: That's affirmative, Gordon. I guess I should have mentioned that sooner. Yeah. We got the thud and we got the talkbacks on barber pole, then immediately back to gray. But we did feel - feel the thud.

a14-0040738.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0040738.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 8 minutes into the flight. We show 14 at an altitude of 14,294 nautical miles [26,472 km] away from Earth. Discussions are continuing in the Mission Control Center concerning our docking problem. A probe and drogue model, if it has not yet been brought in, will be brought in shortly to aid in the discussions. We show 4 hours, 9 minutes into the flight; continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0041138.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: 14, Houston. Go ahead.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0041138.text: Do you want me to leave the television running or shall I take it down now?

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Ah, Stand by. Like to leave it running, Ed. But we're not seeing the booster right now. It's in the lower left corner, just barely. But we'd like to keep it running for a future use.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0041138.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Houston, 14. And turning the Pyros and SECS - and SECS Logic, Off.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Roger.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0041138.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 14 minutes. The color converter is - is off the line at the moment, being recycled. We're showing black and white at this time.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Apollo 14, Houston. Over.

a14-0041138.speaker: Roosa
a14-0041138.text: Go ahead.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Okay, we'd like to essentially try the docking again with the normal procedures prior to going to more drastic alternate procedures. We'd like you to reconfigure the DAP . R 1 should be 11102 for docking. We'd like you to go to Extend/Release and hold it for at least 5 seconds, and then return to Retract and proceed with one more try at a normal docking. Over.

a14-0041138.speaker: Roosa
a14-0041138.text: Okay, we'll put a narrow deadband in and we'll go Extend for 5 seconds at least and back to Retract and bang it again.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0041138.text: As you heard, CapCom Fullerton passed along to Stu Roosa and other crew members of 14 that we're going to make another docking attempt with the established procedures prior to reconsidering alternate plans. We're at 4 hours, 16 minutes now into the flight. We show Apollo...

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: And, 14; Houston. Make your closing rate on this try, not - not fast, not slow, just a normal closing rate.

a14-0041138.speaker: Roosa
a14-0041138.text: Okay. We'll try it. I thought that's what I had the first time, but we'll give it a go.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Roger. The first time looked that way to us. We'd just like to try it again.

a14-0041138.speaker: Roosa
a14-0041138.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: 14, Houston. When you go to Extend/Release for the - at least 5 seconds so would you read the talkbacks to us?

a14-0041138.speaker: Roosa
a14-0041138.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: And, Houston, we'd like to bring SECS Logic, On, and get another Go for pyro arm.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Stand by. [Pause.] We're ready for Logic, On.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Logic is On. [Long pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: 14, Houston. You're Go for pyro arm. [Pause.]

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Roger. Go for pyro arm.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0041138.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 14 pressing on now with another attempt at docking. We show the spacecraft now at a distance of 15,821 nautical miles [29,300 km] away from Earth. We'll stand by and continue to monitor; 4 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Houston, 14. Are you ready for the Extend/Release position of the switch?

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: That's affirmative. Go ahead, Al.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Okay. Going in Retract, and Extend/Release on my mark. Five seconds.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Mark. [Pause.] My barber pole stayed gray, back to Off. Barber pole's still gray.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Roger; understand.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Back to Retract. Barber pole's still gray.

a14-0041138.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0041138.text: Roger. I understand the talkback stayed gray all the way through.

a14-0041138.speaker: Shepard
a14-0041138.text: Affirmative.

a14-0041138.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0041138.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 27 minutes now into the flight. We show Apollo 14 at a distance of 16,889 nautical miles [31,278 km] away from the Moon - away from the Earth. There has been no voice communication with the Apollo 14 crew for some time as the 14 crew is pressing on for another attempt at docking and in Mission Control, a probe and drogue assembly is on hand, and discussions are continuing here as to possible alternatives. We're at 4 hours, 28 minutes into the flight; continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0043056.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0043056.text: Okay, Houston, we're starting to close on it now.

a14-0043056.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0043056.text: That's Ed Mitchell making the report at 4 hours, 31 minutes that they're starting to close in again at - on another attempt to dock with the Lunar Module. We presently show Apollo 14 at a distance of 17,453 nautical miles [32,323 km] away from Earth.

a14-0043056.speaker: Roosa
a14-0043056.text: I'm going to tap it one more time.

a14-0043056.speaker: Roosa
a14-0043056.text: Okay. That's at least - [garble] tap it. Well, I'm going to tap it there. [Garble] allow a little for the [garble] real world [garble].

a14-0043056.speaker: Shepard
a14-0043056.text: All right. Verified we're in Retract. I'm going [garble].

a14-0043056.speaker: Roosa
a14-0043056.text: My alignment is good. Stand by.

a14-0043056.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0043056.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 33 minutes. You heard that report of no latch. In the control center, we have a probe and drogue assembly. Looking very closely over it are backup commander Gene Cernan along with John Young and Chet Lee the Mission Director, and John Llewellyn, who's on one of the flight control team. We're at 4 hours, 34 minutes and we show Apollo 14 at a distance of 17,729 nautical miles [32,834 km].

a14-0043056.speaker: Shepard
a14-0043056.text: Houston, 14. I'm sure you're thinking about the possibility of going hard suit and bringing the probe inside to look at, as we are.

a14-0043056.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0043056.text: That's affirmative. We may have one more procedure to try prior to going to that. Stand by 1 now.

a14-0043056.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0043056.text: That was Al Shepard who made the suggestion apparently being considered aboard the spacecraft, as it - as it certainly is here at Mission Control, that of depressurizing the cabin, and - of bringing the probe inside for closer scrutiny. We're at 4 hours, 36 minutes into the flight. We show 14 at a distance of 17,994 nautical miles [33,325 km] away from Earth.

a14-0043056.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0043056.text: We'd like some more words on the exact appearance of the drogue, the scratches, and so forth. [Garble].

a14-0043056.speaker: Roosa
a14-0043056.text: Okay, I'll give you - try to give you the best. As I look at the probe - and then you all can figure out where the docking latches are from there; but as I look at the probe in the docking position, the prominent thing - are we have three scratches about - oh, maybe a couple of inches long, and they're really - well, the top one's about - essentially 12 o'clock, maybe 11:30, and then they're spaced, you know, equally around the ring, about 120 out. Now, there is one other scratch that I didn't see before, that I must have put on this last attempt. I noticed it as we backed out, and it - Well,

a14-0043056.speaker: Shepard
a14-0043056.text: Houston, all these scratches are radial, and they're right up at the very apex of the drogue.

a14-0043056.speaker: Cernan
a14-0043056.text: Hey, Stu. This is Gene-o. Do you read?

a14-0043056.speaker: Cernan
a14-0043056.text: Okay. We - we got one more idea down here, before doing any hard suit work, and - let me throw it out at you, and you come back with your impressions. We're thinking of - of attempting to - to dock actually without the aid of the probe, which requires some pretty fine alignment. We're thinking that maybe you could go ahead and go through a normal plus-X and put the probe in the drogue, and while you're holding a - This will help you with your alignment - and while you're holding a plus-X, go ahead and blow a bottle and try and retract the probe. Now, if the probe retracts, it should retract we

a14-0043056.speaker: Shepard
a14-0043056.text: Ah, Gene-o. Let me see if we understand you on that. Your - your thought is to blow one of the bottles to retract the probe after we're aligned up and just before contact - or wait until we contact, and then thrusting, and then retract the probe.

a14-0043056.speaker: Cernan
a14-0043056.text: Okay, Al. We're - we're thinking that actually, if you use the - Leave the probe extended until you actually contact, that - that any small, minute misalignment, at least in translation left, right, up, or down, will be taken out as the probe centers in the hole of the drogue. If you can keep a plus-X going at that time and then retract the probe, hopefully, your alignment will stay fairly close and - and we may pick up a couple of the docking latches. Now, as I said, we've got some reservations. We're not - we're not sure, actually, if the probe is going to retract, so you might keep that in

a14-0043056.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0043056.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 4 hours, 43 minutes now into the flight. You heard the discussions between Gene Cernan, now at the CapCom position and Al Shepard. The bottle reference, this bottle of gaseous nitrogen, which activates a pneumatic system that retracts the probe. This is perhaps a consideration that will be pursued at this time. We're at 4 hours, 43 minutes. We presently show Apollo 14 at an altitude of 18,928 nautical miles [35,055 km].

a14-0044552.speaker: Shepard
a14-0044552.text: Okay, Houston. We'll review what we're going to do for you. See if it is the right thing. Stu is going to make the approach; close at a very slow rate until the initial contact. He's going to call out at that time and apply plus-X. I will then go to the Retract Prime 1 position.

a14-0044552.speaker: Cernan
a14-0044552.text: That - that's it, Al. That - That should - should do it if that - that probe does actually retract, and if our alignment is good enough, the possibilities are pretty good of picking up the docking latch.

a14-0044552.speaker: Shepard
a14-0044552.text: Okay. You - Your theory is, it is going to retract because you feel the capture latches are locked.

a14-0044552.speaker: Cernan
a14-0044552.text: No. I - Actually, the impression here is that it is not going to retract.

a14-0044552.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0044552.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 47 minutes now into the flight. Pete Frank, over the Flight Director's loop, advised his EECOM and his Flight Planning Officer to consider procedures for the hard suit, if we are unsuccessful in this upcoming attempt.

a14-0044552.speaker: Shepard
a14-0044552.text: Okay, Houston. We're on our way in now and we're going to try the plus-X until it's - After its initial contact, try the plus-X until it's settled down for perhaps a second or two and then go through the retract cycle at that time.

a14-0044552.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0044552.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 4 hours, 50 minutes now into the flight. The Booster systems engineer has just advised Pete Frank, our Flight Director, that his predicted lifetime on the booster is 13 hours, 18 minutes. The first part of the hardware to degrade would be the batteries and that's a predicted lifetime now, of 13 hours, 18 minutes on the third stage. We're at 4 hours, 51 minutes into the flight. We show Apollo 14 presently at an altitude of 19,930 nautical miles [36,910 km]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0045456.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0045456.text: Okay, Houston. We're about 12 to 15 feet away.

a14-0045456.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0045456.text: Roger, Ed. We got a very good picture.

a14-0045456.speaker: Roosa
a14-0045456.text: About a foot. Here we go.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: I don't know. I got - got a barber pole. We got a hard dock.

a14-0045456.speaker: Roosa
a14-0045456.text: I believe we got a hard dock, Houston.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: We noticed no response for practically 3 seconds after initiating Prime Retract 1. We then got barber pole on both - went gray on both at the hard dock.

a14-0045456.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0045456.text: It didn't even wiggle when you hit it. Right in there.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: Okay. Shall we proceed with the checklist? [Long pause.]

a14-0045456.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0045456.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You heard that report. There was a cheer in Mission Control when that report came from Al Shepard. We're at 4 hours, 58 minutes; standing by. We show 14 at 20,700 nautical miles [38,336 km] away from Earth.

a14-0045456.speaker: Cernan
a14-0045456.text: Roger. We'd like you to proceed on now with the normal hatch and tunnel procedures. [Pause.]

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: That's in work, Houston. We'll keep you advised. [Long pause.]

a14-0045456.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0045456.text: And, Houston, I'm turning the TV off now.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: Roger. We want to just verify that you're still all hard suited before proceeding with the - the tunnel procedures...

a14-0045456.speaker: Cernan
a14-0045456.text: Not hard suited, but completely suited up before proceeding the - the tunnel procedures.

a14-0045456.speaker: Roosa
a14-0045456.text: Roger. We will - Roger, Houston. Why don't you review the procedures again as we go down the checklist here, and we'll check with you again when we get to that point. We do watch the cabin pressure pretty closely, you know.

a14-0045456.speaker: Cernan
a14-0045456.text: Al, can you just give us a - a qualitative feeling of what it sounded like when those docking latches did go? Did you get a - a sort of ripple-bang or are you convinced you got quite a few of them?

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: Yeah. It was a ripple fire, Gene-o. I'm convinced we did quite a few.

a14-0045456.speaker: Cernan
a14-0045456.text: Yeah. That - that sounds pretty familiar, Al. It - it sounds like you're really probably - I wouldn't be a bit surprised to see if you got them all.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: Yeah. I think we got quite a few, Gene-o. It looked - It was a good hard dock.

a14-0045456.speaker: Cernan
a14-0045456.text: Beautiful. Tell Stu that session he had this morning paid off.

a14-0045456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0045456.text: Yes. And we're going to buy him his present from here.

a14-0050515.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0050515.text: Houston. Delta-P at 2.0. We're starting a - a Delta-P stable check. [Pause.]

a14-0050515.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0050515.text: Ah, Ed. Would you repeat your last, please.

a14-0050515.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0050515.text: Rog. We're starting to check the Delta-P for 3 minutes.

a14-0050816.speaker: Shepard
a14-0050816.text: Houston, Apollo 14. We have lost 1/10th of 1 pound per square inch by the Delta-P gauge during the 3-minute period. We'd like to proceed as we are. [Pause.]

a14-0050816.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0050816.text: Ah, you're clear to Go with that.

a14-0050816.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0050816.text: Apollo 14, Houston. We'd like you to verify the H 2 Fans, Off.

a14-0050816.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0050816.text: Belay that, Houston. They're Off now.

a14-0050816.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0050816.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We're at 5 hours, 13 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. The present distance reading for Apollo 14 is 22,503 nautical miles [41,676 km] away from Earth, and following that successful hard docking, Apollo 14 is proceeding on with our basic mission plan. The crew of course will have a chance to look at the docking mechanism during the translunar coast period while Antares and Kitty Hawk are docked. We're at 5 hours, 14 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0051718.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0051718.text: Have some RCS quantity numbers - just - it should make you feel good. You used 131 pounds so far, which is 62 pounds below nominal, but you're still 211 pounds above the redline. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0051718.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0051718.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You heard those...

a14-0051718.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0051718.text: Roger, Houston. We got - We used 131 pounds, which is 62 pounds below nominal. And say again how much above redline?

a14-0051718.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0051718.text: You're still 211, 211 pounds above the redline.

a14-0051718.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0051718.text: And, Houston, we got all the docking latches.

a14-0051718.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0051718.text: Roger. Understand; you got them all. Very good.

a14-0051718.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0051718.text: Al's checking carefully now, but that's his first report.

a14-0051718.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0051718.text: Those were Reaction Control System usage rates passed along to the crew by CapCom Gordon Fullerton. Responding from the spacecraft was Ed Mitchell. We're at 5 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight. We presently show 14 at a distance of 23,125 nautical miles [42,828 km] away from the Earth. Traveling now at a speed of 12,486 feet per second [3,806 m/s].

a14-0052216.speaker: Roosa
a14-0052216.text: Okay, Houston. We got all the latches, and everything was fine. All we had to do was just tap on number 2 and 8 to lock the handle down.

a14-0052216.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0052216.text: Roger, Stu. If you haven't bled the nitrogen with the red button, don't for a minute here.

a14-0052216.speaker: Roosa
a14-0052216.text: Oh, you caught us in time. We have not bled it.

a14-0052216.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0052216.text: Okay. Stand by. I want to make sure that - What EECOM wants to do here.

a14-0052216.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0052216.text: Okay, after a massive discussion here, we've decided - have you go ahead with the procedures as you see them in your checklist there. Verify the Extend Latch Engaged indicator, not visible, and then go ahead and bleed the GN 2 .

a14-0053456.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0053456.text: Roger. In 5 to 10 minutes, the S-IVB fuel pressure should get up to the point where it'll vent. It's through a non-propulsive vent - it shouldn't affect you - much. Over.

a14-0053456.speaker: Shepard
a14-0053456.text: Okay, in 5 to 10 minutes. Thank you. And we're just about to put the hatch back in.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay, Gordon. Is there - just want to make sure that we're all talking on the same frequency on this ejection and - and the maneuvering and everything. Have we got any changes to any of those procedures? [Pause.]

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: I guess what I'm wondering is - after this long a time, is the S-IVB still in the same condition, and so forth and so on.

a14-0053753.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0053753.text: Okay, Stu. Stand by. I'll get a good summary of that.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Gordon, be advised. We're on page L-37 and ready for pre- LM Sep and ejection.

a14-0053753.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0053753.text: Roger. Essentially, I'd like you to go through procedures and - as you would have nominally. The - the only anomaly with the booster is - right now - is the - that we have lost the downlink from the Launch Vehicle Digital Computer, and so your visual indications of its attitude and maneuvers are the only ones that we'll have. We have no read-out on booster attitude down here. And, actually, we've lost many of the downlink parameters on the booster; however, it shouldn't affect the evasive maneuver and targeting to impact. Over.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay, Gordon. That - that - that's what I was wanting to clarify before we pressed ahead so we'll - we'll press right on down and - as nominal and give you the call when we see it and so forth.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0053753.text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours, 44 minutes. At the present time in Mission Control we are preparing for a shift handover. Flight Director Milton Windler is coming on to relieve Flight Director Pete Frank. That handover will occur following LM extraction. A short while ago, the Flight Director was asked when LM extraction would occur. His response was, whenever the crew is ready. The crew is proceeding to extract the LM in the normal manner at this time, and following LM extraction, there will be a change of shift briefing in the large Auditorium in building 1 at the Manned Spacecraft Center

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Okay, circuit breaker SECS Arm, two, closed...

a14-0053753.speaker: Shepard
a14-0053753.text: Okay. Wait - wait a minute, baby. [Garble].

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Yes, we sure do. [Garble]. Let's forget that.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: No, let's get your last circuit breakers now.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Well, this is the first circuit breaker.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Circuit breaker SECS Arm, two, closed; verify.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: You need a Go for pyro arm.

a14-0053753.speaker: Shepard
a14-0053753.text: Houston, 14. We'd like a Go for pyro arm, please.

a14-0053753.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0053753.text: Yes, you have a Go for pyro arm.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0053753.text: The Go for pyro arm indicates the crew is preparing for LM separation. We'll continue to attempt to recap. Returning to live conversation in the event the crew or the CapCom speaks up. The normal docking procedure would be for the probe mechanism to engage the drogue in the Lunar Module. There are 3 small latches in the tip of the probe which extend after passing through a hole in the end of the conical drogue mechanism. This is soft docking. At this time, a pneumatic system actuated by nitrogen pressurization draws the two vehicles together pulling the - retracting the drogue or rather retrac

a14-0053753.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0053753.text: We have a report now that the crew is thrusting minus-X which would indicate that they are extracting the Lunar Module from the S-IVB at this time.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: I guess that was a Go.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Could have been a No Go. [Garble]. Okay, the pyros are armed.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: TVC Servo Power number 1, AC 1/Main A.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Give me a mark when you get set.

a14-0053753.speaker: Shepard
a14-0053753.text: Let's take a look at the 83. Copy down minus 0.7, 0, 0.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: These O 2 tanks there are closed?

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: No, I think that's surge tanks...

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Okay, there it is. Tank 3. Want the heaters off?

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Houston, got a Cryo Press light in the - O 2 tank 3.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Look outside, Al, if you want to see something beautiful.

a14-0053753.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0053753.text: Roger. We're - we estimate that's probably stratification.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Rog. Sorry, that's also tank 1 and 2 that just dropped down.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Look at those big pieces floating around there.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0053753.text: Our telemetry data indicates that the LM is clear, that the crew is maneuvering now to the attitude for the evasive maneuver.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay, let's keep us honest, Ed.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Com - Computer Activity light out. Do a Verb 66.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay. That's Safe. Let's get our maneuver going.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Okay. Let's get on through the checklist. SECS Logic, two, Off.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Circuit breakers SECS Arm, two, open.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay. I've got the Arms, off; the Logics, Off; and Arm circuit breakers, Open.

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Okay. I'm pulling the S-IVB / LM Sep open.

a14-0053753.speaker: Roosa
a14-0053753.text: Okay. CMC , Auto, Rate 2, and Rate Command...

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Okay. And I'm going to verify the [garble] O 2 ...

a14-0053753.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0053753.text: Launch Vehicle/ SPS Indicator switch at GPI .

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Apollo 14, Houston. We'll be standing by from you for a - that you have the S-IVB visually and a Go for the yaw maneuver.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay, Gordon. It's just now coming out from behind the LM for me in the - in the left window here. About another 15, 20 seconds, we ought to have a good view of it.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: And - Okay, we're well clear, Gordon, if you want to go ahead and do the yaw maneuver at your convenience.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger, Stu. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0055323.text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours, 55 minutes. The crew now maneuvering into the proper position for the APS evasive maneuver. In some of the conversation, you heard reference to the fact that data from the S-IVB is limited, and this lack of data has complicated the...

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: 14, Houston. We just sent a checkout command to the booster which looked good. So we're getting ready to start the yaw maneuver now.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay. Why don't you give me a mark when it's coming?

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: All right, will do. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: 14, Houston. We'll be commanding at 55 plus 30, about 5 seconds from now. Ready...

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Mark. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay, she - she's moving, Gordon.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger, Stu.

a14-0055323.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0055323.text: The S-IVB moving into the proper position for the APS evasive maneuver.

a14-0055323.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0055323.text: Our communications officer reported a drop out in data. They're checking to determine the cause of it. The concern mentioned previously about the - controlling the S-IVB for the APS evasive maneuver refer to the fact that a multiplexer apparently has failed in the S-IVB Instrument Unit. The primary concern here is that in performing the maneuver, there are certain systems that flight controllers don't have as good a visibility into as they would prefer. However the fact that the S-IVB responded to the yaw maneuver command properly indicates that the systems are responding as they should and th

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Well, Gordon, the maneuver looks like it's going well. She's sure maneuvering away from looking at us, and it's a beautiful sight.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger, Stu. It sounds good to us. We had some question about our command capability and it sounds like it's okay.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Oh yeah. She's going away from us.

a14-0055323.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0055323.text: Following the Auxiliary Propulsion System maneuver, and the propulsive venting of the liquid oxygen aboard the S-IVB , there will be targeted - a burn determined, or targeted to impact the S-IVB on the lunar surface at approximately 33 degrees west and 20 degrees south, which is near the Apollo 12 landing site, and it is expected that this maneuver will be carried out as planned. You heard Stu Roosa on that last exchange report that the S-IVB was responding properly to commands and appeared to be coming around in the proper attitude.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Apollo 14, Houston. Would you give us Omni Delta? [Pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0055323.text: Okay, you have it, Houston.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Go ahead.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: With a Go from you up there, we'll plan to initiate the APS evasive burn at 6 plus 04 even. Over.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay. Yeah, it's well boresighted away from us, and we'll be standing by.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger.

a14-0055323.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0055323.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 2 minutes, 18 seconds; a little less than 2 minutes away now from the scheduled Auxiliary Propulsion System evasive maneuver on the S-IVB . CapCom Gordon Fullerton advised the Apollo 14 crew that that maneuver would occur at 6 hours, 4 minutes with the liquid oxygen dump scheduled to occur at 6 hours, 25 minutes, 20 seconds.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Apollo 14, Houston. The evasive maneuver should be going now. How does it look?

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Rog. We - we see the booster moving.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Now the last thing you can do for us on this, because of our lack of determining the booster attitude, is, as it fades out of view - if you can determine if it is still looking stable. Over.

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay. We can sure handle that, and you got some venting there, too, as you started that maneuver.

a14-0055323.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0055323.text: Roger. That's normal. I was expecting...

a14-0055323.speaker: Roosa
a14-0055323.text: Okay.

a14-0060807.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0060807.text: Apollo 14, Houston. Would you go to Manual and Wide on the High Gain, but stay in Omni Delta?

a14-0060807.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0060807.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 9 minutes. We've completed our shift handover now at Mission Control. Flight Director Milton Windler and his team of Maroon flight directors, flight controllers. The Flight Dynamics Officer has just advised the Flight Director that he does not anticipate a mid-course correction being required at the opportunity for mid-course correction 1. This would mean that the mid-course would not be made until the midcourse correction 2 opportunity. At the present time Apollo 14 is traveling at a speed of 11,237 feet per second [3,425 m/s]. The spacecraft altitude is 28,

a14-0060807.speaker: Roosa
a14-0060807.text: Okay, Gordon. I'm sure - sure you all have been - been talking about it. Do you want me to press ahead with the maneuver to the P52 attitude and go into that?

a14-0060807.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0060807.text: Roger, Stu. That's affirmative. We'd like you to go through with the normal procedures as shown in the Flight Plan down to that P52 at 5 hours and 40 minutes, but at that point we're going to deviate slightly in order to save some RCS . We would - do not want you to do the fuel cell purge or the waste water dump. We're planning to have you - or - or - and we do not want you to do the - go into PTC . At that point we're planning to do the P23 which will be a little early, and we'll have a new attitude for that. And then we'll go into PTC . Right now it looks like midcourse 1 is not likely to be

a14-0060807.speaker: Roosa
a14-0060807.text: Okay, now at 5:50 you say, do not do the fuel cell purge or the waste water dump?

a14-0061613.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0061613.text: Roger. As soon as you get to your attitude there, we'll be ready to uplink a new REFSMMAT to you.

a14-0061840.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0061840.text: Houston, 14. Do you want me to start a battery B charge?

a14-0061840.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0061840.text: Ed, that's affirmative. Go ahead with the battery B charge.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Go ahead.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Hey, Gordon. I can - got a beautiful view of the S-IVB now, out of the left-hand window, and she's stable as a rock.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger, Stu. [Long pause.]

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: And, Houston, I've initiated battery B charge.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger, Ed. Would you give us Omni Charlie, Ed?

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: You have it.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger. And at about 6:25:20, the LOX dump should start on the S-IVB . You might keep an eye on it at that time. I'll give you a warning about 10 seconds prior.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Okay.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0062245.text: CapCom Gordon Fullerton was advising the crew that the dump of the liquid oxygen remaining in the S-IVB will occur at 6 hours, 25 minutes, 20 seconds Ground Elapsed Time. This is the propulsive venting of the liquid oxygen which is aimed to increase the separation distance between the Lunar Module and the booster third stage and also is targeted to impact the S-IVB on the lunar surface near the Apollo 12 seismometer.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0062245.text: We're now at 6 hours, 25 minutes; some 20 seconds away from the liquid oxygen dump.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Apollo 14, Houston. That LOX dump should start at about 10 seconds.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0062245.text: Booster reports the dump is initiated.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Apollo 14, Houston. The LOX dump should be complete now. Did you see anything of it?

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: Yeah. It's a beautiful sight, Houston. The Sun was shining from the side; it was streaming out. We tried to get a couple of Hasselblad shots of it from the corner of the window. It's really fantastic.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger, Al. [Long pause.]

a14-0062245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0062245.text: That was Apollo 14 commander, Al Shepard reporting a very spectacular sight with good sunlight on the liquid oxygen particles streaming out of the nozzle of the S-IVB . The LOX dump is scheduled to be followed by an additional...

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: Okay, Houston. You have P00 and Accept.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger, Al. We'd like you to try to bring up the High Gain now. Use a pitch of plus 28 and a yaw of plus 317. Over.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: Roger. 28 and 317. [Long pause.]

a14-0062245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0062245.text: Once the High Gain Antenna is brought into play, we should see a marked increase in signal strength. The LOX dump from the S-IVB will be followed by an additional maneuver to target the S-IVB to the proper impact point. That maneuver, performed with the Auxiliary Propulsion System.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: Okay. You're in Auto and locked up, Houston.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Ed, this is Houston. We're having a little problem with our read-out of High Gain Antenna angles here. Would you read out your onboard pitch and yaw angle?

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: Rog. I have a pitch of plus 29 and yaw of about 320 - 330.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: Say again the Yaw.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: About 330.

a14-0062245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0062245.text: 330. Roger.

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: I'm not having any trouble at all with weightlessness.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: I'm not either, Al.

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: How are you doing, Stu?

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Well, so far, so good.

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: Really very comfortable.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Yes, I - I guess I'm a little surprised at - at the fighting to stay down...

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: Yes.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: ... if any.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: Well, I think a lot of this is due to these hoses we got on here. Once we get rid of them, it'll be a little different.

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: There are a jillion stars out there.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: I think you've got a whole bunch of little things to look at.

a14-0062245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0062245.text: Venting of the S-IVB .

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: In fact, you've got a - Let me help you with that [garble].

a14-0062245.speaker: Roosa
a14-0062245.text: Okay. I think we'll start - I'm going to start clearing my pockets out, in preparation to get this suit off.

a14-0062245.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0062245.text: Good show.

a14-0063036.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0063036.text: 14, Houston. We have the REFSMMAT and trunnion bias zero in there. It's your computer.

a14-0063036.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0063036.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 33 minutes. We'll be coming up soon on a change of shift press briefing. At that time we will take down the live air to ground circuits and record any conversation with the spacecraft for playback following the change of shift briefing. One bit of information from the flight surgeon. Flight surgeon reports that Commander Shepherd's biomedical data, primarily heart rate, resumed spontaneously at 1 hour, 30 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. At that time, the CapCom asked if he did anything to fix the sensor and Shepherd replied nope. The readings on all three crewme

a14-0064124.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0064124.text: Rog. Did you get our Noun 93s?

a14-0064124.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0064124.text: Ed, would you give us the torquing time?

a14-0064124.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0064124.text: This is Apollo Control at 6 hours, 45 minutes. At the present time, Apollo 14 is traveling at a speed of 10,555 feet per second [3,217 m/s] and at a distance of 32,283 nautical miles [59,788 km] from Earth. Change of shift briefing is ready to begin now in the MSC News Center. We'll record any conversations with the spacecraft during this period of time and play them back following the press briefing. Also there will be questions from Cape Kennedy following the - following the briefing during the course of the question and answer period. At 6 hours, 46 minutes; this is Apollo Control.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Apollo 14, Houston. Over,

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Go ahead.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Okay. If you haven't already, we'd like you to continue on through the rest of the procedures in the Flight Plan after the P52 down to 6 hours, except don't do the O 2 fuel cell purge or the waste water dump.

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. That's what we're planning to do.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: And, then, Ed, I have a - a longer update; I want you to do a P23, the one that's scheduled for about 9:50 in the Flight Plan - correction 9:30, and if you'd turn to that, I'll give you some new stars and other information to go there. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Stand by. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: All right Houston, I have the Flight Plan open to 09:30.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger. Stand by 1. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Okay, Ed. On the P23, the optics Cal attitude is the same as listed there. Like you to change the P23 sighting attitude to roll, 184; pitch, 2... [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Hold it, hold it.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Okay.

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. I'm ready; go again.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Okay. It's listed there at 42. Roll, 184; pitch, 283; and yaw, 310. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. The sighting attitude is 184, 283, 310.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: That's right. And we have a change in the order of doing the stars, plus a couple of substitutions. I'd like you to use the listed star number 3, that's Gamma Centauri, number 53. I want you to do that star first. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Hold it a minute.

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay, 53, Gamma Centauri is first.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger. And then the star that's listed number 2, number 2 - 36, will be the second star.

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Roger. Delta Ophiuchi.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Okay. And then the third star is a different one, a new one. It will be star 161, Iota Centauri - and Earth far horizon. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay, star 3 is 161, Iota Centauri, EFH .

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger. The Noun 70 for that star is the same as the Noun 70 on star number 1. It ought to be easy just to write it down. That'll be 00 all balls on the first register, all balls on the second register, and 00120 on the third register. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Understand.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: And Noun 88 is completely different. First register, minus 75603; second register, minus 27129; and third register, minus 59566. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Roger, stand by a minute. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. For Iota Centauri, Noun 70 is all zeroes, all zeroes, 00120; Noun 88; minus 75603, minus 27129, minus 59566.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger, Ed. Readback correct. Okay, the fourth star will be star number 24, Gienah, Earth's far horizon. And Noun 70 will be: first register, 00024; second register, all balls; third register, 00120; and you don't need a Noun 88 for that one. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. The fourth star is 24, Gienah, EFH ; Noun 70 is 00024, all zeroes, and 00120.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger. That readback's good. After you finish that P23, we'd like you to do the O 2 fuel cell purge and the waste water dump. And then the - the activity to follow is still under discussion here; we're talking over possibly removing the drogue and taking a look at it at that time and possibly cranking up the TV to give us a picture of it back here. So the decision to start PTC after finishing the P23 will depend on whether we're going to request you to give us a TV shot of the drogue and probe. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Okay. Understand, and the - following this P23, you want us to press on with the O 2 fuel cell purge and waste water dump that's listed about 11:25. Is that correct?

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: I guess it's listed there, and it's also the same thing you skipped back there at 5 hours and 55 minutes. I guess that's the...

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Do you want us to do it immediately after the P23, or wait until 11:25.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: Roger. Stand by. I'll check on that to be sure. Do that immediately after the P23, Ed.

a14-0065046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0065046.text: Rog.

a14-0065046.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0065046.text: And one other thing, while you have a pencil in hand, is a 'Lift-off plus 15' P37 block data when you're ready.

a14-0070056.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0070056.text: Houston, go ahead with the P37 for lift-off plus 15.

a14-0070056.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0070056.text: Okay, Ed. GET of ignition is 015:00; Delta-V T , 5700, minus 165; GET for 400K, 045:04. Go ahead.

a14-0070056.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0070056.text: Roger, Gordon. We didn't quite understand when you wanted us to start this P23 that you passed the info on.

a14-0070056.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0070056.text: Okay. Stu's going to get out of his suit here, and we'll be ready in a few minutes.

a14-0071526.speaker: Roosa
a14-0071526.text: All right, Houston; 14. How do you read?

a14-0071526.speaker: Roosa
a14-0071526.text: Okay, Gordon, I just wanted to check and make sure that I was back on the comm here.

a14-0071526.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0071526.text: This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 25 minutes. During the change of shift briefing, we advised the crew that it is being considered to have them remove the probe and drogue assembly from the docking tunnel, pull it down into the Command Module and activate the television so that we on the ground and the crew can get a good look at that particular piece of equipment. A decision to do so will not be made in all probability for another 30 to 40 minutes. At that time, it will then require something like an additional two hours to get the necessary lines up between the receiving end - the receiving

a14-0072914.speaker: McCandless
a14-0072914.text: Roger, Stu. When you get ready to commence your P23, we have a change to the sighting attitude, based on your current estimated time of starting. Over.

a14-0072914.speaker: Roosa
a14-0072914.text: Okay. And, hey, could you give me an estimate on - on this? Are you wanting us to press on into that right now, or do you want us to go ahead and get the suits stowed, so forth?

a14-0072914.speaker: McCandless
a14-0072914.text: That's - that's really your option, Stu. Whenever you conveniently get ready to run a P23, why don't you check with us, and we'll make sure you've got a current attitude? Over.

a14-0072914.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0072914.text: This is Apollo Control at 7 hours, 38 minutes. That completes the playback of the taped conversations between the spacecraft and Mission Control. We'll now continue to follow for any live conversations with the crew. The capsule communicator at this time is astronaut Bruce McCandless. McCandless relieved CapCom Gordon Fullerton. At the present time, Apollo 14 is traveling at a velocity of 9,776 feet per second [2,980 m/s] and the spacecraft is 37,248 nautical miles [68,983 km] from Earth.

a14-0074509.speaker: Roosa
a14-0074509.text: Okay, Bruce. How do you read?

a14-0074509.speaker: McCandless
a14-0074509.text: Go ahead. [Pause.] Apollo 14, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a14-0074509.speaker: Roosa
a14-0074509.text: Okay, Houston. I'm getting ready to start the - this P23, and - and I guess that last P52 will still be good for this, and I'll start into the Optics Cal attitude and then get your Verb 49 attitude to start after that.

a14-0074509.speaker: McCandless
a14-0074509.text: Okay. And I'll check and see if we want to update our attitude from the one I got here in front of me, and we'll pass it up to you when you're ready.

a14-0074509.speaker: Roosa
a14-0074509.text: And, Bruce, I guess I want to verify we do not need another P52 . It's been - what - an hour since that last one?

a14-0080154.speaker: McCandless
a14-0080154.text: 14, this is Houston. We'd like you to acquire us with the High Gain Antenna. Pitch, minus 75; and Yaw, plus 99. Over.

a14-0080154.speaker: McCandless
a14-0080154.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Change Yaw angle to plus 120.

a14-0080154.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0080154.text: Okay, Houston. We've locked up Auto Track.

a14-0080531.speaker: McCandless
a14-0080531.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Ed, we'd like you to read out the Pitch and Yaw position meters on the High Gain Antenna for us, if you would, please.

a14-0080531.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0080531.text: Roger. The Pitch is reading - minus 90, and Yaw is 150.

a14-0080531.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0080531.text: No, make that about 180 - I mean about minus 80 and 150.

a14-0080948.speaker: Roosa
a14-0080948.text: Okay, Bruce, how about that attitude for the P23?

a14-0080948.speaker: McCandless
a14-0080948.text: Roger, Stu. The attitude will be roll, 179; pitch, 280; yaw, 310. Over.

a14-0080948.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0080948.text: This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 12 minutes. At the present time, the crew aboard Apollo 14 is preparing to begin a series of star sightings. They will do this in computer program 23. Taking sightings and marks on 3 stars to update the onboard guidance system's knowledge of where it is and where it's going. At this time, here in Houston at the Manned Spacecraft Center and also at North American in Downey, California, teams of engineers are in the process of putting together a set of procedures and evaluating the tasks involved in running through a set of checks on the probe and drogue assemb

a14-0080948.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0080948.text: This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 30 minutes. Apollo 14 now traveling at 9,163 feet per second [2,793 m/s]. Spacecraft is 41,842 nautical miles [77,491 km] from Earth. The Flight Dynamics Officer reported that there appears to be a very small amount of venting occurring on the S-IVB . The venting is not probably causing any significant affect to the trajectory to the vehicle, however, it does affect the tracking data on it, and makes it difficult for the Flight Dynamics Officer to get a good vector on the S-IVB and from that to compute a predicted impact point. However, it is possible to comp

a14-0084523.speaker: McCandless
a14-0084523.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. For your information, the booster people are planning an APS burn on the S-IVB at 9 hours GET even. Over.

a14-0084523.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0084523.text: Houston, 14. Have you any idea where we should look to see it? [Long pause.]

a14-0084523.speaker: McCandless
a14-0084523.text: Stand by on that one, Ed. And, if we can get some good angles and stuff for you, we'll send them up.

a14-0084523.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0084523.text: Okay. We've just been moving around here. We've lost track of it.

a14-0084523.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0084523.text: This is Apollo Control at 8 hours, 59 minutes. We're standing by now for the beginning of the S-IVB Auxiliary Propulsion System maneuver which will target the Saturn third stage to an impact point near the Apollo 12 seismometer.
