That will be a 4-minute and 12-second burn targeted to put the third stage in at about 1.56 degrees south latitude and 33.25 west.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Ed, this is Houston. Coming up on the S-IVB APS burn, and - we don't have a good attitude for you to look out right now.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Okay. We'll kind of look around and see what we can see.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Roger.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Give us a hack on it, Bruce.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Roger. It's going now. It's about a 4-minute burn.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Houston, we've been unable to spot the S-IVB . [Long pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: 14, this is Houston. You can try looking out the right-hand side window and - with your line of sight depressed a little bit from the straight-out position.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: I guess where the engine bell lies.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Rog. The Sun's coming in that window. [Pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Okay. That's probably going to make it pretty difficult to spot.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Makes it a little hard on the eyes. [Long pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Bruce, we've been sincerely busy with housekeeping up here. We haven't had a chance to - describe anything we've been seeing. We'll get around to that after a while.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Say again what you're going to get around to.

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: I was saying, we'll get around to - doing a little description for you after a while.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0085900.text: Booster Officer reports the burn is complete.

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: And the S-IVB burn has been completed, Ed. [Long pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: Thank you, Bruce.

a14-0085900.speaker: Shepard
a14-0085900.text: Bruce, we've been wondering if you found your headset all right when you got back to the MOCR. [Pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: McCandless
a14-0085900.text: Yes, I've got it on. I didn't notice anything wrong with it. You may be a little subtle for me, but go ahead. [Pause.]

a14-0085900.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0085900.text: You obviously found it. It is working.

a14-0091855.speaker: McCandless
a14-0091855.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. I have a Flight Plan update for you.

a14-0091855.speaker: Shepard
a14-0091855.text: Okay, Houston, go ahead with your Flight Plan update.

a14-0091855.speaker: McCandless
a14-0091855.text: Roger, 14. We have a P52 that was previously scheduled in the Flight Plan at 9 hours GET . We'd like you to hold off on that P52 until after PTC is established, and then run it while in the PTC mode. After your P23s are complete here, we'd like you to perform the oxygen purge and waste water dump. Also perform the Delta-V test and null bias checks, as called out in the Flight Plan at 9 hours and 20 minutes GET previously. And then you can deactivate the primary evaporator at your convenience. And we'll be having instructions for you on what we want to do on - with respect to the probe and drog

a14-0091855.speaker: Shepard
a14-0091855.text: Okay. You want the P52 originally scheduled for 9 to be done after PTC is commenced. You want O 2 purge and water dump, and [garble] now and we'll do the Delta-V test and null bias check here momentarily, as soon as 23's been completed. We'll talk about the probe and call you back.

a14-0091855.speaker: Roosa
a14-0091855.text: Okay, Bruce. I just wanted to say a word about that P52 that we had just before the P23 there. Went to that P52 attitude and PICAPAR - I went to pick the star that was occulted by part of the LM . So you probably saw me dial in another star. And the stars weren't probably separated too far, as far as the criteria goes. So if anybody's looking at that, that's the reason.

a14-0091855.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0091855.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 27 minutes. Apollo 14 now 46,539 nautical miles [86,190 km] from Earth, travelling at a speed of 8,544 feet per second [2,604 m/s]. We're still awaiting the arrival of a list of questions and procedures from the engineering support room. These questions will be passed up to the crew, asked of the Apollo 14 crew, and used in part as a basis for a decision as to whether or not to ask the crew to remove the probe and drogue assembly from the docking tunnel of the Command Module.

a14-0092700.speaker: Shepard
a14-0092700.text: Regarding the probe, I don't think we'd mind taking it out tonight, discussing it with you, letting you look at it, and then leaving it out for the night.

a14-0092700.speaker: McCandless
a14-0092700.text: Okay, 14. We copy. And as I mentioned earlier, we haven't really gotten all the inputs yet on what we want to do, whether we'd like to do this tonight or whether we might want to wait until tomorrow, but I'll get back to you as soon as we - we have and we'll incorporate your feelings into the decision down here and send them back to you. And did you copy on my Flight Plan update? We'd like to get the primary evaporator deactivated whenever it's convenient with you all. [Long pause.]

a14-0092700.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0092700.text: That last remark came from Al Shepard. Shepard stated that the crew would not mind removing the probe and drogue assembly tonight, but they would prefer not to have to reinstall it tonight before beginning their sleep period. And as you heard, CapCom Bruce McCandless advised the crew that the decision has not as yet been made as to whether or not the crew will be asked to remove the drogue and probe assembly. Discussions are going on at this moment around the Flight Director's console and we're still awaiting the engineering data which will also serve in part in making that decision. At 9 hour

a14-0093408.speaker: Shepard
a14-0093408.text: Houston, on the EMS null bias check, we had a start at minus 100 and terminate with minus 99.4.

a14-0093408.speaker: McCandless
a14-0093408.text: Okay, Al. We copy. You started with minus 100 on a null bias check, and you terminated with minus 99.4.

a14-0093408.speaker: Shepard
a14-0093408.text: That's correct. The O 2 purge has been completed and the waste water dump is in progress.

a14-0093408.speaker: McCandless
a14-0093408.text: 14, this is Houston. Would you prefer to take time out to have something to eat or press on with the drogue operations now?

a14-0093408.speaker: Shepard
a14-0093408.text: I think we could do both simultaneously.

a14-0093408.speaker: Shepard
a14-0093408.text: [Garble] the drogue, Bruce, is to get it out, look at it, discuss it with you, and give you some time to think about it, and tie it down here with us while you're thinking about it.

a14-0093408.speaker: McCandless
a14-0093408.text: Roger. We're tentatively looking at taking the probe out, doing that, tying it down, and we may want to take the drogue out, but we thought you could just lock the drogue back in place, and then the hatch, to go to sleep for the evening.

a14-0093408.speaker: McCandless
a14-0093408.text: Okay. And be right back at you in about a minute with the hot smoking word. [Pause.]

a14-0093408.speaker: Roosa
a14-0093408.text: Hey, Bruce, are we going to get in - start PTC before we start in on the drogue?

a14-0093408.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0093408.text: Houston, 14. This is a pretty fine snow storm we have going on here.

a14-0093408.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0093408.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 39 minutes. The decision that's been made with respect to the drogue and probe is that the crew will be asked to remove the assembly. They will also be asked to unstow the television camera, get television coverage of it. However, the television lines will not be put up between Goldstone and Houston. In order to avoid a 2-hour delay, the TV signal would be recorded at Goldstone for playback later. And the evaluation that would be done this evening would be a verbal evaluation from the crew with the TV to be recorded for playback at some later time. At 9 hours

a14-0093408.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0093408.text: This is Apollo Control at 9 hours, 42 minutes. There's been a slight modification to that plan as far as the TV is concerned. The crew will begin as soon as convenient to remove the probe and drogue assembly. However the lines will be brought up from Goldstone. This will probably require an hour to an hour and a half and any television that is received at the time the lines are up will be released live. And television, until that time, will be recorded. And so there is a possibility that we will get some live television toward the end of the probe and drogue activities aboard the Command Modul

a14-0094200.speaker: McCandless
a14-0094200.text: 14, Houston. We're showing about 15 percent on the waste water on telemetry now.

a14-0094200.speaker: Shepard
a14-0094200.text: Rog. We've just shut it off. We're showing 22.

a14-0095300.speaker: McCandless
a14-0095300.text: Okay, Ed. Here's what we would like to do on the probe removal - or actually the whole probe inspection shooting match. We'd like to remove the tunnel hatch, of course, and let you make a quick visual inspection there to see if there's anything that looks significantly amiss. If you see anything, we'd like to photograph it; and, in this whole sequence, we would like to have you power up the television and send a picture down, which we'll receive at - at Goldstone and record, although we still have about an hour or an hour and a half before we could be configured to receive the television back

a14-0095300.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0095300.text: Better hold up a minute, Bruce.

a14-0095300.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0095300.text: This is Apollo Control at 10 hours, 1 minute. Our Network controller has just reported what is perhaps the fastest hour and a half work we've seen in some time. He reports that the lines are up and ready to receive live television from Goldstone, so hopefully, when the crew is ready to begin removing the probe and drogue assembly we'll have live television of that activity.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Go ahead, 14.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Roger. Can you give me the changes of this probe removal procedure so that I can copy it on page S2-5?

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Roger. Actually we'll be looking at page S2-6 for the changes, that is, the section that applies to both TLD and LOD. Over.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Okay, I'm ready to copy.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Okay. At the top of page 2-6, the first step, "Probe umbilicals - disconnect and stow". We'd like you to verify proper connection of the umbilicals before you disconnect and stow them. And I guess you might take a look for bent pins, contacts, all sort of stuff. Down at about the sixth line down where it says "Capture latch release handle lock - rotate counterclockwise to unlock." We'd like you to verify that it is locked prior to unlocking it. You got that one? [Long pause.]

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Okay, go ahead.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Down about five lines further, you have "Capture latch release handle - pull, rotate to unlock, 180 clockwise," and we'd like you to pay particular attention to whether there is an unusually high torque required to unlock the capture latch release handle in this step. [Pause.] And we'd also like you to verify the absence of, or report, any damage to the pyro cover or to the capture latch release handle. And the pyro cover that we're talking about is the - it looks like an extruded metallic shell just forward of the capture latch release handle there. It's the one that bears the decals on it th

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Okay. Damage to the pyro cover and what else?

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Any damage to the capture latch release handle? [Pause.] And then as you pull it out, we'd like to know if you notice any unusual forces required to remove the probe. [Pause.]

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Okay. Let me read it back.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Okay, go ahead.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: At top of page S2-6, "Probe umbilicals." Before we disconnect and stow, we want to verify that the "yea verilies" are properly connected.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Yea, verily.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: And there's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 "Capture latch release handle lock"; before rotating counterclockwise to unlock, I want to verify again that that is locked.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Roger.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: And that you would like for us to pay attention to the torque required to loosen any of these items - oh, that's the capture latch release handle; and you want us to observe for any damage to the pyro cover or the capture latch release handle and to observe any obvious damage that's apparent to the capture latches or the probe end.

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Roger, Ed. And we currently have the lines from Goldstone back to the building up here, so I think that we'll probably be ready to support via TV almost in real time. And for onboard photography, we're recommending use of the electric Hasselblad set on f/2.8, 1/125th of a second at 3½ feet, magazine O for Okmulgee, which is stowed in Alpha 13, and you might verify the f-stop with the spotmeter set at ASA 64, if you have the chance. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Okay, Bruce. I got that, I believe. The electric Hasselblad at 2 8, 125th, 3.5, magazine O for Opinaca, it's stored A-13, and we'll check it with the spotmeter. How long will you have Goldstone coverage, Houston? [Long pause.]

a14-0100100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0100100.text: Ah, [Long pause.] 14, this is Houston. We'll have Goldstone coverage for about another hour and a half. If that's any problem, we can reconfigure to pick up Honeysuckle. And the shutter speed is 1/125th; that's 1 slash 125. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Roger, Houston. One twenty fifth.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0100100.text: Getting edgy already down there.

a14-0100100.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0100100.text: This is Apollo Control at 10 hours, 13 minutes. We're still standing by for the crew to begin the operation of removing the probe assembly from the docking tunnel of the Command Module and we do expect that we'll have live television coverage of at least a portion of that activity. We have 1 hour, 50 minutes of Goldstone acquisition time remaining and before we expect to lose acquisition from Goldstone and pick up primary coverage from the Honeysuckle site. At the present time Apollo 14 is 50,322 nautical miles [93,196 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 8,234 feet per second [2,510 m/s

a14-0101300.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0101300.text: Bruce, it'll probably be 15 minutes or so before we finish getting some chow, and we'll start up into that tunnel for you.

a14-0101300.speaker: McCandless
a14-0101300.text: Roger. We're standing by down here. We've got the color converter going so we can watch you in glorious living color. And just give us a yell when you're ready to go.

a14-0101300.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0101300.text: That was Ed Mitchell reporting that it will be about 15 minutes before the crew is ready to begin the probe removal operation.

a14-0102022.speaker: McCandless
a14-0102022.text: 14, this is Houston. When you get around to the hatch removal in the tunnel, we'd like to get a LM / CM Delta-P reading prior to your equalizing the pressure. Over.

a14-0102022.speaker: Roosa
a14-0102022.text: Rog, Bruce. We'll give you that.

a14-0102022.speaker: Swigert
a14-0102022.text: Stuart, how is your peanut butter?

a14-0102022.speaker: Roosa
a14-0102022.text: Hey, Big Jack, not enjoying any peanut butter.

a14-0102022.speaker: Swigert
a14-0102022.text: Coz you're doing a good job.

a14-0104547.speaker: McCandless
a14-0104547.text: Roger. If you're about wound up on eating, I've got a correction to the inflight erasable load of T ephem for you, and we'd like to suggest a change to the DAP to open you up to a 5-degree deadband to save a little fuel. Over.

a14-0104547.speaker: Shepard
a14-0104547.text: Okay. We'll call you back in a minute.

a14-0105209.speaker: Shepard
a14-0105209.text: Okay, Houston. 14's ready to copy T ephem .

a14-0105209.speaker: McCandless
a14-0105209.text: Roger, Apollo 14. This is a correction to the inflight erasable load procedure for T ephem as found on page G9-4 of the G&C Checklist. Under column B, line 04 now reads 33304, and should be changed to read 35242. Line 05, under column B, now reads 07000, and should be changed to read 03262. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0105209.speaker: Shepard
a14-0105209.text: Okay. Page now - 9-5, that is. How about giving it to me again? 9-4, that is. Go ahead.

a14-0105209.speaker: McCandless
a14-0105209.text: Roger. That's page 9-4. Under the OID line number 04 in column B for Buffalo, you'll find the entry 33304; that should be changed to read 35242. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0105209.speaker: McCandless
a14-0105209.text: Right. And the next entry directly below it on OID line 05 now reads 07000, and that should be changed to read 03262. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0105209.speaker: McCandless
a14-0105209.text: Roger. Readback correct. And on your DAP , we're recommending an R 1 load - Okay, I see that you've got it already. Sorry about that.

a14-0105209.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0105209.text: This is Apollo Control at 10 hours, 59 minutes. We're standing by for the Apollo 14 crew to begin removal and evaluation of the probe assembly. We do anticipate having live television coverage through Goldstone. And our Network controller is making arrangements for satellite coverage from Honeysuckle so that we would have television through Honeysuckle also after we hand over to that site. At this time, Apollo 14 is 53,866 nautical miles [99,760 km] from Earth. The spacecraft velocity is 7,900 feet per second [2,408 m/s]. And we'll continue to stand by.

a14-0110525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0110525.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a14-0110525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0110525.text: Roger, Houston; 14. I've got the camera set up and we're starting to work on the tunnel now. When you're configured for television, we'll let you have it.

a14-0110525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0110525.text: Roger. We're configured, and let me see if we're ready to have you send it down. [Pause.] Roger. Let her rip.

a14-0110525.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110525.text: We're now getting a television picture.

a14-0110525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0110525.text: Stu, this is Houston. Before you equalize, would you give us the LM / CM Delta-P ?

a14-0110853.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0110853.text: Okay, Houston. We're starting to bring our pressure up until [garble] in the tunnel.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: We haven't yet been able to make out who is up in the tunnel working in the hatch area, removing the hatch.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: That's Ed Mitchell giving us the reports on the pressure differential.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: The spacecraft now 54,477 nautical miles [100,891 km] from Earth.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: The greenish looking object floating on the end of the white tether is what is referred to as tool E. It's a hex-head screwdriver type tool.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0110853.text: Houston, we're starting to bring the hatch out now and put it on the foot of the couch.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0110853.text: You're not getting very much light down there, Houston, but that's the hatch going under the left-hand couch.

a14-0110853.speaker: McCandless
a14-0110853.text: Roger, Ed. Even with the low level of light, we're getting a pretty good picture here, especially after it's color converted. [Long pause.]

a14-0110853.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0110853.text: Can you see anything up in the tunnel, Houston?

a14-0110853.speaker: McCandless
a14-0110853.text: We really aren't seeing much in the way of the docking mechanism there. Here we go. That looks better.

a14-0110853.speaker: Roosa
a14-0110853.text: Okay, Houston, as we start the inspection, we find that the probe umbilicals are properly secured.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: That was Al Shepard reporting that the probe umbilicals are properly connected. That was one of the things that we had asked him to verify before removing the probe assembly.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: Our best guess at this time is that Stu Roosa is the crewman working in the hatch area.

a14-0110853.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0110853.text: Activation of the handle allows the probe mechanism to collapse inside the tunnel and makes it possible for the crewman to remove the assembly.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay, Bruce; I don't know how well you can follow with the TV camera down there, but I didn't see anything obviously wrong with the umbilicals, and the capture latch release handle lock was in the Lock position.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. Thank you, Stu.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0112231.text: And it appears that the 83-pound probe assembly is collapsing, sliding down out of the tunnel now.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay. The capture latch release handle turned very easily, Bruce.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger; out.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: You didn't notice any damage to the pyro cover or anything like that, did you?

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: No, I - I didn't, Bruce. I - I looked it over here with a flashlight and, gee, I can't - can't see anything out of the ordinary. We'll - we'll drag it down and take a look at the outside of it. But, I didn't see anything wrong with - with the pyro cover or any of the connections or anything like that.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: And, Stu, while you're at it, would you say that the force that it took to remove the probe up there from the tunnel area was high, low, or indifferent - or nominal?

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Well, you know it's the first time I've done it without gravity helping a little bit - and pushing back, but I - I wouldn't say it was exceptionally hard. I sort of braced myself on the bottom of the tunnel and gave a pull and she came loose. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0112231.text: I can see the head of Commander Alan Shepard just behind the probe.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. We'd like you to examine the probe head as you're now doing with particular emphasis on any evidence of unusual shearpin shearing in the bushing hole there at the end, or foreign material in the capture latch release button area or foreign material or damage anywhere in the areas of the capture latch hooks. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay. We'll give it a go. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: All right, Bruce. The first [garble] we looked we don't see anything obvious about it.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay...

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: If you could give us some instructions as to where you'd like to look, we'll try to play the camera right in on it for you.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: And, Bruce, up here in the very tip of the probe - you know where the - the tower hooks on it, it looks clean. I don't see anything fishy about that right off the bat.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: All right. Is that the bushing on the end you're describing to me, Stu?

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Yeah. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, 14, we'd like to get some closeup photos of the probe head around the capture latch release button of each capture latch hook; and if you find any scratching or damage up there - of that area in particular, also.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay, Bruce. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Houston, looking at the drogue, we see that there are three scratches - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - that are rough to the touch [garble] broken the surface of the drogue. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Al, this is Houston. You're coming through very weakly. Can you, maybe, put the mikes closer to your mouth? I think that might be the problem.

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Okay, I was looking up and away from the mike when I was talking but, I was in the - up in the tunnel. I'm looking at the drogue and there are these three scratches which we described before that have - that feel rough to the touch. They've probably scratched the surface of the drogue - perhaps a fourth of an inch. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Al, this is Houston. You mentioned the dimension associated with these scratches - You mentioned a quarter of an inch. Was that width or depth of penetration, or length or what? Over.

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Yes, I was trying to describe the depth of penetration, and it's very difficult because we don't have any kind of gauge on it, but it has scratched the surface to a depth of perhaps - I don't know - 3 or 4 thousandths maybe. Very definitely scratched. It's rough to the touch. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: MCC
a14-0112231.text: : Now, I'm confused, CapCom. Is that - the scratch is of 3 or 4 thousandths?

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. Understand you're saying they're about 3 or 4 thousandths of an inch deep and on the order of a couple of inches long?

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: That's right. They're very light. They all - as I said before - radial scratches leading away from the apex of the drogue and some are about 2 inches long, one's about 1 inch long, one's about three-quarters, and one's about one-half inch long. These are apparently the marks made by the capture latches as they made the docking attempt and then backed in - cut into the surface of the drogue. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger, we copy. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, when you get through taking some photos up there, we'd like you to take the capture latch release handle, pull, rotate it counterclockwise to the Cock position and then manually depress all three capture latch triggers at the base of the capture latch hooks, simultaneously, and verify that the capture latch release button should move forward to the lock position flush with the probe - bushing.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay. Why don't we do that and then when we get all through, we'll go through and get the pictures you want.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: And we're going to bring the drogue out, too, so you can take a look at it on the TV. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger, Stu; and after you do get it out, we'd like you to hold the TV steady on the area of the drogue where the scratches are for a couple of minutes and do likewise again on the capture latch area on the probe.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Ah, Houston; I'm moving the television camera in on the drogue now. Al's going to put a light on it. It is pretty dark.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0112231.text: We're now looking up into the docking tunnel towards the Lunar Module.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: 14, this is Houston. We're getting a picture, but the illumination level isn't very good and I guess I - I for one can't see any scratches right here.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Roger; it is pretty hard to see it, Houston. It's the light level. [Pause.] We're going to try another little trick here. Let's see if we can get you some light.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: All right, Houston. We're going to move in on the - You're looking at the center of the drogue now and the scratches - you can see Stuart's thumb there. He's going to point to them and we'll see if we can get enough light for you to see them.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger, we - we got that last one, Stu, and we got the one you're pointing at now. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: And, Bruce. I think that this illumination will give - illumination will give it to you if you'll let me hold it for a minute here.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. We can see about five or six of these radial scratches in the present scene - right - right where you're looking there, about three of them. One... [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Yeah, that's - that's affirmative, Bruce.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, now, I guess that at the 4 o'clock position you got about three scratches and then at 8 o'clock, you've got one. Do you have anything up at noon? [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: That's affirmative, Bruce. There's one long one at 12 o'clock noon.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: From the looks and from the feel, I believe it appears that the probe hit the drogue almost dead center every time we tried to make contact. But, it just rebounded right off of it.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger; we copy.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay, we're going to put the drogue back in place if you're through with it now.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Negative, we'd like you to hold it out for a minute or so. We ultimately want to wind up fit checking the drogue and probe here.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, back on the probe, we'd like you to take the capture latch release handle, pull, rotate counterclockwise to the Cock position or a 150-degree rotation.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Okay, I've done that.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, now manually depress all three capture latch triggers at the base of the capture latch hook simultaneously and verify that the capture latch release button in the end of the probe moves forward to the Lock position; that is flush with the probe pushing. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay, you want us to push all three of them simultaneously, is that right?

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: That's right. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: All right. Say it again, and verify what?

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, the little button right at the tip of the probe which is the capture latch release button from the LM active side - where you got your finger - should pop out flush when you trigger all three of these latches simultaneously.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Got it. Is it flush? Okay I'm going to pull back in and it came out - it appears to be almost flush. [Pause.] Stu says that's counted as flush, the way it is now. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: We're going to repeat it, Houston. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: 14, Houston. We're requesting Medium Beamwidth on the High Gain Antenna and we're going to have to handover from Goldstone here shortly.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: [Garble] we repeated that, and it - it comes out - flush.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: In looking at that button, do you notice anything unusual about it - any burrs, any bending, or any way it could be hanging up on something?

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: [Garble].

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Say again, Ed. We had some static.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Stand by. We are looking at it now.

a14-0112231.speaker: Roosa
a14-0112231.text: Al's taking a look at it. The top of the button looks smooth. Of course, you can't see down below it. But it seems to keep from knocking - releases fairly easily. [Pause.] It doesn't appear to be sticking at all.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. I guess that's what we really wanted to know about it.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: 14, Houston. If you could - on the TV pictures - refrain from using the flashlight in close here, I think we've got enough light to - to see it with the ambient light.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Maybe you do. We don't seem to.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. We got 30 seconds to handover; so we're going to - just go into a standby mode here for a minute or so until Honeysuckle picks up.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: And, Ed, now that you've got the capture latches in the Locked position out there on the end of the probe, we'd like you to push as hard as you conveniently can in zero-g on each of the capture latches and verify that they do not depress.

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Right. We've done that. We'll do it again, and they don't.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Houston, they're not going to go in that way.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. They shouldn't. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay, 14. Now we'd like you, using tool B or some other suitable tool, to depress the capture latch release button in the end of the probe there to cock the capture latches.

a14-0112231.speaker: Shepard
a14-0112231.text: Roger. Stand by.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0112231.text: Our Network controller reports that we are now getting a television signal from the station at Honeysuckle Creek, Australia.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Houston, we can cock the capture - capture latches by pressing in the button on the end of it.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Roger. And now that you've got the drogue out, we'd like you to position the drogue and push it over the capture latches until the capture latch release button extends; and, I guess we'd like you to do this several times and try applying different combinations of offset, side load, and torque on the thing, and check it up for any indications of dragging, binding, or anything it might be giving the problem that you experienced a few hours ago. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay. Say again now how you would like - like us to cock the capture launches in the way we just did by depressing the button on the end of the probe. And then fitting it over - into the drogue several times and repeat this operation. Is that correct?

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: That's correct. If you put the probe in a fixed place and then put the drogue over it, you could sight in through the hole on the end of the drogue and keep a good eye on things.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Roger; understand. [Long pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: 14; and, one of these times when you have the drogue on over the end of the probe, you might try just holding the drogue in position and wiggling the capture latch release button in and out several times. In this condition, it won't do anything but it will allow you to assess the possibilities of binding or sticking of that particular part of the mechanism. [Pause.]

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Okay, Houston.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: Houston, I'm going to get rid of the TV camera for a minute. It's not doing us any good and it's taking all three of us to handle it.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay. Roger.

a14-0112231.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0112231.text: And it appears we may have to get on the LM side to do this. There's not quite enough room here to work.

a14-0112231.speaker: McCandless
a14-0112231.text: Okay.

a14-0115615.speaker: McCandless
a14-0115615.text: Ed, this is Houston. Have you had any - luck, I guess you could call it - in getting the probe and drogue to bind by applying lateral forces to the drogue?

a14-0115615.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0115615.text: Not yet. Stand by; we're getting ready to try it again now.

a14-0115615.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0115615.text: Hey, Bruce, there just wasn't any place that worked handily with that. We're going to put the drogue back in - Al's on the other side - and then we can put it up in there right.

a14-0115615.speaker: McCandless
a14-0115615.text: Okay. By the other side, do you mean over in the LM ?

a14-0120038.speaker: Roosa
a14-0120038.text: Okay, Bruce. We cycled it - oh, about four or five times, and it goes in just so easily. The capture latches dock and hold it, and we've tried it by putting the capture latch release handle at 150 and putting it up and they move in. We've tried it by leaving it - you know, the yellow - and cocking them by pushing in on the end of the probe on the probe release plunger. And it works both ways, just real fine.

a14-0120038.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120038.text: So, what you're trying to tell me is you still haven't come up with anything that would be the problem.

a14-0120038.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120038.text: Would you pass over to Al that, while you've got the probe and drogue in the tunnel there and mated - He's on the other side - and keeping them engaged, would he push the capture latch release button in and out several times and see if he can make it stick up against the bushing by pushing sideways, or anything of that sort, on it while it's being pushed in and out.

a14-0120447.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120447.text: 14, this is Houston. While you're up there in the tunnel, we'd like to get a roll angle read-out on - from the index mark as you come back through; and, with respect to further procedures, I guess we got a - a write-in comment down here which is a step that says further instructions will follow tomorrow. [Pause.]

a14-0120447.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0120447.text: Didn't quite understand all that, Bruce. But try it, try us again.

a14-0120447.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120447.text: Okay, we're asking for a docking tunnel roll index reading at your convenience, and...

a14-0120447.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120447.text: You've exhausted our imaginations for right now on troubleshooting the probe. We'll work on it some more overnight and be back with you in the morning.

a14-0120447.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120447.text: And would you confirm that Al was unsuccessful in getting the capture latch release button to bind up against that bushing in the end of the probe?

a14-0120447.speaker: Roosa
a14-0120447.text: That's a - that's a negative, Bruce. We've cycled it several times; and he pushed on it and tried to jimmy it; and we - The thing slides in just so easily and locks up; and, when he pushes on the - on the plunger, why she releases very easily; and we can't seem to find any bind or get it to malfunction for us at all. [Long pause.]

a14-0120447.speaker: McCandless
a14-0120447.text: Okay. Well, holding the - holding the probe in place there, we were wanting him to just take and cycle the capture latch release button in and out several times, trying to - doing his best to bind it up against anything he can find there in the way of the internal surface of the bushing. I guess you're telling me that he was unable to.

a14-0120447.speaker: Roosa
a14-0120447.text: Okay. Well, we hadn't really run that specific test. We'll try that.

a14-0121112.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0121112.text: Houston, we're bringing Al back through. We cannot force it to malfunction at all. So, you'll have to think about it overnight.

a14-0121112.speaker: McCandless
a14-0121112.text: Roger, 14. We'll do that. We recommend that after you get Al back on the Command Module side, you reinstall the drogue and the Command Module hatch and keep the probe over in the Command Module. We believe we've seen enough TV data for the time being, so you can shut down the television at your convenience. And we would like to get photographic documentation of the capture latch release button, of each capture latch hook, and of any areas of scratches or visual damage on the probe, Ed. [Pause.]

a14-0121112.speaker: Roosa
a14-0121112.text: And, Houston, the docking roll index is plus 0.9.

a14-0121112.speaker: McCandless
a14-0121112.text: And, Stu; this is Houston. You're cleared to start getting set up for a PTC at your convenience. We'll be watching the rates; and, on this first PTC initiation, we'll probably want to go very close to the full 20 minutes of rate damping, although we expect that on subsequent ones during the mission, we'll have a better feel for it and just be able to cue you as to when to initiate the roll based on the rates that we're observing. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0121112.speaker: Roosa
a14-0121112.text: Okay, understand. And we don't mind waiting 20 minutes.

a14-0121112.speaker: McCandless
a14-0121112.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. When you do close the hatch in the LM , we'd like you to give us a mark so we may confirm the Floodlights, Off, over.

a14-0121112.speaker: McCandless
a14-0121112.text: Roger. We weren't intending to rush you on it. Just when it happens, give us a yell.

a14-0121112.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0121112.text: This is Apollo Control at 12 hours, 20 minutes. We're in the process now of handing over shifts. Flight Director Gerry Griffin and his team of flight controllers coming on now to replace Flight Director Milton Windler. During the shift that is just ending, the Windler team came on just after the Apollo 14 crew had successfully completed docking on the sixth attempt. That occurred at Ground Elapsed Time of 4 hours, 56 minutes, 46 seconds. And following that, the Saturn S-IVB was successfully configured for the Auxiliary Propulsion System evasive maneuver and the subsequent LOX dump and midcours

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: I've got a comm configuration for you to set up in here for PTC .

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: Okay. You can set the High Gain Pitch and Yaw indicators to Pitch, minus 52; and Yaw, 270 degrees and then select Omni Bravo.

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: Okay. And then Track to Manual, and Wide Beamwidth.

a14-0123108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0123108.text: Rog, Freddo. We were busy with the probe at 11 hours, and we're inquiring about turning off the waste storage vent valve and shifting our heater configuration on the O 2 tanks. [Long pause.]

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: Okay, Ed. Waste Storage Vent can go to Close and on the heater configuration, 1 and 2, to Off; 3 to Auto.

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: Did you all by chance vent the batteries back at 11 hours, then?

a14-0123108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0123108.text: Neg, Fred. I'm getting ready to do that now.

a14-0123108.speaker: Haise
a14-0123108.text: Okay, Ed. I was going to suggest you do that before we get the PTC , so we get all that closed up.

a14-0124619.speaker: Roosa
a14-0124619.text: Okay, Fred. Al's closed the LM hatch and he verified the floodlights went out - Went out before the hatch closed.

a14-0124619.speaker: Haise
a14-0124619.text: Okay. They say they saw it here on the power...

a14-0124619.speaker: Roosa
a14-0124619.text: That may have been - Say again.

a14-0124619.speaker: Haise
a14-0124619.text: They saw it down here, too, on the power, I guess.

a14-0124619.speaker: Roosa
a14-0124619.text: Okay. And I'd like to clarify one thing. Seemed like Bruce implied that we would keep the probe in - in here with us, and we'd just like to store it in the - in the drogue for the night. It's so easy just to open the hatch and get it back out again if we want to dissect it tomorrow or something. [Long pause.]

a14-0124619.speaker: Haise
a14-0124619.text: Yeah, that sounds all right, Stu.

a14-0124619.speaker: Haise
a14-0124619.text: Okay, I'd like to verify that you have the Waste Stowage Vent to Close now. [Long pause.]

a14-0124619.speaker: Roosa
a14-0124619.text: Okay. That's verified, Fred. We're still venting the battery.

a14-0125635.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0125635.text: Freddo, the battery vent seems to have stopped at a reading of about 2 and a half volts. It dropped very quickly to that and it's been staying there. Can you tell if the vent is complete?

a14-0125635.speaker: Haise
a14-0125635.text: Okay. Did you correct that, Ed, and say 0.25?

a14-0125635.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0125635.text: That's right; 2 and a half units, Freddo; 0.25 volts.

a14-0125635.speaker: Haise
a14-0125635.text: Okay, 14. That reading will be okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0125635.speaker: Haise
a14-0125635.text: 14, Houston. Did you copy? The 0.25 reading is good enough, Ed.

a14-0125635.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0125635.text: Thanks, Freddo. And battery vent is terminated.

a14-0131108.speaker: Haise
a14-0131108.text: Okay. If you can give us Accept there, we'll pump you up a state vector and I have P37 block data for you.

a14-0131108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0131108.text: Okay, Freddo. Go ahead with the P37.

a14-0131108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0131108.text: I thought you were reading me a P37 block data.

a14-0131108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0131108.text: All right. Let's start over again. GET I .

a14-0131108.speaker: Haise
a14-0131108.text: Okay. GET I , 025:00; 4971; minus 165; 069:12. That's GET at 400K. [Long pause.]

a14-0131108.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0131108.text: How many are you going to read me up?

a14-0131108.speaker: Haise
a14-0131108.text: Okay. The next one: 035:00; 7548; minus 165; 068:35; and the third one is 045:00; 5725; minus 165; 092:58; and the last one, 060:00; 5242; minus 165; 117:02. [Pause.]

a14-0131108.speaker: Haise
a14-0131108.text: Okay. And remarks. The second through the fourth sets are, Ed, the 35-hour, 45-hour, and the 60-hour block data assumes a midcourse 2. [Pause.]

a14-0131108.speaker: Haise
a14-0131108.text: That's affirm, Ed. And we're still watching your rates here. We'll give you the word when we're ready for the PTC .

a14-0131108.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0131108.text: This is Apollo Control; 13 hours, 20 minutes Ground Elapsed Time in the flight of Apollo 14. The crew presently setting up the Passive Thermal Control drift rate of the so called barbecue mode of...

a14-0132000.speaker: Haise
a14-0132000.text: And, Apollo 14; Houston. You can go back to Block on the computer.

a14-0132000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0132000.text: Okay, Fred, and we got the hatch back in, and when I put the probe up for stowage, I looked again at that pyro cover that Bruce had asked me about before, and I can't see anything wrong with the probe anywhere.

a14-0132000.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0132000.text: Another comment by Stu Roosa on the continuing mystery of why the docking probe malfunctioned in the earlier attempts right after Translunar Injection to dock with the Lunar Module. Attempts to duplicate this failure in flight as well as here on the ground have been fruitless so far. The training model of the probe and drogue are sitting on the floor in the aisle next to the spacecraft communicator's console here in Mission Control. Meanwhile, the tests in flight have been postponed or suspended until after the rest and meal period for the crew of Apollo 14. The spacecraft is now 63,937 nautic

a14-0132000.speaker: Haise
a14-0132000.text: It looks like you quit moving around in there, Ed. The rates are down. I guess y'all can crank up PTC .

a14-0132000.speaker: Haise
a14-0132000.text: Just a reminder. You might make sure you've - brushed your teeth and all that kind of stuff before tucking her in there, before you crank up that PTC .

a14-0134057.speaker: Roosa
a14-0134057.text: Okay, Fred. I'm going to spin it up. I'm going to use B/D roll if that's agreeable with you.

a14-0134406.speaker: Roosa
a14-0134406.text: Hey, Fred, I guess we've already said everything we can to try to help you all out on that probe. We're sitting here trying to run back over. I want to make sure that we're not overlooking something that might give you a clue. And, when we did our docking, as - as I was thrusting plus-X and then Al hit the retract, he said the talkbacks came back barber pole for - a time period; you know, like a couple of seconds before - and then went gray again when we got the - the dock. Now I'm just tossing that in. I think we called that, but I just wanted to make sure we've covered everything. [Long paus

a14-0134406.speaker: Haise
a14-0134406.text: Okay. We - we had already gotten that, Stu, from your previous comments.

a14-0134406.speaker: Roosa
a14-0134406.text: Okay. I just thought maybe there in the rush of things, you know, we might not got it in. I can't think of anything else to - to add, I guess. [Long pause.]

a14-0134406.speaker: Haise
a14-0134406.text: Okay, Stu. I guess we got nothing else on the drogue/probe business. Just wanted to verify that you get the LiOH canister changed, and your PTC startup looks good.

a14-0134406.speaker: Roosa
a14-0134406.text: Okay, Freddo. We got the LiOH changed at, let's see, let's check the time; 13:07.

a14-0134406.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0134406.text: This is Apollo Control; 13 hours, 50 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. And that last exchange of conversation between Command Module Pilot Stu Roosa, and spacecraft communicator Fred Haise here in Mission Control. Stu thought of one item that perhaps he did not mention during the earlier discussions of the docking probe problem. It turned out he had mentioned them, but that had to do with the indications of some devices in the cabin called talkbacks. They're little striped devices that show through a little window and when they're still they have stripes, when they're spinning they turn grey becaus

a14-0135748.speaker: Haise
a14-0135748.text: Okay. You can terminate battery charge now.

a14-0140653.speaker: Haise
a14-0140653.text: Ed, for some reason, we're showing your PTC has gone out of the - gone out of the box, there; so in a bit, here, we're going to need to reinitialize, but would like to continue with the roll here until we get in good shape on the omnis again.

a14-0140653.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0140653.text: Roger. Stu [garble]. Wait until we finish this P52 .

a14-0141109.speaker: Haise
a14-0141109.text: Okay, whenever you get a chance, after the 52 there, I guess you can stop the PTC and reinitialize; we're in good Omni; read you now.

a14-0141109.speaker: Haise
a14-0141109.text: And, 14; Houston. We're not really sure what caused the PTC to diverge. It looked like a pretty good start unless you either vented something or maybe something continued to vent from a while back.

a14-0141109.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0141109.text: That's the more likely - we had a continuing vent.

a14-0141109.speaker: Haise
a14-0141109.text: Go ahead. And we got your Noun 93s.

a14-0141109.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0141109.text: Oh, gosh. Did you give them the torquing time of 14:12:50?

a14-0142553.speaker: Haise
a14-0142553.text: 14, we're having a little trouble with data dropout in your present position. We'd like Omni Charlie. [Long pause.]

a14-0142553.speaker: Roosa
a14-0142553.text: Say again, Fred, will you? You busted up on that one.

a14-0142553.speaker: Haise
a14-0142553.text: Okay, Stu. We're having data dropouts. We'd like Omni Charlie.

a14-0142553.speaker: Roosa
a14-0142553.text: Okay, Fred. Try us again real slow. You're - you're just coming in syllables.

a14-0142553.speaker: Haise
a14-0142553.text: Okay. We would like Omni Charlie, Omni Charlie.

a14-0142553.speaker: Roosa
a14-0142553.text: Okay, there's Omni (cough) Omni Charlie. How's that?

a14-0142553.speaker: Haise
a14-0142553.text: Okay. How do you read me now?

a14-0142553.speaker: Haise
a14-0142553.text: Roger. We were having some data dropouts on High Bit Rate there, Stu, and we - before we get ready to crank up PTC , we'll have you go back to Bravo then.

a14-0143354.speaker: Haise
a14-0143354.text: Okay. We're showing O 2 flow pegged high down here. Just wondered if you're getting that on board, too.

a14-0143354.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0143354.text: We thought we'd stopped all - stopped all of the venting, but we apparently are still venting somewhere we're not aware of.

a14-0143843.speaker: Haise
a14-0143843.text: Just a question. Did I understand you to say that you had checked, and you got all of your vents closed up now?

a14-0143843.speaker: Shepard
a14-0143843.text: That's affirmative, Freddo. We're looking right now to see if we can find where this is going. Stand by to mark.

a14-0144413.speaker: Haise
a14-0144413.text: 14, Houston. Did you change anything now? We're seeing the O 2 flow dropping off a bit.

a14-0144413.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0144413.text: Did you see any marked change? We just...

a14-0144413.speaker: Haise
a14-0144413.text: Well, it was up over 0.9 there, Ed, and it's down around 0.7. Gone back up now, though; 0.8 something now. [Long pause.]

a14-0144413.speaker: Haise
a14-0144413.text: Okay. Our - original thoughts were that it might be a 'ducer. If you haven't already done so, you might run through ECS MAL 1a and see how you come out of that one. [Pause.]

a14-0144413.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0144413.text: Well, Freddo, we can see the venting right now. We think we've got an actual problem.

a14-0144413.speaker: Haise
a14-0144413.text: Okay. What side of the spacecraft, 14?

a14-0144413.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0144413.text: Now it's coming out the port side.

a14-0145153.speaker: Haise
a14-0145153.text: Okay. We saw it drop off. I guess you cycled the Regs, Ed. So that would indicate the 'ducer's okay. You might check again the valve on top of the urine receptacle and make sure that guy is closed off.

a14-0145153.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0145153.text: Yeah, we're rechecking those now [garble] Freddo.

a14-0145153.speaker: Roosa
a14-0145153.text: Yes, Fred, I did that. And, in fact, I even closed the - the waste management dump just to see if Myrtle was leaking, but it didn't do any good.

a14-0145559.speaker: Haise
a14-0145559.text: Okay. You seeing any more venting overboard at this time?

a14-0145559.speaker: Roosa
a14-0145559.text: That's affirmative, Fred. I was just sitting here watching it - just - it - it comes in spurts. Just about 30 seconds ago, we got a nice splash, and there's some right now. Looks like it's coming, you know, from over in the area of the - of the normal dumps.

a14-0145856.speaker: Haise
a14-0145856.text: Gee, that oxygen flow looked like it had settled down there around 0.4, and then all at once it started - it jumped up again there just a half a minute ago or so. And, it looks like it's back down again. Did you all move anything else in that area?

a14-0145856.speaker: Roosa
a14-0145856.text: Yeah, Fred. We went back, cleaning up after that malfunction, and we had the Water Glycol valves Off and the emergency Regs, and Suit Demand; we didn't see any effect when we went through it. And then we just went and opened them up again, here?

a14-0145856.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0145856.text: It's settled down on our meter at 0.6 pounds an hour now, Freddo.

a14-0145856.speaker: Haise
a14-0145856.text: Ah, I guess we're happy with that O 2 flow you got now. It looks pretty stable, and the vehicle rates look okay to crank up a PTC again. We think we have got a handle on what happened except in - what really caused the first O 2 Flow High. Must be something you readjusted. [Pause.]

a14-0145856.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0145856.text: I don't know that we can have a good answer for you. Stu and I were just talking about. We think quite possibly the - urine dump is leaking. We got it cycled now and shut clear off. Let's see if that helps any.

a14-0150839.speaker: Haise
a14-0150839.text: And, 14; Houston. We'd like Omni Bravo.

a14-0151123.speaker: Shepard
a14-0151123.text: Houston, this is Al. We're going to presleep checklist now. We thought we'd drop off a little bit early tonight.

a14-0151123.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0151123.text: Houston, we're bringing direct O 2 valve, On, to pump the cabin up to 5.7 [psi] now.

a14-0151603.speaker: Haise
a14-0151603.text: We're configured down here to take the E-memory dump any time. Stand by 1. I'm going to check the - how the Omnis are. [Pause.]

a14-0151603.speaker: Roosa
a14-0151603.text: Okay, Fred. We ought to have you now. How do you read? [Pause.]

a14-0151603.speaker: Haise
a14-0151603.text: Okay. Loud and clear, Stu. Stand by 1.

a14-0151603.speaker: Haise
a14-0151603.text: Okay. We're ready now, Stu, for the E-memory. They're all set.

a14-0151603.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0151603.text: Houston, onboard readouts, if you're ready to copy.

a14-0151603.speaker: Roosa
a14-0151603.text: Okay, Fred, here comes the Verb 74. [Garble] 4. Now.

a14-0151603.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0151603.text: Okay. Bat C is 37. Pyro Bat A, 37.45; Pyro Bat B, 37.45; RCS A, 88; B, 90; C, 87; D, 91. [Pause.]

a14-0151603.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0151603.text: This is Apollo Control. The crew of Apollo 14 at the present time is going through their presleep checklist, a little earlier than scheduled in the Flight Plan. Spacecraft being tracked now through the Madrid tracking station of the Deep Space Network. The crew earlier had called and said they wanted to go to sleep a little earlier and prior to that, there were a flurry of questions back and forth about spurious high flow rate of oxygen in the Command Module, higher than normal that is, not excessively high, caused by some valve being open perhaps in the waste management system. Apparently it

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Houston, do you read 14?

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Houston, do you read 14?

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Go ahead, 14. [No answer.]

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Go ahead, 14; Houston here. [No answer.]

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Apollo 14, Houston. How do you read? [No answer.]

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: 14, Houston. How do you read? [Long pause.]

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Houston, do you read 14?

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: 14, Houston. Read you loud and clear.

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read 14?

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: 14, Houston. How do you read me?

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Oh, you're loud and clear. There was a lot of static and no reception on - I guess that other antenna.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Okay. We had to drop Madrid and try to reacquire there to get you back. Could you verify that you are on Omni Bravo there, Stu?

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: That's affirmative; Omni Bravo.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Okay.

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: And if you don't have anything else for us, we're about to secure here.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Stand by 1, Stu.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Just one more thing, I'd like to confirm the H 2 fans, Off. [Pause.]

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Okay. Well, they were on; they're off now, Fred.

a14-0153732.speaker: Haise
a14-0153732.text: Roger, Stu. I guess you can take the rest of the day off.

a14-0153732.speaker: Roosa
a14-0153732.text: Okay.

a14-0153732.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0153732.text: This is Apollo Control at 15 hours, 47 minutes Ground Elapsed Time and apparently the crew of Apollo 14 has retired for the night. That last conversation between Stu Roosa and spacecraft communicator Fred Haise here in Mission Control. The flight surgeon on the Gold team, Dr. Willard Hawkins, said he couldn't really tell yet from his biomedical data at his console who was asleep yet. He said it appears that spacecraft Commander Shepard is now nearing sleep status but he couldn't really tell. We'll take down the air to ground circuit and if there are any further conversations after the sleep pe

a14-0160207.speaker: Haise
a14-0160207.text: Yes. Right, Stu. One last thing. Looks like maybe an O 2 tank number 1 heater is on. Tank 2 switches should be number 1 and 2, Off; number 3 on Auto. [Long pause.]

a14-0160207.speaker: Roosa
a14-0160207.text: Okay. 3 is Auto, and 1 and 2 O 2 tanks are Off.

a14-0160207.speaker: Haise
a14-0160207.text: Okay. We'll leave you alone, now.

a14-0160207.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0160207.text: ...minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Even though the crew had been tucked in for the night, they came back with a short exchange of somewhat less than a minute with spacecraft communicator Fred Haise here in Mission Control. We'll play the tape back now.

a14-0160207.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0160207.text: This is Apollo Control. That wraps up the short piece of tape that was accumulated after the crew supposedly had sacked out for the night. Apollo 14 now 74,589 nautical miles [138,139 km] out. Velocity, 6,406 feet per second [1,953 m/s]. And at 16 hours, 7 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control

a14-0255755.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0255755.text: Good morning, how are you? Or is it afternoon?

a14-0255755.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0255755.text: I'm fine. How are you up there?

a14-0255755.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0255755.text: We're up and brushed our teeth and shaved, and we're just looking forward to a fine day.

a14-0255755.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0255755.text: Roger, Ed. We saw somebody get up and walk in his sleep and work the DSKY there about an hour ago.

a14-0255755.speaker: Roosa
a14-0255755.text: Just need to get a little practice, Gordon.

a14-0255755.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0255755.text: He just had a restless finger.

a14-0255755.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0255755.text: Okay. We've got a site handover coming up in about a minute and a half.

a14-0255755.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0255755.text: Roger. We'll wait for that, and then I'll go ahead and give you the complete propulsion checks and postsleep checklists.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Go ahead, Ed.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: I have some dosimeter readings for you.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay. We've handed over, and - I'm ready to copy here - postsleep.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Okay. Alan dosimeter, 16037; Stu is 01034; mine is 05038. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. We got Al 16037, Stu at 01034, and you with 05038.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0260206.text: Apollo Control at 26 hours, 3 minutes. You heard that conversations with - those conversations with the crew. The crew sounding alert and wide awake. The launch vehicle debriefing time will not be changed, however, it it appears likely that other events in the Flight Plan preceding that may very well take place at the leisure of the crew. We're at 26 hours, 4 minutes into the flight. We show Apollo 14 at a...

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Okay, Houston. I read you now.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. I think we rotated between a couple antennas there. Got you loud and clear now.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: For my sleep, I slept for about 4 hours straight and then another 2 or 3 intermittently, and I feel very good.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Now, about the same for me and feel like [garble].

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Al, this is Houston. You're very, very weak. Would you repeat?

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. I had a sleep cycle about the same for me. I slept soundly for 4 or 5 hours, and then intermittently for another 2 - and we feel excellent up here.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger, Al. For some reason, you're not nearly as readable as Ed is, and it sounds like - well, I guess I can't really say what the problem is there on - on your mike. You're getting a lot of - interference when you start and stop a transmission - I got no suggestion on what to do to improve it. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. How do you read this?

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: That's a lot better, Al.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. The mike was a long way away from my mouth. [Garble] Did you get the sleep report?

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: I think we got it. Four to 5 hours good sleep and a little bit intermittent after that. Is that about it?

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: That's correct. The general condition is excellent.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Al, you're still - breaking up. I really can't give you a good description of what - is wrong, but - you're just not very readable.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Okay. Stand by on that one, Houston. We'll work on it.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay, Ed.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: And, Houston. I'll go ahead and - start charging Bat A with your concurrence, and we have changed the LiOH canister.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. That's - affirmative. You can go ahead with that, and - also give us the - LM / CM Delta-P as shown at the 27 hours there, when it's convenient.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: [Garble]. [Pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: And, Gordon, this is Stu. How do you read?

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: You're loud and clear, Stu.

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Okay. I guess on my sleep I'll split it with you about half. I'll say I got 5 hours.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: My mattress was hard.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. When you're ready to copy, I have some words on - some changes we've figured out for the Flight Plan.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Stand by a minute. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead with your changes in the Flight Plan.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay. Before we start, one reminder is that - when you went to sleep, we didn't get any presleep checklist. If there was anything - out of the ordinary there, we'll - presleep report that was - and - we'll take any - Stand by, I'm getting some words from the surgeon here. Okay. Just disregard it. Just trying to - We'll need the - both the pre- and postsleep reports from here on out. Okay, on the Flight Plan, if you're ready. [Pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. We're going to delay the launch vehicle systems debriefing until 28 hours. And - the P23, which is scheduled at 28:30, we're going to cancel, which will save us some RCS . On - along that line, the results of the last P23 that Stu did, the horizon that he shot at was 28 plus or minus 5 kilometers, and - that's right on the preflight values so an update will not be required. And your average error for pointing error was 3 arc minutes, which rank is right in there with the best ever recorded, and - the expert gives you a pat on the back, Stu, and said it was an outstanding job. [Long paus

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Ah, Jove! Thank you, Gordon.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay. On with the Flight Plan. The Delta-V test and null bias check and the P52 ; we're going to delay that until 29:10 GET . [Pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. So far, I have that we do the launch vehicle debrief at 28 hours to 27 hours [sic]. We're delaying the null bias and the P52 at 28:10 until 29:10; We're canceling the P23 at 28:30.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: That's affirmative, Al. And - and then further after that, we're going to delay the exit of PTC until 29:55. And when we do exit PTC , go right into the midcourse 2 PAD attitude. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. PTC to 29:55 and then set up for midcourse 2.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger. And all other activities will be nominal, except - on the waste water dump - you want - We want you to dump to zero per cent quantity.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay. Dump the waste water to zero.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay. We have one additional question for the launch vehicle systems performance debriefing. We can either give it to you now so you can think about it, or wait until you get around to it to give it to you. Your choice.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: We will take it now.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay. The question is, you announced during the docking attempts that you thought the booster was maneuvering a little bit. We'd like you to expand on the direction of the maneuver: the type of maneuver, lateral or oscillating, or any other words to that effect; the approximate time the maneuver was first observed, whether it was before the first docking attempt, between the first or second, or if you can relate it to any other activity; any observed vents from the launch vehicle during the maneuver; and anything else unusual or unexpected that you noticed. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay, question number 10. Describe the type, direction, and the time relation of the booster maneuvers during docking, and any events that we noticed during maneuvers.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger; and I was just thinking as I read it that, on that time, we can probably go back on the tape and find out when you mentioned it as far as tying down the time accurately, and that might be easier for us to get than you.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay, that would probably help us; thank you.

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Hey, that - that's no sweat, Gordon. I - I remember the - the comment when I made it, and what the circumstances were.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Okay, Stu. I think that takes care of all the words they got for you right at the moment. [Long pause.]

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Go ahead, Ed.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0260206.text: Our LM / CM Delta-P is 0.3, and I'm standing by for a Command Module consumables update.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Roger, Ed. Copy 0.3. We don't have the figures on that update, yet. One thing I didn't mention is that - we are planning to do a midcourse 2, as is shown in the Flight Plan and that - we'll do it such that it will require a clock update as scheduled at about 54 hours and 30 minutes in the time line.

a14-0260206.speaker: Shepard
a14-0260206.text: Okay.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: It'll be a roughly 40-minute...

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Looks like we...

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: ...roughly a 40-minute...

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Say again, Gordon. How much?

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: It'll be roughly 40 minutes, and I still haven't got used to which direction it is. Actually, it's like - going into daylight saving time. It'll - move your clock ahead.

a14-0260206.speaker: Roosa
a14-0260206.text: Okay, Gordon. Looks like we get to send that T ephem update after all.

a14-0260206.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0260206.text: Rog.

a14-0260206.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0260206.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 26 hours, 15 minutes. The midcourse correction 2 is scheduled for a Ground Elapsed Time of 30 hours, 36 minutes, 7 seconds with a Delta-V of 71.3 feet per second [21.7 m/s] performed with the Service Propulsion System engine, and a burn duration of 10 seconds. This will force the trajectory to arrive at the Moon on time, on time Greenwich Mean Time, thus requiring the, the GMT lift-off update. We're at 26 hours, 16 minutes continuing to monitor; and we show Apollo 14 at 106,915 nautical miles [198,007 km] away, and traveling at a speed of 4,865 feet per second [1,483 m

a14-0262820.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0262820.text: Ed, I've got that consumables update now, if you're ready to copy. [Long pause.]

a14-0262820.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0262820.text: Roger. GET , 26:00; RCS total, 86; quad A, 85; quad Bravo, 86; quad Charlie, 86; quad Delta, 87; H 2 tank 1, 87.98 percent; H 2 tank 2, 85.7 percent; O 2 tank 1, 93.4 percent; tank 2, 92.6 percent; tank 3, 54.6 percent. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0262820.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0262820.text: Okay, I read back GET at 26 hours; RCS total, 86 percent; quad A, 85; B, 86; C, 86; D, 87; hydrogen tank 1, 87.98; 2, 85.7; oxygen tank 1, 93.4; 2, 92.6; 3, 54.6.

a14-0262820.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0262820.text: Roger, Ed. Your readback is correct. And we have had considerable discussion today about the docking probe. There are still four questions as a result of all these discussions that we would like to put to you - the crew. It'll probably take some discussion to answer them. There's no hurry. Don't let us interrupt breakfast there. When you're ready, we'd like you to take these questions and comment on them.

a14-0262820.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0262820.text: Okay, Gordon. We'll probably be through here in another 45 minutes, and we'll jump right into that one then.

a14-0262820.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0262820.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 26 hours, 37 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. We now show the spacecraft at a distance of 107,892 nautical miles [199,816 km], traveling now at a speed of 4,827 feet per second [1,471 m/s]. In approximately 20 minutes we will have a shift change here in Mission Control. The Maroon shift replacing the Orange shift of flight controllers; the Orange team headed by Pete Frank came on duty at about 19 hours Ground Elapsed Time. Until the last hour when Mission Control, in fact, received a call from the crew, Mitchell, Roosa and Commander Al Shepard had s

a14-0264959.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0264959.text: Say, Gordon, do you have any choice news items for us today?

a14-0264959.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0264959.text: Ah, gosh, I think you all been making all the news. I haven't heard anything very significant and don't have any good summaries for you right now.

a14-0265236.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0265236.text: I do have one story here, I'll read from the front page of The Houston Post, this morning's edition. The headline is, "Mrs. Shepard ate an omelette during docking problem." And the first paragraph is dateline Cape Kennedy, Florida; "Mrs. Louise Shepard sat in her motel room eating an omelette while her husband and the two other Apollo 14 astronauts worked with a faulty docking latch that for a time threatened their Moonflight." [Pause.]

a14-0265236.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0265236.text: She was sure calmer than we were.

a14-0265236.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0265236.text: That was Ed Mitchell who responded 'she was sure calmer than we were.' We're at 26 hours, 54 minutes into the flight. Apollo 14 now 108,668 nautical miles [201,253 km] away from Earth. The present velocity, 4,798 feet per second [1,462 m/s].

a14-0265236.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0265236.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 7 minutes. We've completed the Change of Shift handover here in Mission Control. Flight Director Milton Windler now sitting at the Flight Director's console replacing Flight Director Pete Frank. Our Capsule Communicator on this shift will be astronaut Bruce McCandless. At the present time Flight Director Windler's going around the room checking the status with each of his flight controllers and reviewing the overall mission status. Apollo 14 at this time is traveling at a velocity of 4,773 feet per second [1,455 m/s] and we've continued to watch that velocit

a14-0272015.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0272015.text: Houston, Apollo 14.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Apollo 14; this is Houston, your friendly Maroon Team on station. Go ahead.

a14-0272015.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0272015.text: Well, hello, Bruce. How you doing today?

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Okay, Ed. How about yourselves?

a14-0272015.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0272015.text: Great, thank you. Bruce, these questions that are being proposed on the probe operation, should I copy them, or shall we just let you go ahead and talk about them and then we'll get back to you?

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Well, I think probably the easiest thing to do would be to start going through them one at a time, and, if you feel like you need more time to discuss it or to recall the exact things you went through, why we can just take the time as we go along. There's no big rush on it. It'd probably be easier than your trying to prepare a formal report or something and voice it down. [Long pause.]

a14-0272015.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0272015.text: Okay.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
