a14-0272015.text: And we're just finishing up the...

a14-0272015.speaker: Shepard
a14-0272015.text: We'll be...

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: We're just finishing up...

a14-0272015.speaker: Shepard
a14-0272015.text: It'd be a little while before we're ready to go that way.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Okay. We're just finishing up the change-of-shift briefing down here and it'll probably be 5 or 10 minutes at least before we're ready to roll on it, too.

a14-0272015.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0272015.text: That's good.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: Hey, Bruce, did you get a good night's sleep? You put in a hard day yesterday.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Yes. I got up about 1:30 or 2 o'clock this afternoon. Felt real good.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: Rog.

a14-0272015.speaker: Shepard
a14-0272015.text: We're happy to discover there really is a patch after all. We're constantly reminded of it.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: That there really is a what, after all?

a14-0272015.speaker: Shepard
a14-0272015.text: [Garble] is a patch.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Yeah, how about that; that's a beautiful one.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: Hey, Bruce, would you pass on to Ray that it was not 100 percent at the bench check.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: That's to Ray, that it was not 100 percent at the bench check. You mean the equipment...

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: [Garble].

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: ...equipment loaded on board was not completely represented at the bench check?

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: That's affirmative.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: We've got the backup crew...

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: I don't know why, but we...

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: We've got the backup crew commander standing here monitoring the system.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: We seem to be finding a few things around that we didn't see at our bench check and a few crew preference decals.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Yeah. How was breakfast, by the way?

a14-0272015.speaker: Shepard
a14-0272015.text: It was great. We ate every scrap.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: Hey, it sure was.

a14-0272015.speaker: McCandless
a14-0272015.text: Yeah. And I found my headset all right this morning, too, but there was a little difference from last night.

a14-0272015.speaker: Roosa
a14-0272015.text: Okay. You keep us posted on that headset.

a14-0274213.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274213.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Go ahead. Over.

a14-0274213.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274213.text: We're standing by for the booster launch phase discussion and the probe discussion any time you're ready to go.

a14-0274213.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0274213.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 44 minutes. You heard Al Shepard ask the CapCom whether or not we're ready to proceed with the continuing analysis of the probe, and we are preparing to proceed with that analysis. Last evening, on this shift, a series of 12 questions were forwarded to the crew after removing the probe in a preliminary analysis. We'll be picking up where those 12 questions left off, with a series of additional questions, and with additional Apollo program and NASA management officials here in the control center to participate in the evaluation.

a14-0274213.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274213.text: Say, Bruce, how far away is S-IVB from us?

a14-0274213.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274213.text: Stand by; I'll see if I can get you a figure on that.

a14-0274213.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274213.text: Yeah, and on the same subject, if you got any - say, give us a roll angle during PTC and some place to point the optics, I wonder if we could see it.

a14-0274213.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274213.text: Okay. I'll see if we can get that.

a14-0274213.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0274213.text: Among the interested officials here in the control center at the present time, who will be participating in this probe evaluation are Apollo Program Director Rocco Petrone; Donald K. Slayton, Director of Flight Crew Operations at the Manned Spacecraft Center; Sig Sjoberg, Director of Flight Operations at MSC; and Apollo 14 backup commander, Eugene Cernan. Also astronaut Tom Stafford has just walked into the control center and is at the CapCom console at this time.

a14-0274213.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0274213.text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 48 minutes. Apollo 14 now traveling at a velocity of 4,704 feet per second [1,434 m/s] and we show the spacecraft 111,159 nautical miles [205,866 km] from Earth. In addition to those officials here on the floor of the control center, we also have Dr. George Low, Acting NASA administrator in the viewing room; and Charles Mathews, Deputy Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight alongside Dr. Low in the viewing room. We have a series of four planned questions which will be asked the crew in addition to follow up questions I'm sure that their responses wi

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Go ahead.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger. We'd like to pick up the discussion on the docking probe situation now, if you're ready.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay, stand by just 1 here. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay, Bruce. I guess we're all hooked up and ready to go. [Pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: 14, this is Houston; go ahead.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Rog. I think we're all hooked up and ready to go.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger. I guess number 1 question would be, is - was there ever more than one bottle selected on the docking probe, and if so, which ones.

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: That's negative. We used primary one, and the only one we used.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger; very good. How many times was the Extend/Release position of the docking probe extension/retraction switch operated, and for when and about how long was it held in these positions? Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: Well, it was operated per Flight Plan for the initial extension, and the dock latch worked normally. We felt a jar, a good solid thump, but it went on out and then it was not operated again until after the problem started. At the ground suggestion, we went to Extend/Release and then back to Retract - I think twice - no more than twice. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, so - grand total, I guess we could say that you've had three cycles to the Extend/Release position; the one nominal one, and the two after the problem started developing? Is that correct?

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: Let's call it no more than four, Bruce. We did one of them on our own, so one normal and no more than three additional.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger. We copy.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: And, Bruce, no response at all except for the first one, which went normally.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, and on the first one there, you were actually causing the probe to extend, were you not?

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: That's affirmative. We extended it, and, as Al said, we heard her clunk in and the talkbacks did their thing, flashed barber pole and then went to gray, as advertised.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, then on the subsequent ones about all we'd be operating is the capture latch cocking motor.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: They probably wouldn't feel that in the form of a mechanical shock or anything like that. And...

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Rog.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: You may want to kick this next one around before you answer us on it and make sure you got all the details lined up. We'd like you to go through the procedure in as much detail as you can on the final docking, including the switch positions, talkback indications, the dynamics, the order of your contact with the - with the LM drogue, the plus-X thrusting, the barber poles, the bottle selection, and the actual probe retraction. I think you mentioned yesterday that you had a 3-second delay in probe retraction, and we'd like to know when that 3-second delay was measured, starting, that is, from th

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: Okay. I'll start off by saying that all the switches were per checklist. And, of course, those were one of the first things that we verified at - when the problem occurred, at your suggestion as well as our own. And - everything was normal up to the point where Stu made his first contact. I'll let him take it on in from there.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay, Bruce, why don't we just back up a little bit, and you - you asked for the specific one where we got the - the docking, but let's go back to the first one, and everything looked just real fine coming in on it. I'd say the - the whole docking operation was just so much like the CMS that it was hard to believe. I mean the - the procedures, and the view, and the response of the vehicle, and I'd say I had 2/10ths of a foot per second closing speed. And then, the reaction when I hit the drogue was just exactly like the - you know, the docking trainer that we had where you didn't hit the captu

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger. The one over there in building 5?

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Yeah. That's the exact response I got. On the first one, I - I clunked into it and - you know - and then I could tell that I was slipping out, and, of course, Al didn't call the barber pole. So, at that time, I did the natural thing and jabbed it with a little plus-X, and drove it into the drogue, and we were lined up good, holding plus-X and the - the alignment - you know - still good on the - on the target just like - you know - you can do in the docking trainer. Okay, and then I realized that it hadn't made contact, so I let her back off. At that time we called you, and I said, "Well, I'll

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Stu?

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: I came in, I'd say probably about a tenth, maybe 0.15, in that area, two-tenths, maybe a little less, contacted it and, at contact, the - the attitude stayed fairly good. There was maybe a degree and a half, 2-degree pitchup movement on the COAS . I then applied the plus-X and held it. At that time, I put it in the center of the drogue, and the COAS and the reticle and the translation were all just looking real good, and so I gave the cue to Al to retract, and he hit the Retract switch at that point. And then I'll let him take it from there. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Stu, before you press on, where in this sequence of dockings did you actuate the Extend/Release switch position again? Over.

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay. It would be after the second attempt. We - It was per your suggestion - the ground suggestion, and we went through the extend/release - in through there - No, wait a minute, we tried it ourselves after the second one, didn't we? [Pause.] Okay, consensus here is, after the first one, we went back to Off and then back to Retract. And then after the second one, we went to Extend and then back to Retract. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, and did you do anything with the Extend/Retract switch after the last unsuccessful docking but prior to the final successful one? [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: I don't think we did, Bruce. We did - We told you everything we did with that switch, after the [garble] first [garble] one time when I [garble] from Retract to Off and then back to Retract again.

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, now, in going through this sequence, did you ever move the docking probe retract, that is, the Bottle Select switch off of Primary 1; that is, did you recycle the switch or do anything in this sequence, or just leave it in that position once you'd initially selected it? [Pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: Well, we don't touch that switch until we get the capture latches. We stay to the Off position until...

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay.

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: 'Til we [garble].

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Roger. Copy. Okay. So we're coming up on the final successful docking here, and you told us that you got this 1½, 2 degrees pitchup on the COAS that looked pretty good. You applied plus-X and held, and I think that's where I broke in. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: Roosa
a14-0274800.text: Okay, and then on the plus-X then that - that brought the - you know - the COAS right down and the alignment - then everything was fine and translation was - was real good all the way except - except like I say, for that - you know - small pitchup - a degree and half or whatever it was, right at contact as the - as the probe sliding into the drogue. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay, and did you...

a14-0274800.speaker: Shepard
a14-0274800.text: And when - when Stu called out Retract, I went to Retract position on Primary 1. And it looked pretty normal from there. Just long enough - to - for you - to say to yourself, "Well, it hasn't worked." And then it went barber pole and gray and simultaneously there we got the feeling that we'd hard docked. So it's probably about a 3-second time period from the time I went to Primary 1 until I had the barber pole, and approximately a second later after that, to gray and the hard dock. [Long pause.]

a14-0274800.speaker: McCandless
a14-0274800.text: Okay. Stand by.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: Go ahead.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. Were you thrusting plus-X all the time from initial contact until the time that you got the hard docking? Over.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: That's affirmative, Bruce. Once I got her in the drogue - you know, we'd talked among ourselves, and we told Al to hold off until I'm thrusting and I'm satisfied with the alignment. So when we made contact and I thrusted and it looked like we were - Everything was good, and I - I held a positive plus-X all the way until we got the - the latches.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay, now. From contact, when you started thrusting plus-X, did you feel anything after the initial contact that would indicate that you'd moved on in and seated the probe in the center of the drogue? Specifically, do you feel that at the time that you selected Retract, the probe head was in such a position in the drogue that you should have already been in a barber pole position on the talkbacks? Over.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Well, Bruce, the - the probe was obviously in the drogue, but - you know - there's no way of knowing. But the feeling among us here and - my feeling is that, no, I don't think we had capture latch lock until after we went to Primary. Now, I - You know; I'm sure y'all have looked at it and you've got people down there tearing the probe apart, but I don't even know if it's physically possible. But I don't feel that we had any capture latches in that hole until that last operation when we went to Primary and drove the beauty in there.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. Do you feel like the - the probe head was in such a position - do you feel like the position of the probe head changed on you any after you went to Primary?

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: No. No, I was watching the - the LM - I was plus-X-ing and Al called "Primary," and we started closing on it and there was no movement; no. [Long pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. We copy. No movement after - after you started the plus-X and got yourself seated in there until such time as the bottle fired; that is, no - no more closing movement. Is that correct?

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: That's affirmative. As far as I can - you know - tell, we were there, thrusting, holding steady - Okay, do you read me, Bruce?

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. Reading you loud and clear, Stu.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Okay. And - you know, we got - We're sitting steady in the drogue, plus-X, everything looking fine. We hit the Retract switch and we start moving together. I didn't hear anything nor see any action until we heard the latches close.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. But while you were sitting there then - the talkback was gray and then 3 seconds after you went to Primary, approximately, it went barber pole and the nominal sequence started.

a14-0280525.speaker: Shepard
a14-0280525.text: Well, I was looking at the talkbacks, and that's about the only thing we saw as we pointed out before. About 3 seconds after the initiation of the primary contact - of the Primary Retract switch to the 1 - number 1 position, they went barber pole for perhaps a quarter or a half a second and then went gray simultaneously with the hard dock. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Hey, Bruce?

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Go ahead, Stu.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Okay. And on that one, we've sort of hassled this out. I guess it's something we need - We're probably going to get to, but we - Yesterday, you know, we called it a ripple fire and we felt like we had them all, which we did; but it really felt like the - the latches - we got a couple or, you know, it's hard to say how many; but we got some latches and then at some discrete time, maybe a quarter of a second or something like that; then we got the rest of them in a ripple. So, I think we got the docking latches in two distinct times, separated by, you know, a very small amount. But at least it w

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay, Stu. We copy that and I guess one last point on this - this final docking sequence. Did the closure of the two vehicles start when you selected Primary and continue for some period of time with the barber pole indication appearing during this period of closure, or did the flash to barber pole and then back coincide with the beginning of the closure for hard docking? [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Hey, let us talk about that one for a second, Bruce.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: Bruce, let me give you my opinion from the right seat. We're coordinated, I think, on the way this happened. I saw us move in as in previous attempts. We hit, moved just a little bit to improve alignment as the drogue forced the probe toward the center, and we started to bounce - it looked like we bounced - started to bounce back out. Stu hit the plus-X thrust and held it for what appeared to be right in the middle of the drogue with thrust. He called the Retract. Al hit the Retract, and a moment after that, it seemed like we started to move together. Al then called barber pole, called gray, a

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. We copy that, Ed. Thank you.

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: No. We did not [Answering Al or Stu]. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: And I wonder if you could comment on the thrusting activity immediately after contact for each docking.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Okay. As I said on the first one, I - was going along...

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: I think we're referring - We're referring more to the nature of stable - attitude control or stabilization thrusting other than the plus-X. I think you've pretty well covered the plus-X for us.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Oh, that's the only thrusting I did. That's all it took to - to align it. I did no other movements either with the RHC or the THC after contact except plus-X.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. We copy that.

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: Bruce, the probe was sufficiently close to the center of the drogue on each of those contacts. I believe that the marks that we pointed out to you on television yesterday represent the initial contact of the probe. It could not have been more than an inch and a half or 2 inches from the center of the drogue at that time on any of the contacts.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: All right. It looks like Stu was right in there in the center from what we could see on the - the TV last night on those contacts.

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: That's affirmative. It looked the same way out the right window.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: 14, this is Houston. In the process of making the docking yesterday, we advised you to check some circuit breakers, which you did. Did you at any time cycle any of these circuit breakers, that is, open and then reclose them? Over. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Okay. All we did was check them. That's the group 4 and the docking probe circuit breakers. I just checked them, you know, by pushing on them; but, no, we did not pull any and then push them back in.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. We copy. And that about winds up our queries on the docking-probe situation. We'll be ready to go on the - the launch-vehicle debrief here in a minute or so. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Shepard
a14-0280525.text: Okay, Bruce.

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Okay.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0280525.speaker: Shepard
a14-0280525.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Roger. Last night on the docking probe removal, after you took the preload off the probe, could you tell whether the probe head was, in fact, locked into the drogue at that time or not? [Long pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: No - I - It - it - it appeared to be, Bruce. I took the preload off. In fact, I think Al made that question and we both looked up around at the probe head to see if we could see anything that looked unusual about it or whether it looked like it was out or anything, and - and it did not. Everything looked - looked normal. [Long pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Could you - could you feel and tell whether the head of the probe was locked into the drogue or not? [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: No. I guess the answer to that would be we don't know. [Long pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: But now, I guess as you've realized, after I collapsed the - the probe, it definitely was.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Okay. You say after you collapsed the probe, the head of the thing was definitely locked in there?

a14-0280525.speaker: Roosa
a14-0280525.text: Yeah. It was hanging in there and I had to apply a little tug to - to get it out. I went right by the decal on the checklist, and I think you asked at that time about the force that it took to bring it out; and it appeared, you know, reasonably normal for the first time that I had done it in - in zero-g. It didn't appear to be anything funny about it. [Pause.]

a14-0280525.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0280525.text: Bruce, let's make it clear. There is no question about the capture latches being through the drogue. But the question of whether they were locked or not is the one we don't know the answer to.

a14-0280525.speaker: McCandless
a14-0280525.text: Right. That, of course, is the question that we were trying to get out here just now.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. At GET of 28 hours and 30 minutes, you are approximately 1,180 nautical miles. That's 1 1 8 0 nautical miles away from the S-IVB . If you'd care to look for it, we suggest you use a P52 program with a star code of zero and load the - the following numbers in Noun 88, if you're ready to copy.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Go ahead.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. Noun 88 values are 1, minus 31505, minus 87189, minus 37491. Read back. Over.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay. We'll plug in minus 31505, minus 87189, minus 37491.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. Your readback's correct and we'll probably, at the end of the launch vehicle systems debriefing here, have some more numbers for you if you want to - if you don't acquire on this first pass.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: And we're ready to press on with the debriefing. If you've got your Flight Plan handy, you can just proceed down through the questions, and we'll interrupt if we find anything that's unclear or, if you prefer, I can ask them to you in a panel discussion-type thing and you can answer back. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: We'll go ahead with the [garble] questions in the Flight Plan. Stand by 1 minute.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, Houston. On question number 1, regarding significant changes in the noise level, the only change in noise level that we noticed was during the first part of the launch on the S-IC , when we had the initial noise of ignition and the buildup in noise during Max Q . And, of course, the associated... [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, Houston. I think we're coming up on an antenna switchover for you. You seem to be fading down into the mud.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Are you reading, now, Houston?

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay. We're reading you better signal strengthwise, Al. We still seem to be getting a little bit of breakup from your comm carrier. Can you reposition the mike? See if that helps any.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. I have the mike right in front of my mouth right now. Is that better?

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. [Pause.] I think we better take it from the top again.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, from the top. The only significant change in noise level we noticed was, as mentioned, due to the burning of the engine in the atmosphere, that is, the ignition, of course, a buildup of noise there. And the noise level increased through Max Q , and then a drop off. Other than that, with respect to - to the noise itself, we had no problems at all in our communications at any time during the stages of the flight. Does that satisfy everybody on question number 1?

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: That's affirmative. Press on. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. Number 2. On the S-IC , we noticed no significant changes in noise level and vibration, other than what we just discussed. S-IC we felt was a real fine ride, nothing unexpected. The S-II , we noticed a change in vibration, a sort of a slight pogo, which started at 8 plus 40. Nothing of really any great magnitude. And on the S-IVB to orbit burn, we noticed no significant changes in the noise and vibration level. We noticed nothing unusual on S-IVB during TLI ignition. However, we did notice the beginning of a slight hum, low hum, or buzz toward the end of the TLI burn. That's it for numbe

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: We have no questions right now on that, Al. We're closing our loop down here with the Huntsville Operations Support Center, so it takes us a - a few seconds to a minute or so to get a response back. Why don't you press on with the question number 3? If we get any queries, why, we'll reopen the previous ones.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. On number 3, nothing unexpected in the way of transients that - on which we had not been briefed. As a matter of fact, it went pretty much according to the way we had expected it through all the events mentioned in question 3, that is, ignition and staging, engine shutdown, mixture ratios, and so on. We did experience a little more abruptness with the cut-off of S-II . The S-II SECO, I think, we [garble] a little more than we expected. Otherwise, everything was pretty much the way we'd kind of planned them. Question 3.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. Question 4.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. Stu is ready for you on question 4.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay, Bruce. I got a good look at that shroud, of course, station keeping with the S-IVB , and you couldn't see all of it; but, as we moved around, you could see a good portion of it back around behind the - the LM and every place that I could see and Ed also and Al - Al was looking through the hatch window part of the time, and everything looked just tight as a drum. We saw no loose pieces of the shroud anywhere. Nothing out of the ordinary, and after Sep - as the - I mean after ejection and the booster came into view - came into my window pretty much of a head-on view, and we were out a litt

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. We copy.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay. Going on to - going on to number 5. We experienced good communications throughout the entire powered flight and launch. We've been able to hear the ground on all the calls, and we had no comm problems at all.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: [Under McCandless] How about you, Jim? Any comm problems from us?

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: How about you, Jim? Any comm problems from us?

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Negative. We experienced no comm problems. [Pause]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, question number 6. Was there visible venting? Stu, do you want to take over, now?

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay. We didn't see any - anything unusual other than those that you called; and when you called the venting while we were station keeping, well, of course, it came on, rather beautiful sight. And the only other thing was when you gave a mark for the APS evasive burn, why, I noticed the booster venting and it appeared to be the same area as it had been venting during the station keeping phase; and the answer came back that that was expected, and so forth; and that was the only thing out of the ordinary. Other than that, everything was fine and all the other vents you called. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay, on to number 7. And I guess that one may still be open.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Yes, I was just trying to whip off a fast answer for you on that one, but we don't have any. So I guess that Al will tell you the last time that we - we saw it.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Well, I guess the last time we saw the S-IVB was with the eyeball, naked that is, and it was during the propulsion venting. It was kind of a tough angle for us to see because of - it was just very low on the edge of the window number 1. However, the Sun angle on it was good; it was stable when it was venting, as near as I could tell, approximately, a couple of miles away. We took a few pictures of it with the Hasselblad, so we may be able to see the beautiful conical-shaped pattern coming from the venting; but as far as control was concerned, it was going in the right direction and appeared to

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. We copy. [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, number 8. Stu, you want to take that one?

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay, I guess the guidance obviously was good and the velocity was - was real fine. It looked like, during the - during the boost phase, they were running a - maybe 2, 2½ miles, maybe 3 miles low along my profile, looked rather consistent; but we obviously arrived at the right place, so the - and the velocity cut-offs were right on the money and the TLI guidance, I think, was within 10 feet, 17, or something like that. You've got the numbers, but it looked real good, and the only thing I can comment there was it looked to me like we were going into Earth orbit insertion maybe a couple o

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: All the way on the profile I should say. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.text: Okay, are you ready for number 9?

a14-0282554.text: Roger. Go ahead with number 9.

a14-0282554.text: Okay. The ORDEAL ball at ignition was as advertised at 8 and a half degrees. After ignition, went to the normal pitchdown, the ball settled down very close to zero; and, as the burn progressed, eased on up to about a plus-1 degree; then, slowly on back to zero; then, close to the pitchdown, just prior to - to the cut-off, and I would say somewhere around 2 or 3 degrees negative, that is at 357 and 358 on the ball, prior to cut-off. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay, and we've got one more write-in, Question number 10; and it's based on...

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay, I'll take that one, Bruce.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay, Bruce. That - that came from my comment. And as we were station keeping and watching the venting, it looked to me like the booster had picked up a little right yaw as - as I looked at it. I meant - moving left on me, but then I just mentioned, it looked like it was moving over a little; but then, later on, I decided that that was just the scatter of the two vehicle's deadbands because the IU - the S-IVB deadband all the time was solid as a rock, even during the venting. And after all that venting, when I went back to - to try the other dockings, I expected to have to change my attitude a

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay, Stu; thank you.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: And while the Huntsville people are closing the loop here, we had previously given you a Flight Plan update concerning your waste water dump at 30 hours plus 15 minutes, and our update was that you dump to zero percent. We'd like now to modify that to a nominal dump to 25 percent on the waste water. Over.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, we are now modified; 25 percent it shall be.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger; out.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Could you tell me about Al's comm? You mentioned some dropouts in EKG prior to launch. Apparently you're still not seeing those. Are they in any way associated with these voice dropouts you talked about today? [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, this is Houston. Our belief is that there's no correlation at the present time between your earlier EKG problems and the current degraded comm through Al's comm carrier. We would like to suggest when you have the chance that Al try using the spare comm carrier, and see if that improves communications.

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Okay, we'll shift over.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, this is Houston. We've received some inquiries regarding your answer to question number 2. The Huntsville Operations people would like to get a little more detail on the slight hum or buzz. Was it actually an acoustic or audible noise, or was it felt through the structure of the spacecraft, and can you give us approximately the time that it commenced and duration, that is, did it proceed until TLI cut-off? [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Shepard
a14-0282554.text: Stand by 1, Houston.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay, Bruce. I think the noise is kind of hard to describe, I guess, and maybe make ourselves clear, but it definitely was not an acoustic buzz. It was a high frequency buzz that we felt through the structure; and, I'd say, it probably started - and this is an approximation - say 2 minutes into the TLI burn.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay. And continued through the balance of the burn?

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Pretty much so, yes. Just about the same level. I wouldn't say that it increased any significant amount.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: I realize this is sort of hard to put your finger on. Is there any way you can quantify the level, or give us some feeling for how much of - how high the level was? [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: No. No, I think that's pretty tough, Bruce. In fact, you know - the - the burn was going so well and the ride was so smooth that - you know we - we had time to - to pick it up. I suspect that, you know, it was low enough level that if you had something else on your mind, you wouldn't even have noticed it.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Did this - did this just sort of start abruptly, or build up from the background, do you think?

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Well, Ed feels it was a buildup and I'm not sure. So let's vote that it was a buildup then. That seems to be a majority. And it just came on kind of slow and came up and stayed at low level and - and was there.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay. And the only other question we got back in is at 8 plus 40, this pogo-type thing that you mentioned was - Could you give us a little more detail on direction of motion of it and amplitude. Any more elaboration you have on that would be appreciated.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay. I guess I called out the time on that one in the cockpit. But, it was a pogo; it started to slip out that time because when I - when I felt it, I looked at the clock and it was not of... [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, Houston. We had an antenna changeover here and... [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, Houston. How do you read? [No answer.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: 14, Houston. How do you read? [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay. How do you read, Bruce?

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Loud and clear, Stu. How do you read me?

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Oh, you're 5 square. The static's died down, and - As I was saying, there was no question but what it was a low amplitude pogo starting right at 8 plus 40. However, the magnitude was low enough that it was not affected - did not affect any of our voices; and, you know, a fairly low level will - will do that, so I'd - I'd say, you know, it was pretty small. It was not of any concern, but picked it up just because - you know - thinking about pogo, I guess. [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Roger. Thank you. [Pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: And, Stu, did that last all the way until shutdown of the S-II , or did it die back out? [Long pause.]

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Bruce, I can't give you a positive answer; none of us can. My impression is it was there all the way, but that data really isn't a very good input.

a14-0282554.speaker: McCandless
a14-0282554.text: Okay. Thank you. I believe this concludes our discussion on the booster questions.

a14-0282554.speaker: Roosa
a14-0282554.text: Okay.

a14-0294317.speaker: McCandless
a14-0294317.text: Roger. And I've been asked to remind you that, in connection with the midcourse burn number 2, if there is stratification in the oxygen tanks, you may get a Cryo Low Press light as this is reduced. Over.

a14-0295142.text: Houston, 14. Have you finished with the uplink?

A separate computer processed the information leading to the automatic uplink, and they rounded down to 4.3. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0295142.text: Okay. Those computers ought to talk to each other.

The spacecraft velocity at that point was 4,779 feet per second [1,457 m/s]. We'll cross t

a14-0300600.text: That's kind of wild, isn't it? Noun 20 Enter. 281.2, 353, and 297.5. Okay. There's an Enter. Computer's yours, Leader.

a14-0301434.text: This is Apollo Control at 30 hours, 17 minutes. We now show the spacecraft to be in the proper attitude for the midcourse correction. I would like to go back over one point that perhaps got a bit garbled in the last report, and that is the effects of this maneuver on the trajectory. Without the burn, without the midcourse correction, the spacecraft, as we said would pass about 2,104 nautical miles [3,897 km] from the Moon. Also, its time of closest approach would be about 15 minutes later than desired. With the midcourse correction, we place the time of approach at the time desired which is 82

a14-0302719.text: 14 to Houston. We're in position, standing by for a Go for MCC-2 burn.

a14-0302719.text: This is Apollo Control at 30 hours, 35 minutes. Flight Director Milton Windler has just reminded his flight controllers that we're one minute away now from our first midcourse correction. That maneuver scheduled to occur now in about 45 seconds. The flight controllers here are monitoring their data and we'll be observing the performance of the Service Propulsion System engine and spacecraft systems during the period of this burn. Total burn duration again is planned to be about 10.3 seconds. It'll give us a change in velocity of 71.4 feet per second [21.8 m/s].

a14-0303500.text: And you heard Stu Roosa report a mightly good burn. No necessity to trim out the residuals with the RCS.

a14-0303500.text: 14, for your information, we showed the actual burn time to be 10.0 seconds. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0303500.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0303500.text: Our telemetry data - Our telemetry data shows that the spacecraft onboard computer...

a14-0303500.speaker: Roosa
a14-0303500.text: Hey, Bruce, that was really great. The CMS was never like that.

a14-0303500.speaker: Shepard
a14-0303500.text: Houston. At the end of the burn we're showing fuel, 002; oxidizer, 989; unbalance, 300 decrease.

a14-0303500.speaker: McCandless
a14-0303500.text: Okay. Delta-V C , minus 4.1; fuel, 100.2; oxidizer, 98.9; and unbalance is 300 decrease. Is that correct?

a14-0303500.speaker: Roosa
a14-0303500.text: And if you didn't get the residuals, they're plus 0.2, minus 0, and minus 0.1.

a14-0303500.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0303500.text: Our telemetry data showed that the onboard clock timed that burn at 10.19 seconds which is extremely close to what we showed on the ground, our reading being 10.0 seconds. You heard Stu Roosa comment that the simulator was never like this, a reference to the fact that the onboard guidance system controlled that burn almost precisely as planned. The Flight Dynamics Officer will begin at this point to gather telemetry data on the trajectory to compute a trajectory in order to determine what effect the maneuver had on the trajectory. This is a process that normally requires several hours before t

a14-0304416.speaker: McCandless
a14-0304416.text: 14, this is Houston. We've reviewed the chamber pressure and the SPS engine operation from this last midcourse on the strip charts, and it looks real fine. We'll have some more words for you - for you - later on the reconciliation of the burn times in tenths of seconds. We're curious as to what value you got with your stopwatch. Over.

a14-0304416.speaker: Roosa
a14-0304416.text: Hey, Bruce. What do the strip charts show us P C , two banks? [Pause.]

a14-0304416.speaker: McCandless
a14-0304416.text: We're going to have to convert from percentage of thrust to PSI, Stu. We'll be right at you.

a14-0304416.speaker: Roosa
a14-0304416.text: Oh, no sweat. Don't want to cause you any trouble. I was just curious.

a14-0304416.speaker: McCandless
a14-0304416.text: They're doing it anyway. Just, we hadn't gotten it accomplished for this burn yet.

a14-0304416.speaker: Roosa
a14-0304416.text: Okay. Just wanted to calibrate my gauge.

a14-0304416.speaker: McCandless
a14-0304416.text: You might check your middle gimbal angle, Stu, for the maneuvering.

a14-0305026.speaker: McCandless
a14-0305026.text: 14, this is Houston. For your information, when starting the PTC spinup, we'll use quads Alpha and Delta. Over.

a14-0305026.speaker: Roosa
a14-0305026.text: Okay. We'll use Alpha and Delta for the spinup.

a14-0305026.speaker: McCandless
a14-0305026.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Your average chamber pressure for this last burn was 100 psi even.

a14-0305026.speaker: Shepard
a14-0305026.text: Okay, the average was 100 even. Thank you.

a14-0311426.speaker: Roosa
a14-0311426.text: Okay, Bruce. I tell you, I'm sure not seeing what I expected to on this - dark side of the Earth through the sextant here. The angles that - that you gave me lined up the - the optics pretty much over on the edge of the dark side all right. But through the - through the sextant, there's still a lot of light coming in, and I - with that high-speed black and white, I don't see why we're not going to wipe it out. I - I guess I really expected to see pretty much darkness through the sextant here. [Pause.]

a14-0311426.speaker: Roosa
a14-0311426.text: Okay. And there's another strange thing on the sextant on this sighting, Bruce. We got a...

a14-0312034.speaker: McCandless
a14-0312034.text: Roger. We've been advised that there was some illuminated area of the Earth expected to be visible in the field of view for this dim-light photography. What we'd like you to do is to go ahead using the nominal angles; take your three exposures; and then, if it's agreeable to you, we'll have a new set of shaft and trunnion angles for you and you could squeeze off three more. Over.

a14-0312034.speaker: Roosa
a14-0312034.text: Okay. No sweat. I'll press ahead and take some photos.

a14-0312034.speaker: McCandless
a14-0312034.text: 14, Houston. In your original transmission, did you say that you could see any of the illuminated portion of the Earth through the sextant eyepiece or just that you had some scattered light coming in? Over.

a14-0312034.speaker: Roosa
a14-0312034.text: I've got quite a bit of scattered light. It's negative on seeing any of the - of the lit portion. I - Manually, you know, I've driven it over to the terminator and then the CMC pulls it back to the dark side. We're pointed on the dark side, but there sure is a lot of light showing.

a14-0312034.speaker: McCandless
a14-0312034.text: 14, Houston. Have you already mounted the camera on the sextant adapter? - or to the sextant?

a14-0312034.speaker: Roosa
a14-0312034.text: That's affirmative, Bruce. I'm in the middle of the first frame right now, but it's no sweat to change. I can do anything you want.

a14-0312034.speaker: McCandless
a14-0312034.text: No, no. Don't do that, because we'd have to squeeze off more film at that 24 frame per second prior to dismounting it.

a14-0312034.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0312034.text: This is Apollo Control; at 31 hours, 26 minutes. As you heard, Stu Roosa is preparing to use the Maurer sequence camera, 16-millimeter Data Acquisition Camera aboard the spacecraft for the dim light photography scheduled in the Flight Plan at this time. Roosa will have the camera mounted or actually has the camera mounted at this time to the sextant of the spacecraft. He uses the spacecraft computer to point the optics in the proper direction, which in this case is at the Earth dark side. And he will take three frames, one...

a14-0312034.speaker: Roosa
a14-0312034.text: Okay, Bruce. I've finished the - the 1-minute, the 20-second, 5-second exposures, and I'll just hold here until you give me some more angles if that's what you want.

a14-0312034.speaker: McCandless
a14-0312034.text: Okay, Stu. What we'd like you to do is in your longitude over 2 for a P22, just put in minus 42.5, which was the - the value that was originally in the Flight Plan before we updated you and run three more exposures and that will wind it up. [Long pause.]

a14-0312034.speaker: Shepard
a14-0312034.text: Okay. We'll enter that in long-over-2 like it was originally in the Flight Plan and repeat.

a14-0312034.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0312034.text: That last comment came from Apollo 14 commander Al Shepard. Roosa took the first two frames - first three frames, one exposure at 60 seconds, one at 20 seconds, and one at 5 seconds. These pictures taken with very high speed black and white film, hope to show some of the phenomena on Earth that are visible only in very dim light such as lightning. And as you heard, Roosa will now re - repoint the optics and take three more frames of the same phenomena at slightly different pointing angle. Hopefully, one of the two angles will give a minimum of reflected light into the optics. That reflected li

a14-0313450.speaker: Roosa
a14-0313450.text: Okay, Bruce. I completed the - the pictures. I put the sextant back on and looked at our second one and it's - it's going to be just about the same.

a14-0313450.speaker: McCandless
a14-0313450.text: Roger, Stu. I think that wraps up the requirements for the dim-light photography.

a14-0313450.speaker: McCandless
a14-0313450.text: And just to clear up the situation that I created on giving you a quad Alpha Delta. We are recommending Alpha and Charlie for the PTC spinup and your option on the quads that you used for rate damping.

a14-0313450.speaker: Roosa
a14-0313450.text: Okay. We figured that's what you meant.

a14-0313450.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0313450.text: This is Apollo Control at 31 hours, 42 minutes. The Apollo 14 crew has completed the dim light photography scheduled in the Flight Plan. The next event will be to stabilize the spacecraft and then spin it up at the relatively slow rotational rate of 3 revolutions per hour. This is the Passive Thermal Control mode used to maintain the proper thermal stability - the proper temperatures of the spacecraft, exposing all sides of the spacecraft equally to the radiation from the Sun. At the present time we show Apollo 14 121,264 nautical miles [224,581 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 4,271

a14-0315040.speaker: Shepard
a14-0315040.text: Go ahead, Houston. Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0315040.speaker: McCandless
a14-0315040.text: 14, Houston. You can secure the High Gain Antenna at this time. We recommend a Pitch of minus 5...

a14-0315040.speaker: McCandless
a14-0315040.text: We recommend a pitch of minus 52 degrees, yaw of 270 for securing the High Gain Antenna. Request Omni Bravo for PTC . Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0315040.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0315040.text: Houston, this is Apollo 14. We're reading you loud and clear. Go ahead.

a14-0315040.speaker: McCandless
a14-0315040.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. You may secure the High Gain Antenna now. Pitch, minus 52; Yaw, 270. Request Omni Bravo for PTC . Over.

a14-0320236.speaker: McCandless
a14-0320236.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Stand by for an important announcement. [Pause.]

a14-0320236.speaker: McCandless
a14-0320236.text: Roger. You're Go for PTC spinup now. [Pause.]

a14-0320236.speaker: Roosa
a14-0320236.text: What would we do without you, Bruce? [Long pause.]

a14-0320236.speaker: Roosa
a14-0320236.text: Hey, Bruce. How come we haven't heard any news, like who won at Daytona and things like that?

a14-0320236.speaker: McCandless
a14-0320236.text: Well, we tried for one news summary and most of the news came out to be on the subject of Apollo 14. We figured you guys were probably the ones that had the inside scoop on that, so we'll give a stab at another one.

a14-0320236.speaker: Roosa
a14-0320236.text: Yeah. Tell us what's going on at the races at Daytona.

a14-0320236.speaker: McCandless
a14-0320236.text: Okay. Give us a couple of minutes and we'll have some word for you.

a14-0320236.speaker: Roosa
a14-0320236.text: Oh, no sweat. Just at your convenience.

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: If the workload isn't too heavy up there for you, we've got another set of Noun 88 values for sighting on the S-IVB , if you're interested.

a14-0322910.speaker: Shepard
a14-0322910.text: Okay, stand by and I'll copy them down. [Long pause.]

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: Roger, 14. Noun 88: minus 34293, minus 85901, minus 38013. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: Okay, Bruce, you back with us?

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read? 14.

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: 14, we're approaching an antenna switchover period here. Let me give you a call again in a minute. [Long pause.]

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: Hello, Houston. How do you read 14?

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: 14, Houston. Loud and clear. How me? Over.

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: We're back with you. How about giving me R 3 again, please?

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: Okay, R 3 is minus 38013. Read back. Over.

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: Okay; reading you back from Noun 88: minus 34293, minus 85901, minus 38013.

a14-0322910.speaker: McCandless
a14-0322910.text: Roger; readback correct. These are calculated for a GET of 32 hours, 45 minutes; but should be valid from the present up through about 33:45. You will be able to see the S-IVB when your spacecraft roll angle is between 85 degrees, that's 085 degrees and 020 degrees. If you do see it through the sextant, we'd like you to try to take some pictures, using the same techniques as on the dim-light photography per camera advance, same film magazine, the same exposure times, if you concur. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0322910.speaker: Roosa
a14-0322910.text: Okay, sounds great. I understand this is set up for a time of 32 plus 45:00, however, it ought to be good now and we ought to be able to hack it when our roll is between 085 to 020. And if we lap the big moose, we'll take some pictures of it using the same magazine and the same procedures as the Earth dim light that we just finished. [Long pause.]

a14-0323917.speaker: McCandless
a14-0323917.text: 14, this is Houston. Be advised that the S-IVB is tumbling at a rate of one tumble - that is, one 360-degree tumble - about every 4 and a half minutes, so that the intensity of the object may vary if you see it out there. And even if you don't, we've been considering the speed of the film. We'd like to take same pictures. Perhaps it would show up on photography if you can't see it with the naked eye. And another item, your phase plane plot for PTC - It looks like you've established a very good PTC here. It's curving back around toward the center. We think it's going to hold for quite some time

a14-0323917.speaker: Roosa
a14-0323917.text: Okay, Bruce; copy that. When we get around to the right roll angle, we'll give a Go on the S-IVB . Copy about the PTC , and we'll start a charge.

a14-0325451.speaker: McCandless
a14-0325451.text: Do you see anything out there, Stu?

a14-0325451.speaker: Roosa
a14-0325451.text: Well, we're just now coming out from behind the LM . Looks like I've got something here in the sextant. Let me pull her in the center and see what it looks like. [Long pause.]

a14-0325451.speaker: Roosa
a14-0325451.text: Well, Bruce, I've got two things in the sextant and - You know, it could either be a faint - faint star - I don't see any - any tumbling on them yet, but 4 and a half minutes isn't that fast either.

a14-0325451.speaker: Roosa
a14-0325451.text: Okay, I've lost one of them due to the light coming into the sextant. And I'm about to lose - lose the other object, whatever it was.

a14-0325451.speaker: McCandless
a14-0325451.text: And 14, Houston. We got a little sports news for you.

a14-0325451.speaker: Roosa
a14-0325451.text: Okay, go ahead. You're just in time for dinner.

a14-0325451.speaker: McCandless
a14-0325451.text: Would you rather I croon something soothing to you, like background music, or Ravel's Bolero or something?

a14-0325451.speaker: Roosa
a14-0325451.text: Negative on the music. We got all that we need here. You can just croon some good sport news.

a14-0325451.speaker: Shepard
a14-0325451.text: Why don't you hold on a minute and let Ed get his headset on?

a14-0325451.speaker: Shepard
a14-0325451.text: Okay, Houston. Everybody's on the line.

a14-0325451.speaker: McCandless
a14-0325451.text: Okay, I don't know if it was really all that Earthshaking. I've got the results of the Daytona races. It was won by Pedro Rodriguez from Mexico with his partner Jackie Oliver in a Porsche, and they completed 688 laps of the 3.81-mile course there at Daytona in 24 hours. Ronnie Bucknum and Tony Adamowicz were second in a Ferrari, and Lamak Donohue-David Hobbs team was third. In winning the event, Rodriguez and Oliver averaged over 109 miles per hour for the 24-hour period. And Sunday's Andy Williams, San Diego Open Golf Tournament, Californian George Archer took the honors with a 7-under-par sc

a14-0325451.speaker: Shepard
a14-0325451.text: Okay, very good. Thank you. Keep up the good news.

a14-0325451.speaker: McCandless
a14-0325451.text: Roger. You can tell Ed to take his headset back off now.

a14-0325451.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0325451.text: This is Apollo Control at 33 hours, 10 minutes. We're at a relatively quiet period in the Flight Plan. The crew is scheduled to begin a rest at about 41 hours Ground Elapsed Time. At the present time we show Apollo 14 124,800 nautical miles [231,130 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 4,149 feet per second [1,265 m/s]. The Flight Dynamics Officer reported to the Flight Director a short while ago that tracking seems to be confirming that the midcourse correction maneuver is bringing the spacecraft in a little bit higher above the Moon than had been planned. This would indicate a slight u

a14-0325451.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0325451.text: This is Apollo Control at 33 hours, 31 minutes. We've had no conversations with the crew since our last report about 30 minutes ago. At the present time Apollo 14 is 125,649 nautical miles [232,702 km] from Earth, and the spacecraft velocity is 4,121 feet per second [1,256 m/s]. We're preparing for a shift handover in Mission Control at the present time. And, we do anticipate having a change of shift briefing in the MSC News Center, Probably in about 45 minutes to an hour. Flight Director Gerry Griffin is coming on to relieve Flight Director Milton Windler, and the Capsule Communicator on the

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0333100.speaker: Shepard
a14-0333100.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Roger. We took up a collection here in the Control Room and bought a newspaper, and we got a couple more items, if you're interested.

a14-0333100.speaker: Shepard
a14-0333100.text: Great. Take up another collection and you might buy two.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Oh, we'll buy you a morning paper, too, a little later. On the Daytona race, a few more details. Reading into the article, Rodriguez and Oliver divided the driving chores up about equally ...

a14-0333100.speaker: Shepard
a14-0333100.text: Bruce, hold up just a second.

a14-0333100.speaker: Shepard
a14-0333100.text: Hold it a second.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: Okay, Bruce. Everyone's on the net now. Proceed.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0333100.speaker: Roosa
a14-0333100.text: Go ahead.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Roger. Back in the Daytona, it says that Rodriguez and Oliver divided...

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: 14, Houston. How do you read now? [Long pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Apollo 14, Houston. How do you read now?

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: Loud and clear, Bruce. Go ahead.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Okay. Let me try it once more with vigor. Back in the Daytona Race, Rodriguez and Oliver divided up the driving chores about equally, and had built up a lead of 213 miles at one point in the race. But trouble struck with about 3 hours left when the car's transmission failed as Oliver was motoring around with not a care in the world. Two Ferraris - the one driven alternately by Bucknum and Tony Adamowicz of Wilton, Connecticut, and another under command of two-time U.S. road racing champion Mark Donohue and David Gobbs of England had survived the long night but were out of it as long as the Por

a14-0333100.speaker: Roosa
a14-0333100.text: Damn. That's a - That's a good summary, Bruce.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Yeah. I ought to be a sportswriter. [Long pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: And that was very interesting, Bruce. And the next item here is a headline that says 'Apollo number 4900 to orbit the Earth. [Pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Unknown crew member
a14-0333100.text: (Laughter)

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: 'The Aerospace Defense Command has entered Apollo 14 as number 4900 in its records of Earth orbiting satellites. The ADC, housed inside Cheyenne Mountain, is providing NASA with information on satellites passing near Apollo 14 during its journey to the Moon.' Just thought you might be interested in that.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Well, they say always better late than...

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: As I live and breathe, it's Fred-ly! (Laughter)

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: It's better to be number 4900 than not to be at all (laughter). And, meanwhile, today at New York, "The doors of baseball's Hall of Fame swung open for seven old timers elected by a veterans' committee after the regular ballot of the Baseball Writers Association of America had failed to name any moderns to the shrine. Legendary pitcher Rube Marquard, who shares the record of 19 consecutive victories in a single season, and George M. Weiss, the executive genius who built the New York Yankees into an awesome powerhouse from the late 1940's, led the advance of the old timers. Also named were outf

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: And here's another startling bit of news - from London. The headline says, "Subway riders arrive; can't get out of station." "More than a dozen passengers were trapped in a London subway station for more than an hour early today when the staff locked up and went home." That sound familiar? "When the passengers got off the last train on the Bakerloo line, at the Maida Vale station in Paddington, they found exits blocked by steel shutters and the station deserted. Police were called and they in turn contacted London subway officials. A spokesman for the London Transport said it would investigate

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: Could happen to anyone, anyplace.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Also in the news is this other item from London. That D-day is less than 2 weeks away. They're referring here to the day when England changes to decimalized currency. "A government agency coordinating the switch says everything is going smoothly. 'Our latest survey has shown that since November there has been an incredible improvement in the extent to which people are familiar with the decimal equivalents,' a Decimal Currency Board spokesman said Sunday. On February 15, the new pound, worth $2.40, officially will become worth 100 new pence." [Pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: And the next on the agenda here. "Vehicles are called the top noisemaker." Dateline is from Paris. "Motor vehicles are the chief source of city noise, and only governments can do anything about it. This opinion is the result of a 2-year study by the consultive group on transportation research of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development." Incredible! (Laughter) "This problem is worldwide." [Pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: Seems like you two have a good handle on world events, important world events.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: From Lourenco Marques, Mozambique, this item. "Fresh floodwaters have poured into Portuguese East Africa's cyclone-stricken lowlands today, hampering rescue efforts for thousands of flood victims already marooned 4 days. The central government said 135,000 persons lived in the worst-affected area around Quelimane, administrative capital of the central Zambesia province. Only 24,000 people have been rescued, but Zambesia Governor Lieutenant Gen - Lieutenant Colonel David Ferreira declined to estimate the death toll." Good night, Fred.

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: Very good. Good night, Bruce.

a14-0333100.speaker: Roosa
a14-0333100.text: Tremendous! [Pause.]

a14-0333100.speaker: Shepard
a14-0333100.text: Very nicely done. Very nicely done.

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: We had to censor the best parts.

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: Say again.

a14-0333100.speaker: Haise
a14-0333100.text: We had to censor the best parts.

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: That's too bad.

a14-0333100.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0333100.text: There will be a daily showing, I assume.

a14-0333100.speaker: McCandless
a14-0333100.text: Oh, we'll see what we can do.

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Go ahead, 14.

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Hey, Bruce. I'm going to take some pictures of this S-IVB area this time around. Do you want me to have the two strips at 24 frames per second for 2 seconds and everything just like on the other sequence?

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: That's affirmative, Stu.

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: 14, Houston. If you feel like doing a little paperwork here, I've got an update to the inflight erasable load procedure as a result of the new PIPA bias and gyro compensations uplinked to you just prior to midcourse 2. [Pause.]

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Okay, stand by 1, Bruce. [Long pause.]

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Okay, Bruce, go ahead.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: 14, Houston. Page 9-4 in the G&C checklist, load A for Albuquerque. Under identification number 03, the old value is 77143; new value, 76674. OID 05: old, 00110; new, 00320; OID 07: old value, 76745; new value, 77417; OID 11: old value, 00477; new value, 006 - make that 00063. Read back. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Roger; readback correct. For cryogenic hydrogen management, we'd like to turn the heater in Hydrogen tank number 2, Off, and our calculations show that your pericynthion altitude is currently 67 miles. As the period of our tracking improves, we expect this to work down towards about 60 nautical miles. And we have a question for you. Have you noticed any cosmic ray flashes during your last sleep period or at other times when the Command Module was darkened? Over. [Pause.]

a14-0335000.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0335000.text: One at a time, Houston. You say Hydrogen 2 Heater, Off? Over.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Roger; H 2 tank number 2, Heater, Off. We'll call you when we want it back to Auto or On.

a14-0335000.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0335000.text: Okay, it's Off now. And yea, verily, saw a few flashes. I'm not quite sure what they're ascribed to; but, nevertheless, we saw flashes during the sleep period last night.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Okay, was this...

a14-0335000.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0335000.text: Unfortunately, we were a little bit - we were a little bit too tired to conduct any sort of measured experimenter data with them, but maybe we'll get around to that in the next few days.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Roger. One question, would you say that you were dark-adapted when you saw these, or did you see them before you were well dark-adapted?

a14-0335000.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0335000.text: I will speak for myself. I didn't start seeing them until after I woke up, 3 or 4 hours after going to sleep.

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Hey, Bruce, I had a comment I noticed on that last night. I'd wake up several times and I'd turn on the light to take a look around PTC and that O 2 flow that's been troubling us; and then I'd close my eyes again, and I'd see some flashes real soon after I had been looking at these lights. Now they were rather subdued lights, but you know - I certainly wasn't totally dark-adapted.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Okay, what sort of lights were you using, the floodlights or the integrals?

a14-0335000.speaker: Roosa
a14-0335000.text: Using the integrals mostly; on several occasions, I did have the floods up to check, and then I'd turn them back off again. And it didn't seem to matter much.

a14-0335000.speaker: McCandless
a14-0335000.text: Okay, thank you, 14.

a14-0340709.speaker: McCandless
a14-0340709.text: 14, Houston. For your information. The program alarm was a 404 trunnion angle greater than 90 degrees. No problem.

a14-0340709.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0340709.text: This is Apollo Control at 34 hours, 23 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Gold team Flight Director Gerry Griffin is being briefed by each of the console positions here, each man runs down the items that he has upcoming for this shift. The off-going Flight Director Milton Windler accompanied by his Flight Dynamics Officer Bill Boone, are en route to the Houston News Center where they will have a change of shift briefing for newsmen in the small auditorium. Apollo 14, very little conversation from the crew in the last several hours. Is now showing distance from Earth of 127,737 nautical miles [236,56

a14-0343333.speaker: Haise
a14-0343333.text: I wonder if you can verify for us that you have H 2 tank number 1 to Auto and H 2 tank 2 to Off.

a14-0343333.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0343333.text: This is Apollo Control at 34 hours, 36 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We're anticipating no immediate conversation with the rather quiet crew of Apollo 14; and during the period that the change of shift press conference is under way at the News Center in Houston, the conversations if any will be recorded on tape for subsequent playback. At 34 hours, 36 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a14-0344500.speaker: Roosa
a14-0344500.text: Okay, Fred. We just went through the Hycon and everything checked out real fine and we ended up with magazine W on it.

a14-0344500.speaker: Haise
a14-0344500.text: Okay. Copied. And, you ended up with magazine W.

a14-0344500.speaker: Roosa
a14-0344500.text: Rog. That's per the plan. [Long pause.]

a14-0344500.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0344500.text: Freddo, do they want these times - of these - at this point?

a14-0344500.speaker: Haise
a14-0344500.text: That's affirm, Ed. I guess they'd like the times and they'd like how many frames you used off the other Mag that was on there.

a14-0344500.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0344500.text: Okay. Mag V as in Victor. We started with frame zero and ended with frame 9, before resetting the counter. The LTC clock is on day 764 and 07:30 corresponds to GET of 34:26:42.

a14-0344500.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0344500.text: Say, Houston. We could play a lot of tic-tac-toe in the next two or three pages of the Flight Plan. [Pause.]

a14-0344500.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0344500.text: The next three pages of the Flight Plan are very bare. We can play tic-tac-toe all afternoon on those.

a14-0344500.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0344500.text: ...we just had lunch a few minutes ago; it's afternoon.

a14-0344500.speaker: Haise
a14-0344500.text: Yes, I have to agree with you about the next few pages. They do look pretty slim.

a14-0345250.speaker: Haise
a14-0345250.text: Yes, the photo people would like to know if y'all got the S-IVB pictures using the dim-light Earth-side settings there, and about when you did that - if you remember.

a14-0345250.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0345250.text: Stand by. We took some pictures. Whether we got them or not remains to be seen.

a14-0345250.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0345250.text: Those pictures were completed at 34:03:25, and they were on magazine J for Juliett.

a14-0345250.speaker: Haise
a14-0345250.text: Okay. You got them at 34:03:25 on Mag Juliet.

a14-0345250.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0345250.text: This is Apollo Control at 35 hours, 5 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. During the change of shift press conference some 3½ minutes of air-to-ground conversation was recorded on tape for playback at this time. Presently Apollo 14 is 129,338 nautical miles [239,534 km] out from Earth, traveling at a velocity of just about an even 4,000 feet per second [1,200 m/s]. Some of the major milestones, at least from statisticians point of view; halfway point in time between lift-off and Lunar Orbit Insertion will come at 40 hours, 56 minutes; at which time the spacecraft will be 142,119 [nautical] mil

a14-0351020.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0351020.text: This is Apollo Control. That completes playback of the accumulated tape. We're now live with Apollo 14, continuing to monitor the air-ground loop.

a14-0351346.speaker: Haise
a14-0351346.text: Okay. I have a - an LOI minus 5-hour flyby maneuver PAD for you that we owe you about this time. [Pause.]

a14-0351346.speaker: Haise
a14-0351346.text: You got the good book out, ready to copy? [Pause.]

a14-0351346.speaker: Shepard
a14-0351346.text: Start back with Delta-V T , please.

a14-0351346.speaker: Haise
a14-0351346.text: Okay. Delta-V T , 0396.4, and 0:56, 0391.2; 22, 211.7, 08.7. The next three lines are N/A. Then Noun 81 - Noun 61s are minus 27.86, minus 168.02; 1149.8, 36159. And the last item, GET .05g at 165:12:25. Under comments, GDC align, set stars, Sirius and Rigel, R align 230, P align, 170; yaw align, 002; no ullage. And the burn is SPS docked based on the PTC REFSMMAT . [Long pause.]

a14-0351346.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0351346.text: Okay, I think I missed two items sent over: the Noun 47 weight, and the H P figures there.

a14-0351346.speaker: Haise
a14-0351346.text: Okay, the Noun 44 is at - apogee was N/A; perigee, plus 0021.2. [Pause.]

a14-0351346.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0351346.text: Okay. On the LOI minus 5, SPS / G&N : 63526; plus 0.90, minus 0.33; at 067:59:31.54; plus 0382.3, minus 0104.3, minus 0008.4; 246, 208, 262; H A is N/A, plus 0021.2; 0396.4, 0:56, 0391.2; 22, 211.7, 08.7; boresight star, N/A; Noun 61s, minus 27.86, minus 168.02; 1149.8, 36159; 165:12:25. Sirius and Rigel at 230, 170, 002; no ullage. It's an SPS docked burn with PTC REFSMMAT .

a14-0351346.speaker: Haise
a14-0351346.text: Okay, Ed. Everything's okay, except two items. Apparently the one of us got our flip flops wrong here. For the attitude block, yaw should be 062, and the Noun 33 hours should be 076. [Long pause.]

a14-0351346.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0351346.text: Roger. The hours are 076; Noun 33; and yaw is 062.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Houston, 14. Go ahead.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: I just wanted to see if you all are still around there. You all been looking out the window lately back in this direction? Seen anything interesting?

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: No, I haven't looked out for a while. Got something interesting for us to look at?

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: I was asking you - if you had seen anything from that vantage point. Pretty dark down here where I am right now. [Pause.]

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: It's been an hour or so, Fred, since I took a look at either back in your direction or at the Moon. Let me see if I can see where you are now. [Long pause.]

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: Guesstimation on the terminator ought to be somewhere around India, Pakistan; somewhere in that - along that line.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Okay.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Houston, 14. We have the Moon out the hatch window right now, Freddo.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: Okay.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: And I presume then that the Earth is probably out the port telescope at this moment.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: I guess you'll have to wait about another 20 minutes or so for it to come up in the hatch.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Rog. Yeah, I suspect also it's down just a little bit too far for us to see.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: Let's see, how big a Moon are you seeing there? Is it about not quite a half or something?

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Rog. It's short of a half; and, for size, it appears about like an orange held at - short of - just short of arm's length. About - it subtends about a degree and a half now, a little less.

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: Roger. [Pause.] Yeah, and the board here has you at about 135,000 out now.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Okay, that'll make it slightly over a degree then, I guess. [Long pause.]

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: As you already know, Fred, the Moon starts to take on a little bit of brown - grayish colors about this point, as opposed to being so very bright as it appears from the Earth. You can start to see a little bit of texture here. [Pause.]

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
a14-0361139.text: Yeah, that's a good word to remember, that texture business.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: Yeah.

a14-0361139.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0361139.text: And, Fred, I have the monocular on the Moon now out window 5, and it - it's really starting to look very interesting from this point of view. [Pause.]

a14-0361139.speaker: Haise
