a14-0361139.text: And it'll look a little better in a couple of days.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Go ahead, 14. [Pause.]

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: I have the Home Planet out the hatch window now, and where did you say the terminator is?

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Oh, guesstimation is somewhere between the Sudan and the India.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Rog. [Pause.]

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: And, looking at your position, overhead here, you ought to have - Philippines - mainland, the Far East there, in sight.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: As a matter of fact, I do, Fred. There is quite a bit of cloud cover, and I'm having a little difficulty identifying landmasses. I'll be able to pick it up by the next time around here.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: And, 14; Houston. [Pause.]

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Go ahead.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Yeah. I was trying to give you a sunrise terminator there, Ed. I guess from your - I got some pictures here that tells me that what you're probably looking at is the sunset terminator, and that's running right through Australia and right across the coast of China.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Okay. Rog. That makes a lot more sense of it; I'm pretty sure I had the Australian continent down at the bottom of my lighted area, and looking up across the Philippines. And there's a great deal of cloud cover in that area, but there are a few islands standing out. I believe that I can see the southern tip of India standing out without too much cloud on it.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Rog. India should be right about at the - the edge.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Rog.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Go ahead, 14.

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Is there still a semisizable tropical storm off the east coast of Australia?

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Hey, I'll ask somebody about that one, Ed. [Pause.]

a14-0362135.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0362135.text: Part of it seems to be in darkness right now, but I seem to be seeing about half of a very large - circulating airmass.

a14-0362135.speaker: Haise
a14-0362135.text: Roger, Ed.

a14-0363046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0363046.text: The Home Planet's out of my field of view, now, Freddo.

a14-0363046.speaker: Haise
a14-0363046.text: Okay, stand by one, Ed. We've got kind of a bad comm right now.

a14-0363046.speaker: Haise
a14-0363046.text: Okay, I think we may be back on good Omni now, Ed. Go ahead.

a14-0363046.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0363046.text: I say, I don't have very much viewing time on either the Moon or the Earth. As it swings past the window, it's very low; and I - we only have just a few minutes on each window. But it's a most inviting and magnificent view. I'm very glad we have Earth as a Home Planet. I hope we can keep it so it's inviting. [Pause.]

a14-0363046.speaker: Haise
a14-0363046.text: Roger, Ed. Yes, again looking up at the big board I can - need to get about another 40,000 miles or so, then you'll be more directly in the Earth/Moon plane, and you ought to have them pretty much centered in the window about then.

a14-0363959.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0363959.text: Rog, Freddo. I'm watching - out the rendezvous, right-hand rendezvous window at the thermal skin on the LM . Right now - and it is in full-Sun outside my window - and I observed as the Sun came directly onto it [garble] bands of heat and then cools off and pops back into shape again as the - starts to cool off on the next cycle. It's - it gives a rippling effect as the Sun passes across it. It's very interesting.

a14-0363959.speaker: Haise
a14-0363959.text: Okay, I heard a little bit of your onset there, Ed, before Omni B got us again with the bad comm there. And, I guess LM -8 got built just like LM -7, because I noticed that same sort of a thing there.

a14-0363959.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0363959.text: Yeah. I guess that's what it's all about. The thermal protection - expands from the heat and contracts. And, this is sure doing it on each cycle.

a14-0363959.speaker: Haise
a14-0363959.text: With respect to your weather question awhile ago, Ed, they say they do have a weak cyclonic storm to the west of Australia, but they're not showing anything to the east; and I - maybe I misunderstood, I thought you said you saw it over by the sunset terminator to the east.

a14-0363959.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0363959.text: Rog. It appeared to be up by the sunset terminator, Freddo. A very - like a donut-shaped cloud but several thousand miles across. It might have been too large for just the tropical storm they're talking about. Couldn't be a very widespread circulation.

a14-0363959.speaker: Haise
a14-0363959.text: Ah, I guess they need to go look out the window down there, too.

a14-0363959.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0363959.text: This is Apollo Control 37 hours, 7 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Very sparse conversation coming from the crew of Apollo 14. This crew won't be noted for being verbose. Some gee whiz numbers on the mission: Present distance from Earth, 133,930 nautical miles [248,038 km]; velocity, 3,851 feet per second [1,174 m/s]. At 37 hours, 7 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, continuing to monitor air to ground as long as the crew is awake; this is Apollo Control.

a14-0373034.speaker: Haise
a14-0373034.text: Okay. We're ready to suspend battery charge on A.

a14-0390042.speaker: Shepard
a14-0390042.text: At 39 hours, the LM /Command Module Delta-P is reading 0.75.

a14-0390826.speaker: Haise
a14-0390826.text: Is Ed around with a headset on?

a14-0390826.speaker: Haise
a14-0390826.text: Yes. I'm not maybe clear on a question you had earlier about the ball valves with respect to time in the burn on MCC-2, but I do have some data here. And I think the crux of it is - is that if you use a cue of the ball valves visually showing full Open to full Closed, you'll be shifting your - what you're actually starting and stopping your clock by about a quarter of a second from the actual chamber pressure. But the total Delta-Time is very close. On that burn, you would have clocked 10.15 versus 10.2 via P C . [Pause.]

a14-0390826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0390826.text: Okay. You say had we measured P C we would have clocked 10.15. Is that affirm?

a14-0390826.speaker: Haise
a14-0390826.text: No. You'd have - from 90 percent P C down to 10 percent, you'd have got 10.2 seconds. And if you'd have started your watch with Bank A full Open to the Bank A needle showing full Closed, you'd have measured 10.15. Except in the time - absolute time scale, you would have started and stopped your watch one quarter second to the right. [Pause.] Because there is a lag in the - what I'm telling you is there... [Long pause.]

a14-0390826.speaker: Haise
a14-0390826.text: ...there's a lag in those needles moving by about a quarter of a second from what the actual chamber pressure is.

a14-0395047.speaker: Haise
a14-0395047.text: I know you'll be happy to hear that we won't have a need to do the uplink here at 39:40. The state vector looks in great shape as is.

a14-0395047.speaker: Shepard
a14-0395047.text: Very good. Glad to hear that. You're right.

a14-0395047.speaker: Haise
a14-0395047.text: We won't have to work that in this busy schedule here.

a14-0395047.speaker: Shepard
a14-0395047.text: Okay. We'll proceed to the next item.

a14-0395047.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0395047.text: This is Apollo Control; 39 hours, 59 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Flight surgeon just reported a few moments ago that apparently Lunar Module Pilot Ed Mitchell had unplugged his biomed harness and apparently was preparing to go to sleep. They're somewhat ahead of schedule on this particular item in that the rest period is not scheduled to begin until 41 hours Ground Elapsed Time, which is almost 2 hours from now. One hour from now, I beg your pardon. I don't see how it could be much quieter, whether they were asleep or awake, judging from the past several hours' sparse conversation. Apollo 14

a14-0401325.speaker: Haise
a14-0401325.text: Okay. The PTC is divergent enough that it's not going to make it through the next - this upcoming sleep period. So we'd like for you to stop at about zero roll, and we'll reinitialize. In the interim, you can do any venting or dumping you might have to do and - before cranking it up again.

a14-0401325.speaker: Shepard
a14-0401325.text: [Garble] cockpit at the moment with the food and everything. We'll probably catch you the next [Garble] around. [Long pause.]

a14-0401325.speaker: Haise
a14-0401325.text: Okay. Okay. And either zero or 180 roll will be okay.

a14-0401325.speaker: Haise
a14-0401325.text: And, 14; Houston. Who's the duty cook tonight?

a14-0401325.speaker: Shepard
a14-0401325.text: Ed Mitchell's in the pantry right now.

a14-0402638.speaker: Haise
a14-0402638.text: Okay. We'd like H 2 - H 2 tank number 2 to Auto.

a14-0402638.speaker: Shepard
a14-0402638.text: Okay. H 2 number 2 going to Auto now.

a14-0402638.speaker: Haise
a14-0402638.text: Okay, that's a heater switch, Al.

a14-0402638.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0402638.text: This is Apollo Control at 41 hours, 25 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. According to Flight Surgeon Willard Hawkins and here in Mission Control, the only one still apparently awake is Commander Shephard aboard Apollo 14 and he apparently is settling down into the easy rhythmic breathing of one going to sleep, but Roosa and Mitchell apparently have been asleep for some time. Apollo 13 - Apollo 14 now 143,114 nautical miles [265,047 km] from Earth. Travelling at a velocity of 3,568 feet per second [1,088 m/s]. At this time we will take down the air-to-ground circuit and should the crew wake up and m

a14-0413245.speaker: Shepard
a14-0413245.text: Houston, 14. We are ready with our crew status report and with a Verb 74.

a14-0413245.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413245.text: 14, Houston. Got a new CapCom now. Stand by 1 before you start that - report.

a14-0413245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0413245.text: This is Apollo Control at 41 hours, 33 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apparently not everyone is asleep up there, cause we had a call just a moment ago offering the crew status and on board read outs so we'll play catch up with the tape and go live as quickly as we get through the brief burst of tape. Lets go.

a14-0413245.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0413245.text: New CapCom referred to is Gordon Fullerton who is replacing Fred Haise at the CapCom's console. Some handover going on here in the room. Pete Frank being briefed by the outgoing Flight Director Gerry Griffin, who will be coming to the news center as soon as the handover is complete for briefing on God only knows what, but at any rate he'll be coming over that way. We're standing by live on air-ground at 41:35.

a14-0413607.speaker: Roosa
a14-0413607.text: Okay, Gordon. Fred made his comment before you left, I guess you're - wanting us to reestablish PTC before we sack out. Is that affirm?

a14-0413905.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413905.text: Roger. We're waiting for a good Omni to come up before starting that E-memory dump. One reminder is to complete all dumping before you - try to start the PTC again. And a question. With respect to the O 2 Flow High problems you had yesterday and any that you might have had since, we're wondering if you're doing anything - different than normal procedures as far as the - waste management overboard drain or any other - outside drains that control O 2 Flow High problem. Over.

a14-0413905.speaker: Roosa
a14-0413905.text: That's a negative on the - procedures. We're not doing anything unusual there. And, we haven't had any problems today. The O 2 flow you saw a minute ago was when we were pumping up the cabin to 5 7. And - as far as the ones that - we had yesterday, we really don't have that psyched out.

a14-0413905.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413905.text: 14, Houston. We're ready for the EMOD dump.

a14-0413905.speaker: Roosa
a14-0413905.text: Okay, Gordon. Verb 74, and coming at you.

a14-0413905.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413905.text: Apollo 14, Houston. We're ready to copy your crew status report and onboard readouts. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0413905.speaker: Shepard
a14-0413905.text: Okay. With respect to the crew status, it's excellent. We have a negative medical report. Bat C is 37.0; Pyro A, 37.2; Pyro B, 37.2; RCS A, 87; RCS B, 89; C, 86; D, 88. That was taken at 041:20:00.

a14-0413905.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413905.text: Roger, Al. Would you say Bat - C voltage again?

a14-0413905.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0413905.text: Roger. We copy all those. [Long pause.]

a14-0413905.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0413905.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 41 hours, 53 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. Our displays show Apollo 14 presently 144,049 nautical miles [266,779 km] away from the Earth and traveling at a velocity of 3,540 feet per second [1,079 m/s]. The change of shift has been effected in the Mission Control Center. The Orange team of flight controllers replacing the Gold team. There will be a change of shift briefing in the small auditorium of Building 1 in approximately 10 minutes. This would be a change of shift briefing with Flight Director Gerry Griffin. The modular space station news c

a14-0415805.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0415805.text: Roger. We're within rate limits and it looks like a good place to start the roll rates for PTC .

a14-0415805.speaker: Roosa
a14-0415805.text: Okay. We're going to hang loose here for a few minutes before we spin it up.

a14-0415805.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0415805.text: Stu, when you do get ready to spin up, let us know before you do, and we'll catch it at a good point to start it and give you a Go. Over.

a14-0415805.speaker: Roosa
a14-0415805.text: Okay. That sounds like a good plan. We want to make sure that we've got all the activity quieted down before we spin up.

a14-0415805.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0415805.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 42 hours, 5 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. Our displays now show Apollo 14 at a distance of 144,443 nautical miles [267,508 km] away from Earth. Velocity now reading 3,528.5 feet per second [1,075.5 m/s]. At this time we will take the line down and switch to the change of shift news conference. At 42 hours, 5 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0422840.speaker: Roosa
a14-0422840.text: Okay, Gordon. I think we're through with our - all our venting - for the present time. And any time you say, we'll spin up.

a14-0422840.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0422840.text: Okay. Stand by. I guess we want to wait here a little bit.

a14-0422840.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0422840.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 42 hours, 32 minutes into the flight of Apollo 14. Apollo 14 now at a distance of 145,367.8 nautical miles [269,221.2 km] and traveling at a speed of 3,501 feet per second [1,067 m/s]. Since our last report, CapCom Gordon Fullerton has had only a brief contact with 14, with Command Module Pilot Stu Roosa. We'll play that for you now.

a14-0422840.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0422840.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Surgeon data indicates that the spacecraft commander Alan Shepard, Stu Roosa and Ed Mitchell are still awake, but apparently getting ready to start their rest period. We're at 42 hours, 34 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0424135.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0424135.text: Apollo 14, Houston. It looks good now for starting spinup.

a14-0424135.speaker: Roosa
a14-0424135.text: Okay, Gordon, we'll give it a go.

a14-0424135.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0424135.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 42 hours, 43 minutes into the flight. That brief exchange of - of conversation between CapCom Gordon Fullerton here in Mission Control and Stu Roosa, the Command Module Pilot. We now show Apollo 14 at a distance of 145,757 nautical miles [269,942 km], travelling at an ever decreasing speed or velocity, now reading 3,489 feet per second [1,063 m/s]. We'll stand by and continue to monitor here in Mission Control; and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a14-0425544.speaker: Fullerton
a14-0425544.text: Roger. I'm sorry to have woken you up if you'd dozed off, but we'd like you to check the S-Band Normal Mode Voice switch, Off, and try to go on to sleep then.

a14-0425544.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0425544.text: Apollo Control Houston at 42 hours, 57 minutes, that was Al Shepard responding to CapCom Gordon Fullerton's call. 14 now 146,192 nautical miles [270,748 km] away from Earth. Present speed reading 3,476 feet per second [1,059 m/s].

a14-0425544.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0425544.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 43 hours, 32 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 14. We show the spacecraft presently 147,372 nautical miles [272,933 km] out into space and traveling at a speed of 3,442 feet per second [1,049 m/s]. We've had no contact with the crew of Apollo 14 since our last report. Commander - spacecraft commander Al Shepard, Stu Roosa, and Ed Mitchell now into their rest period. Our flight surgeon is presently monitoring data on spacecraft commander Al Shepard. His data indicates that Shepard is relaxing but probably not yet asleep. At this time we will take our live

a14-0505400.speaker: McCandless
a14-0505400.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a14-0505400.speaker: Shepard
a14-0505400.text: Good morning, Bruce. We're reading you loud and clear. We have completed our postsleep checklist. We have the readouts for you when you're ready to copy.

a14-0505400.speaker: McCandless
a14-0505400.text: Roger. Go ahead with the postsleep checklist.

a14-0505400.speaker: Shepard
a14-0505400.text: Okay. The checklist is complete. We have the following readings for dosimeter, Al, 16041, slept 5 hours; Stu, 01038, slept 7 hours; Ed, 05038, slept 6½ hours.

a14-0505400.speaker: McCandless
a14-0505400.text: Okay, 14. Understand. Al 16041 and 5 hours; Stu 01038, 7 hours; Ed 05038, 6½ hours. Over.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0510310.text: Good morning, Bruce. Go ahead.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. I don't want to interrupt your eat period, but when you have a convenient time, I have a [Flight] Plan update for you. It's a fairly lengthy one. Nothing in the immediate future though.

a14-0510310.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0510310.text: Okay. Stand by. Roger, stand by for about 5 minutes or so, and be advised we completed the LiOH canister change at 51 hours and the LM /Command Module Delta-P at 50:59, plus 0.95. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Understand 0.95 for the Delta-P at 50:59.

a14-0510310.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0510310.text: That's affirm.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Hey, Bruce, I'll take that Flight Plan update. Proceed.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay, Stu, here we go. You may want to just get out the Flight Plan and mark out the items as we go along, or you can copy it down, either way.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: No, I'd rather work on the Flight Plan. You give me the right places to go.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay. Up through 59:20, that's 59 plus 20, everything is nominal. And from there on, you take the LM / CM Delta-P vent at 59 hours and 25 minutes and move that up to 59 hours even. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, we'll move the LM /Command Module Delta-P vent up to 59 even.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. Take the P52 that occurs at 59:45 and move it up 10 minutes to commence at 59:35. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. We'll shoot a P52 at 59:35.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. At 60 hours and 20 minutes, you have a O 2 fuel cell purge and a waste water dump listed. We want to move those up to 59 hours and 50 minutes. That's 59 plus 50. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: You still with me, Stu?

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, Bruce, I moved the fuel cell purge. Yeah, I was just making - getting it all in here, Bruce. Moved the fuel cell purge and the waste water dump to 59:50.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. Delete midcourse correction number 3. Over.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Jolly good. We'll strike out midcourse 3.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay. Now, everything scheduled between the times of 60 plus 55 and 64 plus 10 should be scheduled 1 hour earlier. And if you look at 64 plus 10, the breakpoint there comes after the Verb 48, and we're going to have a write-in that says establish PTC there at 63:10, and the LiOH canister change comes at the nominal 64:12. Over.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. Let me...

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Well...

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: ...read this one again, then. Everything from 61 hours to 64:10 is moved up an hour. Is that affirmative?

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. Starting with the prepared transfer items per LM Activation Checklist and all that stuff.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, we'll move that up 1 hour. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. I've got that. Everything from 61 to 64:10, move up an hour.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. Stand by a second. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger, Stu. At the time of 63:10, following the LM housekeeping activities, reestablish PTC . Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, we're going to PTC at 63:10.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: And perform the lithium hydroxide canister change at the nominal currently scheduled time of 64:12, and pick up the normal Flight Plan timing and sequence afterwards. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. We'll change the canister at 64:12 on time, and then be back on the Flight Plan.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. And I have a 51-hour consumables update for you, if you're ready to copy back at 51 hours.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Stand by 1. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, let her rip, Bruce. [Pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: How do you read me, Stu? I think we're in the process of changing antennas.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: I read you 5 square. I'm ready to copy.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay. GET of 51 hours even; RCS total, 84 percent; Alpha, 84; Bravo, 83; Charlie, 84; Delta, 84; H 2 tank 1, 79.3, 79.7; O 2 tanks, 92, 91, 45. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, got you at 51 hours; total, 84; Alpha, 84; Bravo, 83; Charlie, 84; Dog, 84; H 2 , 79.3, 79.7; O 2 , 92, 91, and 45.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. And you may be interested in knowing that at the present time you are only 20 pounds of RCS fuel below the nominal; so, you're really gaining on it there.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: I'm sorry, Bruce. You - you busted up; would you start over again, please?

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. With respect to total RCS fuel, you are only 20 pounds below the planned RCS budget at the present time, and you are 2...

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. That's broken up pretty badly. I can read we are 20 pounds below nominal.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay, Stu, how do you read now?

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. I'm back with you, and I copied the 20 pounds.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. And that's really closing in on the nominal there. A couple of other items that came up while you were asleep is that we're going to go ahead and exit PTC for the LM housekeeping, since we want to have the TV up for it. And - we're going to go ahead and dump the waste water, anyway; or, wait a minute - wait a minute, I'll run that by again. We need to dump the waste water, which will ruin PTC ; consequently, we're going to come out of PTC for the LM housekeeping and have a good TV attitude to boot. One item is that I believe you went to sleep with 16:20 showing on the DSKY , which was c

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, and say that time again, Bruce.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger; 55 plus 00. Over.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, and we'll blank the DSKY .

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay. No need to blank it now...

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: For sleep that is.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: No, I understand. For sleep - for sleep we'll put it to rest.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger, Roger. [Pause.] And when you all get your breakfast well prepared and you're feeling in a jovial mood up there, why, we'll proceed with the Bruce and Bo show on the morning news.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay, hang on till we all get tuned in. We sure wouldn't want to miss that.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: It'll be a couple of minutes yet. We just got the paper here, and we're editing it right now.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Okay. [Pause.] [S-]IVB, Bruce; I was thinking about that - what you - I could see through the sextant. You know, I had two - it looked like two dim stars in the - in the sextant at that pointing attitude. And, I didn't see any tumbling motion at all on either one of them. And they were separated probably by - roughly half to three-quarters of a degree; I'd say 0.5 to 0.6 of a degree separation between the two, but I really couldn't see anything that would determine whether I was looking at the S-IVB or a star, a faint star.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Roger. We copy, Stu...

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: I really expected the... [Pause.] I guess I really expected the S-IVB to be a little brighter than either one of the two objects that I looked at.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Okay, stand by a second, please.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: 14, Houston, Stu.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Go ahead.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: Yeah. We've just received the intelligence down here that your family is having lasagne for your breakfast. Over.

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: Oh, man; that's - that's good timing.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: We thought you'd enjoy hearing about it. [Pause.]

a14-0510310.speaker: Roosa
a14-0510310.text: There's nothing better for breakfast than lasagne, unless it's a sausage-onion sandwich.

a14-0510310.speaker: McCandless
a14-0510310.text: (Laugh) Very good.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Houston. Apollo 14.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Go ahead, 14.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Roger, Bruce. I have a few observations about the light flash experiment that I'd like to pass on, and perhaps you can generate some information from it that might be useful to us.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Would you stand by a minute, please, Ed.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Okay. Standing by. [Long pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. Ed, go ahead with your commentary on the cosmic ray light flashes, and we'll digest what you've got and give you our views back probably in a couple of hours. Over.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Okay, Bruce. First of all, let me say we all decided to try to dark-adapt, and run the experiment, or at least part of it, last night. I think our experience was that we probably saw one flash after dark-adapting and promptly fell asleep before we saw any more. At least that's true in my case. I think Al and Stu stayed awake a bit longer. However, I think we have seen only three types of flashes so far. What we would probably call a star, a supernova, and a flash - or rather and a streak - and I think that I have seen some - I for - don't recall a name we tagged to them, but reminiscent of the

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Roger, Ed. I think we've copied all of that.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: I'd like to add a few - I'd like to add a few comments on that too, Bruce.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Go ahead.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Hey, Bruce. Do you read?

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Roger, 14. Go.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Okay, Bruce. I'd like to make - You know, you asked yesterday about whether we saw them before we were dark-adapted. So, last night I took my flashlight and shined it in both of my eyes; and, of course, you know, that should ruin your - any dark-adaption that you would have. And in fact, you know, you got the - the residual glow in your eye for a minute and then closed them and, in one case, in less than a minute, I had started seeing the flashes. And on the second time around, I'd say it's probably around 2 minutes before I started picking them up.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Okay, Stu. And were you seeing - when you started seeing them, did you see a number of flashes? Ed reported, I think he saw just about one before he fell asleep.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Well, what we did was we set the timer on 20 minutes, and I heard the timer go off and by that time I had only seen four or five flashes that I could recall. However, at some other periods during the night - That isn't when I did the flashlight routine; that was later on - more toward this morning when I started playing with the flashlight - and I - in one case, I saw one and then followed not too long after that by four or five and then - haven't really picked up any pattern on that. You may see one and then three or four, and you may see one and wait awhile. I can't really - it's a little di

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Okay. We're switching antennas, Stu.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: ...three types. However, my super - supernova, there's explosions in one, and very rare; I'll see a - a - a discrete pinpoint of light for a minute, and then the streaks I've noticed are all - what I would consider over at the periphery of my - of my vision. It - it appears that almost all the streaks are right along the edge of my eye, and I get the - get the impression that the majority of these are running, say longitudinal with the axis of my body. And it seems rare that I see a streak that's right - right in the center of my vision.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: This is Ed. I'm - I have had a little different experience than Stu has. I don't think that I have seen quite as many streaks as he seems to. But I have seen some that appear to be going from right to left, near the center of the field of vision. However, I have mostly been concentrating on trying to identify the types, as opposed to locating them and getting their frequency. I did observe one right after we started to dark-adapt, about 20 seconds. But nothing after that. And, as I say, I think I fell asleep sometime within a couple of minutes after that. [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Do we have any observations from the Commander?

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: No. He's busy cooking breakfast right now.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Oh, Roger. And I guess we just went through an antenna switchover; and we've got some news here, if you all are ready. [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Shepard
a14-0513826.text: I have only one comment. I think the echo of the other - on the light flashes. They do seem to be random, sort of a showery-type pattern. They are visible in a darkened cabin within a very few minutes after turning the lights out - probably as small a time as 1 or 2 minutes. And I've - as far as the characteristics of the flashes are concerned, I've observed about what the other guys have.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Roger. We copy, Al. [Long pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: 14, Houston. Are you interested in some news?

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Roger. Press on.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Okay. From the sports world, "Marquette's streaking Warriors continued to hold forth as the Nation's top-ranked college basketball power, Monday while unbeaten Southern California displaced defending champion UCLA in a runner-up spot. Houston, 15 to 3, is a newcomer to the top 20. The Cougars, who play Long Island U in Madison Square Garden, Thursday night, move into the number 18 spot. USC and UCLA will collide Saturday at Southern Cal." Too bad we don't have a TV uplink for you.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: It'd be pretty nice.

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: 14, this is Bo Bobko. How do you read?

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Good morning, Bo; loud and clear. How are you?

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: Just fine, sir. This is Washington, Associated Press. "The Food and Drug Administration said tests on compressed fish products such as frozen dinners, fish sticks, and fish cakes show mercury content well below the danger level. The FDA said Monday, 'More than 80 samples contained an average mercury level of 0.06 parts per million. Under FDA guidelines, fish with a half part per million is withdrawn from the market.'" [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Seems reasonable to me.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: "The chill blast of a February norther blew into Texas Monday, dropping the temperature sharply after the summer-like weather which closed out last week. January's last day saw temperatures in the 90s at several points in deep-south Texas. And it was one of the driest months ever back here in Houston - here in Texas. The Dallas weather station, for example, measured 0.16 - that's 16/100ths - of an inch of rain against the normal 2.32 inches for January." [Long pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: "The Rarest Atom Particle Reported Found." New York, Associated Press. "Physicists from the University of California reported Monday, they have discovered the rarest and most elusive of the nuclear particles within the atom. They found the particle's track in a photograph of a nuclear interaction, an inch-long footprint it left during its brief lifetime of 15 billionths of a second. The particle is called the antiomegaminus baryon part - antiparticle, the mirror image of matter as we know it on Earth. The discovery is related to the idea that somewhere out there in space there are galaxies mad

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Hey, Bo. I think I saw one of those just go by the window.

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: Grab it, quick.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Hey, Stu...

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: How long did you say the track was that - Bo - how long did they say the track was that they had seen?

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: "An inch-long footprint it left during its brief lifetime of 15 billionths of a second." They said. "We had a standing offer of a case of champagne to whoever found it, Goldhaber said. 'When I get back to the lab I have to deliver.'"

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Do you think Stu qualifies for one also?

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Aw, I let it get away, Bruce.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Hey, that's a pretty great piece of news.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Okay. "On Wall Street, investors bought heavily on Monday giving the Dow-Jones Industrial Average its highest single-day gain of the year. The Dow-Jones average of 30 industrial stocks closed up at 877.81, up 9.31 points, for the biggest one-day jump in '71. Trading was heavy throughout the session, with the New York Stock Exchange ticker backed up a minute or more several times during the day. The tape was 3 minutes late at the close." [Long pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: Washington, UPI. "The administration is considering a pollution tax, such as a levy on emissions of air-polluting sulphur dioxides, in an effort to give industry an incentive to clean up, President Nixon's Economic Report said Monday. The report, prepared by the President's council of economic advisors and sent to Congress under Mr. Nixon's signature, said a tax may be a more effective way to control pollution than direct Government regulation." [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: "At 9:03 tonight, the Apollo 14 crew will begin operating under NASA's own version of daylight savings time. The readjustment of the mission clocks will bring the flight back to the actual real time - parentheses - Greenwich Mean Time - parentheses - for activities as scheduled in the Flight Plan. At 9:03 p.m., the flight will be 54 hours into the mission. However, under the nominal Flight Plan, the 54-hour mark should have been reached at 8:23. To correct this, the crew will move their mission elapsed time clock ahead 40 minutes to coincide with the real-time clock." [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: This is by Francis Dodds, Austin. "A bill creating an upper level college at Clear Lake as a branch of the University of Houston has been approved by the Senate Education Committee. The bill, introduced by Senator Chet Brooks of Pasadena, would create the University of Houston, Clear Lake Campus primarily to serve six area junior colleges. A proposed 360-acre campus is adjacent to the Manned Spacecraft Center. The proposed college must be started immediately, Hoffman said, for two reasons. To be of service to San Jacinto Junior College, Alvin Junior College, Brazosport Junior College, Lee Juni

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: That's pretty interesting news.

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Yeah.

a14-0513826.speaker: McCandless
a14-0513826.text: Rochester, New York. "Brooks Robinson, outstanding player in the World Series with his glove and bat, was named Monday night as winner of the 21st Annual Hickok Professional Athlete of the Year Award. The 33-year-old third baseman of the baseball champion Baltimore Orioles won by a large margin over another veteran, 43-year-old George Blanda, quarterback of pro-football Oakland Raiders. Robinson, who hit 428 in the World Series and made a series of spectacular fielding plays in the five-game triumph over the Cincinnati Reds, received 62 of the 146 first-place votes by a panel of sports writers

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: I'm going home and have dinner.

a14-0513826.speaker: Shepard
a14-0513826.text: I thank you guys.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0513826.text: Still don't understand that bit about changing the time on the Apollo 14 crew. I can't figure what those guys are doing. [Pause.]

a14-0513826.speaker: Roosa
a14-0513826.text: Hey, that was a good newscast. You know you're pretty high in the ratings up here.

a14-0513826.speaker: Bobko
a14-0513826.text: Okay. Thank you. Appreciate it.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0513826.text: This is Apollo Control at 51 hours, 56 minutes. Helping out CapCom Bruce McCandless on reading the news there was astronaut Karol Bobko. And at the present time Apollo 14 is traveling at a velocity of 3,002 feet per second [915 m/s] and we show the current altitude, 162,934 nautical miles [301,754 km] from Earth.

a14-0513826.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0513826.text: This is Apollo Control at 52 hours, 2 minutes. We'll be coming up in the next few minutes on the bistatic radar frequency check. This will be a check of the spacecraft communications frequencies on the Unified S-band and the VHF in preparation for an experiment.

a14-0520200.speaker: McCandless
a14-0520200.text: 14, this is Houston. When you're configured in a suitable VHF mode for the S-170 bistatic radar frequency check, give us a call; and then, we'll secure the S-band uplink for about 5 minutes on you. There's no great rush involved in this.

a14-0520200.speaker: Roosa
a14-0520200.text: Okay. We'll start configuring now and give you a call.

a14-0520200.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0520200.text: The bistatic radar experiment, which will be performed in lunar orbit, will utilize the spacecraft Unified S-band and VHF transmitters to reflect radio signals off the surface of the Moon. And these will be received on Earth and hopefully the...

a14-0520200.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0520200.text: Roger, Houston. We're configured on the Flight Plan at 52 hours. Standing by.

a14-0520200.speaker: McCandless
a14-0520200.text: Roger. We're going to go ahead and secure our S-band uplink. [Long pause.]

a14-0520200.speaker: McCandless
a14-0520200.text: Belay that, 14. We're going to wait until your rotation in PTC brings us around to the point where we can utilize Omni Bravo for the frequency measurement. I'll give you a call just prior to our turning off the uplink.

a14-0520200.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0520200.text: Houston, 14. Speaking of Daylight Saving Time, our Sun comes up very regularly every 20 minutes.

a14-0520200.speaker: McCandless
a14-0520200.text: Roger. We copy. That's probably not unreasonable for the small-size planet you're in right now.

a14-0520200.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0520200.text: Ed Mitchell's last comment about the Sun coming up every 20 minutes refers to the fact that the spacecraft is currently in its Passive Thermal Control mode, or it's rotating at the rate of 3 revolutions per hour or 1 revolution every 20 minutes.

a14-0521907.speaker: McCandless
a14-0521907.text: Apollo 14. This is Houston. We're going to secure the S-band uplink for approximately 4 minutes - 5 minutes at this time. If you need us for anything, just give us a call. We can still receive you. We still have TM , and we would bring the uplink back up. Over.

a14-0521907.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0521907.text: Roger. You're turning the S-band off now. Is that affirm?

a14-0521907.speaker: McCandless
a14-0521907.text: Roger. We are turning the uplink portion of the S-band off at the present time.

a14-0522742.speaker: McCandless
a14-0522742.text: Apollo 14. This is Houston. On S-band, we have the uplink back up. We would like to leave the VHF configured as is, however, until we give you another call about 20 minutes from now. Over.

a14-0522742.speaker: McCandless
a14-0522742.text: Apollo 14, Apollo 14, this is Houston. How do you read?

a14-0522742.speaker: McCandless
a14-0522742.text: Roger. As you may gather, we have the uplink back up at this time. We'd like to remain in the existing VHF comm configuration until we give you another call, however. That'll be about 20 minutes from now. Over.

a14-0522742.speaker: Roosa
a14-0522742.text: Okay. We're easy to get along with. We'll stand by in this configuration.

a14-0523643.speaker: McCandless
a14-0523643.text: Roger, Ed. Down at the Cape, there's a Thor Delta with a NATO communications satellite on it that is about 1 minute and 40 seconds from ignition. If you're in such an attitude that you can view the Cape, you might try a P22 and pick it up in the sextant. Latitude, 28.5; longitude, over 2, 45.5. I say again, 28.5 and 45.5. That's your option. Over. [Long pause.]

a14-0523643.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0523643.text: Okay. I don't think we're going to be around in time. Al's looking at the Earth out the window 5 right now.

a14-0523643.speaker: McCandless
a14-0523643.text: Okay. Maybe you could try the monocular. But that probably doesn't hold much hope.

a14-0523643.speaker: Roosa
a14-0523643.text: Yes, he's got the monocular out now and that's 28.5.

a14-0523643.speaker: Roosa
a14-0523643.text: Okay. 28.5, 45.5. We'll try it. And Al's looking with the monocular now.

a14-0523643.speaker: McCandless
a14-0523643.text: Roger. Longitude over 2 is negative 40.5; negative 40.5.

a14-0523643.speaker: McCandless
a14-0523643.text: Okay, Stu; 3, 2, 1, ignition, down at the Cape. [Pause.]

a14-0523643.speaker: Roosa
a14-0523643.text: Okay. I - I didn't get the optics on; the Earth wasn't quite around. It just went out of the number 5 window just before you come.

a14-0523643.speaker: McCandless
a14-0523643.text: Roger. We just thought we'd send the info up, in case you happened to be in a handy attitude.

a14-0524342.speaker: McCandless
a14-0524342.text: Roger, Al. We thought you might be interested in knowing that we have a Dr. House down here at the Surgeon's console for a few minutes watching the progress of the mission.

a14-0524342.speaker: Shepard
a14-0524342.text: Good evening, William. Glad to have you aboard.

a14-0524342.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0524342.text: We understand that Dr. House is the surgeon who performed the successful operation on Al Shepard's ear which cleared up the inner ear problem and is allowing him to make this flight.

a14-0524342.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0524342.text: This is Apollo Control at 52 hours, 47 minutes. Flight Dynamics Officer Dave Reed has just completed briefing the flight controllers here in the Control Center on the procedures that will be followed and the rationale for the clock update, which is scheduled to occur at about 54 hours, 45 minutes; at which time the clocks and the computer complex here will be reset ahead 40 minutes, essentially placing us back on the Flight Plan, both in terms of Ground Elapsed Time and in terms of Central Standard Time. One of the finer points being considered at the moment is whether to update precisely 40 m

a14-0525659.speaker: McCandless
a14-0525659.text: 14, this is Houston. We've concluded the VHF measurements. You can turn VHF Ranging, and the VHF switches, Off.

a14-0525659.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0525659.text: During the bistatic radar frequency check, which was just completed, the spacecraft VHF signal was being received by [the] 150-foot [46-metre] dish antenna at Stanford, and the spacecraft Unified S-band signal was being received by the 210-foot [64-metre] dish at Goldstone, California. Reception of this - of these signals will allow teams at these two receiving locations to get a frequency calibration which will later be used during the period of orbital science when the bistatic radar experiment is performed from the Command Module. Basically this experiment consists of reflecting the UHF and

a14-0531134.speaker: Roosa
a14-0531134.text: Okay, Bruce, did you get the torquing angle?

a14-0531134.speaker: McCandless
a14-0531134.text: That's affirmative, Stu. [Pause.] And do you have a time for us?

a14-0531134.speaker: McCandless
a14-0531134.text: 14, this is Houston. Loud and clear. We have your torquing angles. Do you have the time for us? [Pause.]

a14-0531134.speaker: McCandless
a14-0531134.text: Apollo 14, Apollo 14, this is Houston; how do you read?

a14-0531134.speaker: Roosa
a14-0531134.text: Okay, read you loud and clear, Bruce. Did you have lockup? Did you get the torquing angles?

a14-0531134.speaker: McCandless
a14-0531134.text: Roger; we've got the torquing angles. Do you have a time at which you torqued for us?

a14-0533039.speaker: McCandless
a14-0533039.text: Apollo 14, this is Houston. We'd like to get battery Bravo on Charge now. Over.

a14-0533039.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0533039.text: This is Apollo Control at 53 hours, 58 minutes. We're now just about 45 minutes away from the scheduled updating of the clocks here in Mission Control. The Flight Plan calls for the GET update to occur at about 54 hours, 45 minutes. However, the precise timing of it is not critical and it'll more than likely be done at some point when we're in communication with the crew and when the timing is right as far as making the changes in the real time computer clock complex. The Flight Dynamics Officer has come up with a new set of coordinates for the predicted S-IVB impact on the Moon. They are as f

a14-0543445.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543445.text: 14, Houston. Got a string of PADs here for you, starting off with a Flight Plan update and then a little later, a T ephem update and two maneuver PADs. When you're ready to copy, let me know.

a14-0543445.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0543445.text: Roger, Bruce. Configured here - we're just finishing up on the experiments. We'll be ready in a minute.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Houston, Apollo 14's ready to copy.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger, 14. On the Flight Plan update, at 55 plus 40 PGET LOU, we'd like you to perform some more S-IVB dim-light photos while in PTC using P52 with the following Noun 88 unit vectors. Now - Stand by. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: 14, this is Houston. How do you read? [Pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay. We're reading you loud and clear.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Okay. Did you copy any of that?

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Just how do you read us; that's the first part we got.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Any of the Flight Plan update?

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Negative. We haven't [garble.] [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Houston, 14. We're not reading you.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Okay. How now, 14?

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay, go ahead.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Beautiful. All right, Flight Plan update at 55 plus 40 PGET LOU, perform S-IVB dim-light photos while in PTC using P52 with the following values for Noun 88. R1: minus 47607, minus 79244, minus 38131. Camera procedures and film magazine will be identical to those for the Earth dark-side photos. The S-IVB should be visible in the sextant between roll angles of 078 degrees down to 005 degrees. Over.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay. At elapsed time of 055:40, we will again take the S-IVB photographs in the P52 , Noun 88, minus 47607, minus 79244, minus 38131, using camera magazine and Earth side - Earth dark-side photographs. The sextant roll angles including 078 down to 005.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger. Readback correct. And that 55:40 time is the post- GET lift-off update time and - we're preparing to give you a lift-off time update now.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Understand. That's the new time.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: 14, Houston. T ephem update. Over.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Go ahead.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger. T ephem : OID 03, 00006; identifier 04, 35223; identifier 05, 16020. The Delta in time is 40 minutes 02.9 seconds added to GET and subtracted for a T ephem . Over. [Pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay. The update identifier 03 is 00006; identifier 04, 35223; identifier 05, 16020, Delta-T, 40 minutes 02.9 seconds, add to GET .

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Houston. Roger. Out. And I have an update to your lift-off plus 60 PAD. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay, go ahead.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Okay. On P37 lift-off plus 60, 060:00, 5381, minus 165, 117:00. Over. [Pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0543754.text: Roger. GETI is 060:00, 5381, minus 165, 117:00.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Readback correct. I have a change to the previously passed SPS / G&N flyby PAD P30 for you. Over.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger. The time of T IG , Noun 33 should be 077:39 minutes 34.44 seconds, and down at the bottom of the PAD, GET of .05g should be 165:52:28, and both of these last PADs assume the GET update. Over.

a14-0543754.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0543754.text: Okay. Noun 33 of the LOI minus 5 is 077:39:34.44 and GET is 0 - .05g, is 165:52:28. The rest remains the same.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Roger. Readback is correct. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: 14, Houston. We observe you're in P00 . If you can give us Accept, we will send you a state vector update to improve your pointing accuracy for the S-IVB photography and a lift-off time update to adjust the GET in accordance with the PADs that we've passed you. Over.

a14-0543754.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0543754.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: And, 14, we're going to hold off a few minutes here on the uplink until we get a good antenna switchover and then we'll be coming at you.

a14-0543754.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0543754.text: Roger. Understand. [Long pause.]

a14-0543754.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0543754.text: The uplink that CapCom Bruce McCandless was referring to is the Elapsed Time update and that will be uplinked via telemetry to the spacecraft clocks and shortly after we would expect the clocks here in Mission Control also to be updated.

a14-0543754.speaker: Shepard
a14-0543754.text: Houston, Apollo 14. The metal composite specimen number 4 has been cooked and cooled and recorded.

a14-0543754.speaker: McCandless
a14-0543754.text: Thanks a lot.

a14-0543754.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0543754.text: The Guidance Officer reports that he's ready now to uplink the revised elapsed time to the clocks onboard the spacecraft.

a14-0543754.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0543754.text: And Guidance and Retro report that we're now updated onboard.

a14-0553356.speaker: McCandless
a14-0553356.text: 14, this is Houston. The uplink is completed. I expect you'll want to reset your mission timers.

a14-0553356.speaker: Shepard
a14-0553356.text: Okay. We'll do that. And we'll also call 17 06 so you can look at T ephem .

a14-0553356.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0553356.text: And our telemetry data now shows the spacecraft Command Module Computer clock to be reading 55:34:30.

a14-0553356.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0553356.text: Once the update is completed here in the Control Center, we'll have one clock which will be designated GET and will be reading the updated Ground Elapsed Time. Next to that, the clock designated TV-5 will be reading the original or actual Ground Elapsed Time and of course will lag 40 minutes, 3 seconds roughly behind the updated GET clock.

a14-0553356.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0553356.text: And we've just had the clocks here in the Control Center updated and we're now on Lift-off Savings Time...

a14-0553356.speaker: Shepard
a14-0553356.text: Houston, Apollo 14. Would you check R 3 T ephem for us?

a14-0553356.speaker: McCandless
a14-0553356.text: Okay. Stand by. Be glad to.

a14-0553356.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0553356.text: This is Apollo Control. Our revised time now reading 55 hours, 46 minutes, 22 seconds. Those Elapsed Time updates were made at following times: 54:53:30 on the spacecraft and that command was uplinked by the Guidance Officer.

a14-0554622.speaker: McCandless
a14-0554622.text: Okay. I've got a few words on the T ephem situation. Probably the most significant...

a14-0554622.speaker: McCandless
a14-0554622.text: ...Probably the most significant part of the whole discussion is that both values of T ephem are correct, and the way that they arrive at this is as follows. The left-hand-most digit of the octal representation of T ephem is coded to include a sign. If you break the left-hand-most digit down into the 3 binary bits, the first bit being zero represents positive. The first bit being a one represents negative. In the value of T ephem update on the PAD, you'll notice that in the R3 load it was 16020 which is a positive 16020. In the value that you read out of the Command Module computer, you will n

a14-0554622.speaker: Shepard
a14-0554622.text: Affirmative. In other words, you want us to leave the loads the same.

a14-0554622.speaker: McCandless
a14-0554622.text: Roger. Either load is correct. The Command Module Computer does not force a positive sign or a negative sign on the octal value but accepts whatever it happens to come up with. So either load is correct. Over.

a14-0554622.speaker: Shepard
a14-0554622.text: Okay. Assuming we have no more updates, how would you like us to update the T ephem into the LM ? Using the 1706 values? [Long pause.]

a14-0554622.speaker: McCandless
a14-0554622.text: 14, this is Houston. I'll catch you when signal strength comes back up.

a14-0555216.speaker: McCandless
a14-0555216.text: Roger. Back on the question of which set of T ephem to load. You can load either one in the LM . If you want a recommendation, we recommend the - the PAD value, but either one would be satisfactory. Over.

a14-0555216.speaker: Shepard
a14-0555216.text: Okay. We'll call 1706 when we make our load. Thank you.

a14-0555724.speaker: Roosa
a14-0555724.text: Okay, Bruce. We've got something in the sextant with those angles. It could be the S-IVB . It's right off to the edge in the sextant field of view and being tracked by the CMC on those angles. And I'll look at it again on the next pass, and then - take some pictures of it after that.

a14-0555724.speaker: McCandless
a14-0555724.text: Okay, Stu. Very good. Could you tell that the object was tumbling, or anything like that, do you think?

a14-0555724.speaker: Roosa
a14-0555724.text: I'll - I'm going to look at it again.

a14-0555724.speaker: McCandless
a14-0555724.text: 14, this is Houston. For your information, the major tumble motion now has a period of 5 minutes and 46 seconds on the S-IVB . Over.

a14-0555724.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0555724.text: This is Apollo Control at 56 hours, 9 minutes. Apollo 14 now 168,880 nautical miles [312,766 km] from Earth, and the spacecraft velocity, 2,842 feet per second [866 m/s]. In Mission Control at this time, we're in the midst of a shift handover. The Flight Director on the shift coming on is Gerry Griffin, and the Gold team of flight controllers, the capsule communicator will be astronaut, Fred Haise. We are planning a change of shift briefing in the MSC news center briefing room, and we estimate that that briefing will be ready to begin in about 15 minutes.

a14-0561639.speaker: Roosa
a14-0561639.text: Houston. 14.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Ah, go ahead, 14.

a14-0561639.speaker: Roosa
a14-0561639.text: Okay. Yeah. You really got the S-IVB boresighted with those angles. Now, the other cycle around - I picked up a star that's also in the field of view, and the S-IVB is tumbling, and you can see it right at the start when it comes in on this one, and then it disappears and comes back in right toward the end. So we're definitely locked in, and with those pointing angles, it's got the S-IVB right near the center of the sextant, and what I picked up the first time around evidently is a star, and it's over toward the edge of field - of the field of view.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Okay. And understand you're going to try to shoot it the next time around, huh?

a14-0561639.speaker: Roosa
a14-0561639.text: Yes. We'll try to get some pictures - I guess I'll try to - I think I'll look at it one more time and try to get a time frame or roll angle where it's visible in the sextant and then try to take the pictures at that time.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Okay. It - that sounds good. It isn't going to be going anywhere.

a14-0561639.speaker: Roosa
a14-0561639.text: Okay. No, we'll be hanging around here for a while.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Go ahead, 14.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: I just wanted to say good morning, Fred. Haven't talked to you today.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Well, good morning. Isn't quite good morning yet. [Long pause.]

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Go ahead, Ed.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: Hey, Freddo, remember yesterday I was talking about the oil-canning effect of the heat contracting and - the heating and cooling of these panels.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Roger.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: And remember you said it looked like same thing that - that was happening to LM -7?

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: That's affirm.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0561639.text: Okay. I just wanted to let you know that I think our oil-can wrinkles are prettier than LM -7's oil-can wrinkles.

a14-0561639.speaker: Haise
a14-0561639.text: Okay.

a14-0561639.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0561639.text: This is Apollo Control; 56 hours, 32 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Here in the control room the Gold Team Flight Director Gerry Griffin is conferring with the various console engineers, finding out what items have to be covered during the next 8 hours of the shift. Each man goes red on the Flight Director's status board and after he completes the conversation the button goes green. The offgoing Flight Director Milton Windier is now in route to the Houston News Center for Change of Shift Press Conference. He is accompanied by his Flight Dynamics Officer Dave Reed. The group should be at the News

a14-0561639.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0561639.text: This is Apollo Control. The Change of Shift Press Conference with the off going Flight Director Milton Windler is going to start momentarily in the small briefing room in the Apollo News Center in Houston. 56 hours, 40 minutes GET ; this is Apollo Control Out and accumulating tape until after the Press Conference.

a14-0564208.speaker: Roosa
a14-0564208.text: Hey, Fred, just for curiosity sake, how far away is the S-IVB ?

a14-0564208.speaker: Haise
a14-0564208.text: Do you have any estimate of how far the S-IVB is away there, Stu?

a14-0564208.speaker: Roosa
a14-0564208.text: Okay, after looking through the optics and judging the size and its relative motion through the celestial sphere, I'd estimate it at 2,178 [nautical] miles [4,034 km] from us.

a14-0564208.speaker: Haise
a14-0564208.text: Well! You might replace the rendezvous radar yet. The number they gave me was 2,400 nautical miles [4,450 km]. And it has an R-dot going away about 1 nautical mile a minute.

a14-0564208.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0564208.text: This is Apollo Control; 57 hours, 3 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We have about a minute and a half of accumulated air to ground voice tapes that were recorded during the Change of Shift Press Briefing which is now finished. We'll play those tapes back. Meanwhile, Apollo 14 is now 170,374 nautical miles [315,533 km] out from Earth; velocity continuing to decrease, 2,802 feet per second [854 m/s]. Let's listen to that minute and a half of tape and then rejoin the air to ground live for any conversation perchance develop between ground and Apollo 14. Let's roll the tape.

a14-0564208.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0564208.text: This is Apollo Control. That completes the brief accumulated tape of the communications between the Apollo 14 and the ground. We're back live now on the air to ground circuit, continuing to monitor as long as the crew is awake. 57 hours, 6 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

a14-0571458.speaker: Haise
a14-0571458.text: Okay. Have you verified the Att Set switch in GDC ? [Long pause.]

a14-0572908.speaker: Haise
a14-0572908.text: Okay. If you can give us P00 and Accept, we'll pump up a CMC clock update.

a14-0573207.speaker: Haise
a14-0573207.text: Okay, FAO would like to know about when Stu took the S-IVB pictures and how much - you got remaining on that sequence camera Mag.

a14-0573207.speaker: Roosa
a14-0573207.text: Okay, Fred. I took them in sort of reverse order but using pretty much the same procedures as that dim light. However, I think I'm going to end up with streaks on the film because you know the way the CMC tracks the objects; but at 57 hours even, I took - I ran 2 seconds at 24 frames per second, 1/500th. Then I took one frame at 1/60th for 20 seconds, one frame at 1/60th for 5. And then at 57:20, I took one frame at a 1/60th for 50 seconds and had to cut it off there; I couldn't get a full minute. And then ran off another strip, and I'm calling it 78 percent left on the magazine. [Long pause.]

a14-0573207.speaker: Haise
a14-0573207.text: Okay, Stu. I copied all of that; thank you.

a14-0575144.speaker: Haise
a14-0575144.text: Got a little configuration change for you on panel 226. We'd like to get O 2 Tank 50-Watt Heater, number 3, Main A, Open. [Pause.]

a14-0575144.speaker: Roosa
a14-0575144.text: Okay. Let's run that again now. It's O 2 , the 50-Watt Heater on O 2 Tank 2.

a14-0575144.speaker: Haise
a14-0575144.text: Negative. O 2 , 3, Main A. 3 Main A, Stu. And the reason is, they want to look at a couple of cycles - with just two elements of the heaters going rather than three. [Pause.]

a14-0575144.speaker: Roosa
a14-0575144.text: Okay. So on O 2 Tank 3, we pull the Main A 50-Watt Heater.

a14-0575144.speaker: Haise
a14-0575144.text: That's affirm. And we'll stay with that configuration through the evening, so they can get at least three or four cycles on it.

a14-0575144.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0575144.text: This is Apollo Control; 58 hours, 2 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 14 currently 171,932 nautical miles [318,418 km] out from Earth. Velocity continuing to decelerate; now at 2,761 feet per second [842 m/s]. Current Ground Elapsed Time for midcourse correction number 4, if it should indeed be performed, is 77 hours, 38 minutes, 24 seconds. RCS burn of about 3 feet per second [1 m/s]. Current estimates on the S-IVB impact; time of 83 hours, 17 minutes, 45 seconds. Latitude, 8.4361 south; longitude, 25.9365 west. Space dis [?] still showing the calculated weight of the spacecraft, the docked

a14-0581420.speaker: Haise
a14-0581420.text: Okay. There's a request from down here to run through a little four-step exercise in having Al check his electrode leads and see if we can find anything early here, so we got time to do something about it before you all get around to the suiting up part of it. And I guess that's at Al's convenience in the next few hours, whenever he thinks he can work it in, maybe. [Pause.]

a14-0581420.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0581420.text: Okey doke. We're finishing up lunch right now. Let Al think it over and see when he wants to try to do it.

a14-0582328.speaker: Haise
a14-0582328.text: Okay. We're ready to terminate charge on battery B.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Houston, 14.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay, 14, stand by 1 until I get a little better comm. I - I can hardly read you now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: 14, Houston. How do you read now?

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay, read you loud and clear. This is Al. I understand you - you're still having a problem with my sensors.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Negative, Al. The situation is - you did have the problem for launch, and then it mysteriously went away. And what they'd like is a visual inspection of the gear to see if we have anything that looks abnormal that we might think about fixing at this time, rather than wait until just before suit-up time, where we'd like to not fiddle with anything.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: I have - I've checked all the sensors, Freddo. They all seem to be firmly in place. They don't appear to have moved. I did have some garble in the gober cable at one time, and that has been changed and now you can compare gober cables. That might have made the difference. I can switch back to that and take a check on that one if you want to.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: No, that - I don't think that's necessary. I might just tell you what they had in mind here and see if you - kind of covered all of the - the places they wanted you to check. Around each of the electrodes, they wanted to know if you had any of the paste that appeared to leak out that you could see stain under the large round pieces of tape you got over them, was the first item. Then, another inspection thing was to look at the solder joints, that's the areas that had the little plastic sleeves over them, to see if you could see anything that appeared to be cracked or coming loose in there. And

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay. We have one that appears to have leaked a little bit. It's the bottom one on the sternum.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay, the bottom one on the sternum. Okay, and I guess the only other square, which should be pretty easy to fill here, Al - he's looking at your data now - is to sequentially put some firm pressure on each of the three sensors for about 10 seconds, giving a call down when you're applying the pressure.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay. Understand you're ready now?

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: That's affirm. They're looking at your data now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay, in the top section of the sternum, I am pressing down the one closest to the right shoulder, now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: And I'm releasing on that one, now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: On the top of the sternum, I'm pressing down the center one, now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Roger, Al.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: And releasing now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay. And the bottom - on the bottom of the sternum, the one who appears to have leaked a little bit, I'm pressing down, now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: And releasing, now.

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Roger.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: [Garble.]

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Okay. I think that fills all the items I got here, Al. [Long pause.]

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay. This is Al, Houston. Understand that we're cleared to continue with the present harness and cable configuration. [Pause.]

a14-0584313.speaker: Haise
a14-0584313.text: Yeah, for the time being that - that's the word, Al. But they're going to look at the data. I guess the bottom one you pushed on showed more change than the others, and they're going to look at it awhile and decide if they want to do anything about that bottom one, I guess.

a14-0584313.speaker: Shepard
a14-0584313.text: Okay.

a14-0585341.speaker: Haise
a14-0585341.text: 14, Houston. I can barely make you out there. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

a14-0585341.speaker: Haise
a14-0585341.text: Okay, 14. Houston. You should be all right now. Go ahead.

a14-0585341.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0585341.text: Okay, Freddo. Inquiring about the LM /Command Module Delta-P test at 59 hours, is that number, 2.7, still good since we have already been in the LM and had a problem with our probe?

a14-0585341.speaker: Haise
a14-0585341.text: 14, Houston. The answer is the 2.7 number is a good one.

a14-0590550.speaker: Shepard
a14-0590550.text: Apollo 14. We have the null bias check, if you're ready to copy.

a14-0590550.speaker: Shepard
a14-0590550.text: Okay, at the end of the 100 seconds, it was reading minus 98.9.

a14-0590550.speaker: Mission Control
a14-0590550.text: This is Apollo Control; 59 hours, 10 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Most recent conversation, very brief exchange some moments ago about some spurious signals or at any rate some problems with one of the sensors on spacecraft commander Shephard's biomedical harness. And they wanted to get the problem sorted out prior to the time the crew suited up for the lunar landing. But apparently it's just some looseness in the sensor and the Surgeon is toying with the idea of perhaps having him put some additional paste underneath the sensor and another piece of tape. This will be resolved at some later ti

a14-0593004.speaker: Shepard
a14-0593004.text: Houston, 14. O 2 heaters configured per Flight Plan?

a14-0593845.speaker: Engle
a14-0593845.text: Apollo 14, Houston.

a14-0593845.speaker: Shepard
a14-0593845.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a14-0593845.speaker: Engle
a14-0593845.text: Okay, Al. First, we got some words for you on the - replacing this lower ECG sensor, and it'll be just taking it off and cleaning it and replacing the same one. [Pause.]

a14-0593845.speaker: Shepard
a14-0593845.text: Okay.

a14-0593845.speaker: Engle
a14-0593845.text: Okay. The materials that you're going to be needing are all in the medical kit over in R-8, and what you'll need is one of those large pieces of tape and one of the ring - rings that fit on the sensor. And the paste that's in the plastic bottle. And all these are in the kit.

a14-0593845.speaker: Shepard
a14-0593845.text: Okay.

a14-0593845.speaker: Engle
a14-0593845.text: Okay. And you can do this at your convenience, Al. There are just a couple of things that we want to make sure you get cautioned on. I'll go ahead and go through the procedures here and if there's anything that you want gone over again, why, just holler. First, remove the tape and the sensor, and clean your skin with one of the wet wipes. And then wipe the paste from the inside of the sensor. Wipe the sensor itself out first, and then pull off the old piece of tape. That's a double stickyback. It looks like that round, double stickyback Scotch tape. Pull that off after you've cleaned the senso

a14-0593845.speaker: Shepard
a14-0593845.text: Okay. I understand. I'll give you a call if I have any questions. That sounds pretty good.

a14-0593845.speaker: Engle
a14-0593845.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a14-0593845.speaker: Haise
a14-0593845.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0593845.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0593845.text: Go ahead.

a14-0593845.speaker: Haise
a14-0593845.text: Okay. We'd like you to put off doing the water dump. In a little bit here, I'll have a Flight Plan update with some instructions to shoot some pictures when we have you do that.

a14-0593845.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0593845.text: Okay. You caught me just in time. I was on my way to the dump valve now.

a14-0593845.speaker: Haise
a14-0593845.text: Read your mind, Ed. Which dump was that?...

a14-0593845.speaker: Roosa
a14-0593845.text: Okay. Did you get the torquing angles, Houston?

a14-0593845.speaker: Haise
a14-0593845.text: We got them.

a14-0593845.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0593845.text: Okay. I trust you're going to put if off until after we've finished with the LM and the TV show, et cetera. Is that right, Freddo?

a14-0593845.speaker: Haise
a14-0593845.text: Yes. I think the pictures they're wanting are from the LM side.

a14-0593845.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0593845.text: Okay.

a14-0593845.speaker: Roosa
a14-0593845.text: And Fred, the time on that torquing was 59:41:10.

a14-0593845.speaker: Roosa
a14-0593845.text: Rog.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: 14, Houston.

a14-0594954.speaker: Mitchell
a14-0594954.text: Go ahead.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Hey, I got a Flight Plan update for you here and a whole bunch of words on shooting the water from the LM .

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay, go ahead. I'm ready for the Flight Plan update.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay. At 60 hours and 40 minutes where you've maneuvered a TV attitude, we need to change the roll angle to 069; and as a result of that, we also change the High Gain angles to minus 66, Pitch; and Yaw, 105. [Long pause.]

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay, Fred. I got the High Gain angles of a minus 66 and 105; and say the new attitude for TV.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay, it's - the only thing changed is the roll angle to 069, so it'll be 069, 090, 000.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay. Now - now some words on the water dump. Like to delay the waste water dump to 62 hours and 30 minutes rather than the 59:50 that it had previously been set at. [Long pause.]

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay, I got it. Waste water dump at 62:30, and say after that.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay, the after that was just to scratch out the 59:50 you had before. Now some words on the...

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: ...on the camera operation. Al and Ed should take over to the LM with them magazine F out of the B-8 cushion and borrow your 18-millimeter lens out of the Command Module. [Long pause.]

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay, and they'll take magazine F out of B-8 and I guess I'll let them borrow my 18 millimeter to take in the LM .

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay, just might make sure they give it back to you. But when they get it over there they can stick it on the LM deck and...

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: They'll have to sign a receipt.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: ...Yeah. And put - the following settings required on the LM deck. f/8, 1/250th, 11 feet, and 24 frames a second. [Pause.]

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay, put the 18 millimeter on the LM deck and set her up f/8, 1/250th, 11 feet, and 24 frames per second.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay. And to run the camera, of course, they're going to need the Sequence Camera circuit breaker closed, and that actually fits in pretty well if they just do all this business right where that's called out on page 116, step 9, of the Activation List. [Long pause.]

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay. They'll need the Sequence Camera circuit breaker in and we're talking about page 116, step 9.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Roger. And if that doesn't quite align with the Flight Plan time I give you, that 62:30, it isn't going to matter that much anyway.

a14-0594954.speaker: Roosa
a14-0594954.text: Okay.

a14-0594954.speaker: Haise
a14-0594954.text: Okay. Now they need a cue from you, Stu, to let them know when you're going to start the dump.
